exchanges.question: Introduction of prepared remarks.
exchanges.answer: Q2 revenue rose 9.3% to $3.3 billion with positive comps and transactions, powered by the Recipe for Growth initiatives. Adam Rymer noted Q2 comp sales grew 2.2% with 1.0% transaction comp, restaurant-level margin reached 25.2%, and adjusted EPS was $0.33, while full-year comp guidance was set to the low single-digit range.

exchanges.question: Can you discuss the lift from bringing back pantry LTOs and whether customer value perception or affordability scores have changed?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle Honey Chicken performed better the second time around, though diminishing returns may hit around the fifth or sixth reintroduction, and menu innovation has been ramped 4x versus a couple of years ago. Brand tracker data in Q2 showed improved affordability scores across all income groups and age cohorts, with value driven by execution, convenience, and protein quality rather than discounting.

exchanges.question: How do you respond to pushback that Chipotle is doing and spending a lot for modest comp growth, and what gives you confidence in picking up momentum into 2027?
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflects early Recipe for Growth benefits from menu innovation, HEAP equipment, throughput, and hospitality. Momentum from rewards engagement, expanded group occasions, and upcoming digital and brand creative initiatives will build and scale into late 2026 and 2027.

exchanges.question: Can you provide more color on the full-year comp guidance to low single digits, the cadence, and the recent trends and challenges seen in July?
exchanges.answer: Traffic improved across Q2 into the first half of July before softening by about 200 basis points in late July around the industry Cyclospora issue. Q3 comps are anticipated around plus 1%, factoring in the continuation of that roughly 200 bps headwind against the year's toughest comparison. Scott Boatwright clarified that Chipotle's food safety protocols remain robust, it is not involved in Cyclospora, does not use the implicated products, and sources lettuce from California.

exchanges.question: What is the expected capital allocation and uplift for store remodels across 1,000 to 1,500 stores, and are you considering leveraging partners in international markets instead of owning?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle is stage-gating remodel tests across locations with investment levels between $100,000 and $300,000 per restaurant, but has no returns to report yet. For global expansion, the company will own and operate Western Europe, while treating the rest of the world as partner-operated or JV models, citing partners Alshaya, Alsea, and SPC.

exchanges.question: What catalyst drove the 18% growth in digital sales, and how does it link to loyalty and register changes?
exchanges.answer: Learn-ins from last year's Summer of Extras led directly to the rewards relaunch, which removed friction in the app and improved flexibility for earning and redemption. These initiatives, along with expanding digital commerce innovation under Arlie Sisson, drove digital acceleration.

exchanges.question: Should we expect all HEAP efficiency to be reinvested into frontline labor, and will it drive positive traffic and satisfaction?
exchanges.answer: HEAP generates 2 to 4 hours of labor efficiency depending on volume, all of which is reinvested in-restaurant to complete morning prep and deploy crew on the line during peak. This efficiency is driving transaction and Max 15 throughput gains, total sales lifts, and better food taste scores, with rollout targeting 2,000 units by year-end and full portfolio completion in 2027.

exchanges.question: Why is 350 company-operated openings per year viewed as the right level rather than a prior ceiling of 400, and what restricts accelerating above it?
exchanges.answer: Opening one restaurant per day (approximately 350 per year) represents manageable, successful growth that aligns with developing capable leaders without risking execution or fracturing the store base. Incremental unit acceleration beyond that will come from partner-operated international expansion, such as Alshaya in the Middle East already reaching 15 locations.

exchanges.question: Where do you see brand positioning evolving under the new CMO compared to the older 'For Real' campaign, specifically around quality and value?
exchanges.answer: The upcoming branding is an evolution of For Real rather than a 180-degree pivot, highlighting fresh in-restaurant preparation, ingredient integrity, and our mission to cultivate a better world. Marketing will emphasize value through abundant, freshly prepared ingredients at an approachable price rather than through price-pointing or discounting.

exchanges.question: Is Q3 underlying trend up about 3% assuming a 2% Cyclospora drag in the 1% guide, and what is system Max 15-minute throughput excluding HEAP?
exchanges.answer: The 1% Q3 comp guide and corresponding expense lines assume that roughly 200 bps Cyclospora drag persists through the quarter. On throughput, non-HEAP in-store Max 15 is in the low-20 range, while digital is in the mid-teens, combining to low-to-mid 30s total entrees per 15 minutes, with HEAP restaurants delivering 2 to 3 entrees higher.

exchanges.question: Can you elaborate on in-restaurant loyalty initiatives and whether the 80% non-loyalty in-store transactions correlate with lower income cohorts?
exchanges.answer: The 80% non-loyalty in-store customer base is broad-based across income levels rather than tied to lower income. To reduce friction at checkout without slowing throughput, a new one-stop payment experience pilots in August that automatically earns rewards and enables enrollment when paying.

exchanges.question: Could you provide more color on upcoming menu additions and whether they are center-of-the-plate or sides?
exchanges.answer: Culinary teams are developing center-of-the-plate items as well as beverages, sides, and desserts. Big ideas are progressing through the stage-gate pipeline and may reach the calendar in the second half of 2026 or into 2027.

exchanges.question: What updates can you provide on frequency and demand among younger and lower-to-middle income cohorts?
exchanges.answer: Younger and lower-income cohorts improved the most in Q2, driven by menu innovation like Honey Chicken and Cilantro Lime Sauce, the Matchday BOGO, and loyalty offers. Scott Boatwright added that Chipotle saw its highest year-over-year wallet share gains since 2024, gaining share every month of 2026 across all income and age cohorts.

exchanges.question: What is the margin outlook beyond Q3, and when will the gap between pricing and inflation close?
exchanges.answer: In Q3, inflation is expected around 3% with pricing near mid-2%, narrowing the earlier dislocation where pricing was 1% against inflation in the low-to-mid 3% range. Beginning in Q4, pricing and inflation are expected to match, eliminating that margin dislocation going forward.

exchanges.question: Did the World Cup generate regional sales benefits, and what prompted pricing expectations to reach the higher end of the 1% to 2% range?
exchanges.answer: Restaurants within 10 miles of World Cup stadiums (approx. 300 stores) saw a 50 to 100 bps comp lift, but the total impact on Q2 comps was less than 5 basis points. The methodical market-by-market pricing rollout showed manageable customer resistance, providing confidence to price toward the top of the range.

exchanges.question: Can you provide incremental color on LTO traffic uplift benchmarks and whether protein LTOs bring in new or existing diners?
exchanges.answer: LTO launches typically generate hundreds of basis points of transaction lift from increased frequency among regulars as well as new customer acquisition, sustained throughout the promotion and demonstrating post-promo customer stickiness. Scott Boatwright added that guest lifetime value rises materially after trying an LTO, and culinary teams are actively working on future center-of-the-plate, side, and beverage innovations.

exchanges.question: Are psychiatry and vaccines core areas Lilly intends to scale through M&A, or were recent acquisitions opportunistic?

summary.overview: Kinsale Capital Group reported fiscal Q2 2026 diluted operating earnings per share of $5.54, up 15.9% year-over-year, alongside an annualized operating return on equity of 24.4%. Gross written premiums fell 5.0% due to persistent softness and aggressive competition in commercial property, though premiums rose 3.7% excluding the Commercial Property Division. Underwriting profitability remained intact with a 75.5% combined ratio, and the board expanded its share repurchase authorization by $250 million.
keyTakeaways: Gross written premiums contracted 5.0% year-over-year, driven by commercial property headwinds, but grew 3.7% excluding the Commercial Property Division.
Management expanded the company's share repurchase authorization by $250 million, bringing total repurchase authorization to $337 million.
Combined ratio came in at 75.5%, supported by 4.5 points of net favorable prior year reserve development and a loss ratio that ran below expectations.
Competitive pressures from London MGAs and traditional carriers continue to weigh on large commercial property and are beginning to seep into long-tail construction and general casualty lines.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS increased 15.9% year-over-year to $5.54, up from $4.78 in Q2 2025.
Net earned premium grew 8.9% year-over-year, while net written premium decreased 1.4%.
Net investment income increased 19.9% quarter-over-quarter, driven by an invested float expansion to $3.4 billion.
The expense ratio rose to 21.7% from 20.7% in Q2 2025, while the other underwriting expense ratio improved slightly to 10.3% from 10.6%.

keyMetrics.comparison: compared to less than 1.0 point in Q2 2025

guidance: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President, and CEO, expects year-over-year gross written premium growth comparisons to be modestly easier in Q3 and Q4 2026.
Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, outlined plans to launch 5 additional product offerings imminently, with 10 more in the pipeline for fiscal 2026.
Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, guided that the Q2 expense ratio of 21.7% serves as a good benchmark run-rate going forward.

qa.question: What drove the improvement in current accident year loss ratio from Q2 2025, and will reinsurance ceding commissions increase after renewals?
qa.answer: Losses came in below expectations due to normal variability across statutory lines, and Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, noted Q2 expense ratio of 21.7% is a solid run-rate guide as potential commission increases would be offset by operational efficiencies.

qa.question: Could Q2 be the trough for commercial property, what drives the 3.7% growth ex-large property, and is business returning to the admitted market?
qa.answer: Pricing direction for 2027 remains uncertain as London MGAs press shared and layered deals, London competition is creeping into long-tail construction and general casualty, and admitted market flow is present but not pervasive.

qa.question: How much inbound submission growth stems from broker initiatives versus pricing, and what are casualty loss cost trends?
qa.answer: Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, stated casualty loss cost trends run in the mid-single digits with low social inflation exposure due to smaller limits, while Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, attributed submission gains to steady hit ratios and the idle broker initiative.

qa.question: When might property pricing reach equilibrium, will the loss ratio drift up from casualty mix shift, and what is the share buyback pacing strategy?
qa.answer: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President, and CEO, stated buybacks are the primary capital allocation tool until top-line growth accelerates, while Salmaan Allibhai noted loss ratios could drift upward over time, but specific property pricing equilibrium timing was not established.

qa.question: How have new product expansions contributed to growth over the past year and what is their future growth uplift?
qa.answer: Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, explained the firm uses a deliberate 'crawl, walk, run' approach to slowly generate submissions and premiums, positioning for expansion when the market hardens rather than seeking immediate volume.

unanswered.question: When might property pricing reach equilibrium and what is the specific pacing strategy for share buybacks?
unanswered.how: Michael Kehoe noted property equilibrium would eventually occur following catastrophe losses and affirmed buybacks as the primary capital tool, but did not provide specific timing milestones or repurchase pacing schedules.

exchanges.answer: Losses came in below expectations due to normal variability and mix across a dozen statutory lines, and loss reserves remain as conservative as ever. exchanges.question: How much are ROEs compressing in E&S casualty given slower growth, and how are you thinking about broker commissions in a soft market?
exchanges.answer: The company manages everything to a 20% ROE or greater and achieved 24.4% for the quarter. Broker commission tensions are normal in a soft market, but Kinsale counters this by offering industry-leading customer service, quote ratios, response times, and broad risk appetite.

exchanges.question: Could 2Q be the trough for commercial property, what is driving the 3.7% growth figure ex-large property, and is business flowing back to the admitted market?

Competition from London is creeping into long-tail construction and general casualty, while flow back to the admitted market exists but is not pervasive.

exchanges.question: How much inbound submission growth is coming from broker initiatives versus pricing, and what are your views on casualty loss cost trends and social inflation?
exchanges.answer: Growth comes from both initiatives like the idle broker program and steady hit ratios driving more bound accounts. Salmaan Allibhai stated casualty loss cost trends run in the mid-single digits, and Kinsale is less exposed to social inflation due to smaller accounts and lower limits, with IBNR released faster on short-tail lines and held conservatively on long-tail lines.

exchanges.question: When might property pricing reach equilibrium, will the accident year loss ratio drift up due to mix shift toward casualty, and what is the pacing strategy for share buybacks?
exchanges.answer: Pricing will eventually reach equilibrium as cat losses occur, though smaller property lines like Agribusiness Property and small business property remain stable. Salmaan Allibhai noted loss ratios could drift up over time, but current losses remain below expectations; Michael Kehoe added buybacks remain the principal capital allocation tool until top-line growth accelerates.

exchanges.question: How have new product expansions contributed to growth over the past year and what is their potential growth uplift going forward?
exchanges.answer: The company takes a deliberate 'crawl, walk, run' pace for new products rather than growing aggressively immediately. They are driving submissions and new premium slowly, positioning Kinsale to ramp up when the market turns.

summary.overview: Chipotle reported Q2 2026 revenue of $3.3 billion, a 9.3% increase, driven by a 2.2% rise in comparable restaurant sales and a 1% increase in transactions. The company highlighted early momentum from its Recipe for Growth strategy, particularly around menu innovation and restaurant execution, despite a late-quarter softening linked to an industry-wide Cyclospora issue.
keyTakeaways: Digital sales grew to $1.3 billion, representing 38.3% of total sales, aided by the Summer of Extras and a revamped rewards program.
The rollout of the HEAP equipment package is accelerating, targeting 2,000 restaurants by year-end, which is improving throughput and transaction growth.
Chipotle is testing a remodel refresh program with investments between $100,000 and $300,000 per restaurant.
The company plans to open 350 company-operated restaurants annually in North America, with additional growth expected from international partner-operated models.
A new one-stop pay system for loyalty members will be introduced in August to reduce friction at the register.
financialHighlights: Revenue increased 9.3% to $3.3 billion.
Comparable restaurant sales rose 2.2%, with transaction comp up 1%.
Restaurant level margin declined 220 basis points year-over-year to 25.2%.
Adjusted diluted earnings per share were flat at $0.33.
The company repurchased $631 million in stock at an average price of $32.55.

Q3 2026 Pricing impact expected in the mid 2% range.

qa.question: Is it still the case that as people revisit LTOs the lift is as good or better than the last time, and are you seeing any changes in value perception regarding generous portions?
qa.answer: Chipotle Honey Chicken performed better the second time around, though there may be a point of diminishing returns after several reintroductions. Our brand tracker showed solid progress across all income groups and age cohorts on value perception, with affordability scores better in Q2 than in the past couple of years. Value is also about convenience, execution, and menu innovation, and we are capitalizing on the emerging protein trend.

qa.question: Could you provide more color on the guide for positive low single-digit comps in 2026, including insights into the third quarter and recent softening?
qa.answer: Traffic improved throughout Q2 and into the first half of July, but we saw a softening of about 200 basis points in the second half of July related to the industry-wide Cyclospora issue. We anticipate Q3 comps around plus 1%, assuming the 200 basis point impact continues, as it is tough to predict how long it will persist. We remain confident in building momentum for the rest of the year, which supports our low single-digit full-year guidance.

qa.question: Is it right to interpret the 1% Q3 comp guide as an underlying 3% trend minus a 2% Cyclospora headwind, and where is Max 15-minute throughput for stores without HEAP?
qa.answer: Yes, the 1% guide assumes the continuation of the 200 basis point impact through the rest of the quarter. For throughput, restaurants with HEAP do about two or three more entrees in their Max 15, while overall in-store throughput is in the low 20 range. When combining in-store and digital, we are in the low to mid-30s on our Max 15.

qa.question: Can you elaborate on the efforts to promote the loyalty program in-restaurant, and do the 80% of in-store transactions without loyalty over-index to lower-income guests?
qa.answer: The non-loyalty transactions do not over-index to lower-income guests; it is broad-based. We are working to make the in-restaurant loyalty experience more frictionless, as the current process of using the app and paying separately is clunky. In August, we will introduce a one-stop pay system where guests automatically earn points when they pay, which will improve execution without impacting throughput.

qa.question: Can you provide an update on how you are thinking about the margin outlook beyond the current quarter and the gap between pricing and inflation?
qa.answer: The gap between price and inflation is easing in the second half of the year as we continue our measured rolling pricing strategy. In Q3, inflation will be closer to 3% while pricing will be in the mid 2% range, narrowing the dislocation seen in the first half. From Q4 forward, we expect pricing and inflation to match, eliminating that dislocation.

exchanges.question: Can you provide an update on trends by age and income in the second quarter, and are any groups improving relative to the higher-income cohort?
exchanges.answer: The younger and lower-income cohorts, which were under the most pressure, have improved the most compared to everyone else from Q1 into Q2. exchanges.answer: The World Cup had a very small impact on the quarter overall, though the 300 restaurants near stadiums saw a 50 to 100 basis point comp benefit during the tournament. exchanges.question: Asked how management maintains confidence in building sales momentum into 2027 despite recent industry slowdowns and tough comparisons.
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflected early results of the Recipe for Growth strategy, particularly menu innovation and operational investments like HEAP. exchanges.question: Asked for additional details on the full-year low single-digit comp guidance, recent Q3 sales softening, and overall trajectory.
exchanges.answer: Q2 traffic improved throughout the quarter into early July before softening by about 200 basis points in late July due to industry Cyclospora concerns. exchanges.question: Asked about capex requirements, returns, and timeline for refreshing 1,000 to 1,500 stores, and whether partner-operated models will be used internationally.

Internationally, Chipotle will own and operate in Western Europe while expanding through strategic partners or joint ventures in other global regions.

exchanges.question: Asked about drivers behind the 18% digital sales growth and how changes in loyalty and in-store payment tie into digital strategy.
exchanges.answer: Insights from Summer of Extras informed the recent Chipotle Rewards relaunch, which reduced friction and increased earn and redemption flexibility. Ongoing digital commerce initiatives are positioned to further accelerate digital revenue growth.

exchanges.question: Asked whether labor savings from HEAP are being reinvested into the production line and how that impacts traffic and guest satisfaction.
exchanges.answer: HEAP saves 2 to 4 hours of labor per day depending on store volume, and all labor savings are reinvested back into restaurant prep and peak line deployment. This reinvestment has driven gains in throughput, total sales, and food taste scores across deployed stores.

exchanges.question: Asked why 350 company-operated restaurant openings per year is considered the right pace rather than higher targets like 400 stores.
exchanges.answer: Opening roughly one restaurant per day aligns with leadership development capacity and maintains operational standards without fracturing the core base. Incremental growth will be driven by global expansion, including partner-operated locations in the Middle East and other regions.

exchanges.question: Asked about the direction of brand marketing under the new CMO and whether ingredient quality and value will be highlighted more prominently.
exchanges.answer: Marketing will evolve from For Real by placing greater emphasis on fresh daily in-restaurant preparation, ingredient quality, and overall brand mission. Value communication will focus on premium ingredients, speed, and abundance at an accessible price point rather than discounting.

exchanges.question: Asked for clarification on whether the 1% Q3 comp guide assumes a 3% underlying trend with a 2% Cyclospora drag, and asked for overall Max 15 throughput numbers.
exchanges.answer: Confirmed that the 1% Q3 comp guide and expense projections assume the 200 basis point Cyclospora headwind continues through Q3. exchanges.question: Asked about efforts to promote loyalty in-restaurant, whether non-loyalty in-store transactions correlate with lower-income guests, and planned frictionless improvements.
exchanges.answer: Non-loyalty in-store transactions are broad-based rather than correlated with lower-income guests. In August, Chipotle will pilot a frictionless experience allowing guests to automatically earn reward points while paying without having to scan a rewards card separately.

exchanges.question: Asked for details on upcoming menu pipeline items, including whether they are center-of-plate, sides, or beverages.
exchanges.answer: Culinary teams are developing center-of-plate proteins, beverages, sides, and desserts. Major menu concepts are currently moving through the stage-gate process, with potential calendar launches targeted for late 2026 or 2027.

exchanges.question: Asked for an update on Q2 and Q3 consumer trends across age and income cohorts, particularly younger and lower-to-middle income guests.
exchanges.answer: Younger and lower-income cohorts showed the most relative improvement from Q1 to Q2, driven by menu innovation like Chipotle Honey Chicken and Cilantro Lime Sauce as well as promotions like Matchday BOGO. Boatwright added that Chipotle achieved its highest YoY wallet share gains since 2024 and gained market share across all income and age cohorts each month in 2026.

exchanges.question: Asked for an update on the margin outlook beyond Q3 and expectations for closing the gap between pricing and inflation.
exchanges.answer: In Q3, inflation will be around 3% while pricing will be in the mid 2% range, significantly narrowing the H1 gap. Beginning in Q4 and moving forward, menu pricing is expected to match inflation, eliminating the margin dislocation.

exchanges.question: Asked about regional sales benefits near World Cup host venues and what provided confidence to target the high end of the 1%-2% full-year pricing guidance.
exchanges.answer: Restaurants within 10 miles of World Cup stadiums saw a 50 to 100 basis point comp lift, but the total Q2 impact was under 5 basis points. Methodical, market-by-market price increases showed low consumer resistance, providing confidence to guide toward the high end of 1%-2% for full-year pricing.

exchanges.question: Asked about LTO contribution to guest frequency and whether high-protein LTOs attract new guests or drive frequency among existing customers.
exchanges.answer: Protein LTOs generate hundreds of basis points of transaction lift during promotions by increasing visits from core guests and attracting new customers whose lifetime value increases after trying an LTO. Boatwright added that second-half innovation will include center-of-plate proteins, sides, and enhanced beverage options.

summary.overview: Deere & Company reported fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues of $12.608 billion, up 5% year-over-year, and net income of $1.379 billion. Performance was supported by $110 million in incremental IEPA tariff refunds during the quarter, bringing year-to-date refunds to $382 million. Based on factory execution and reduced Section 232 tariff rates, Deere narrowed and raised its full-year fiscal 2026 enterprise net income outlook to $4.75 billion to $5.0 billion.
keyTakeaways: Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Ag & Turf, affirmed that early order program intake supports 2026 as the bottom of the ag equipment cycle, but pointed toward a measured recovery rather than a sharp rebound in 2027.

Brent Norwood, CFO, noted that direct tariff expense will drop to $1.1 billion in fiscal 2026 due to Section 232 rates decreasing to 15%, but net tariffs will be an incremental headwind in fiscal 2027 as refund activity ends.
Early order program planter and sprayer intake is tracking up mid-single digits, with factory-installed See & Spray orders doubling to roughly one-third of North American sprayers.

Construction & Forestry demand remained strong with backlogs at four to five months, driven by infrastructure, data centers, and expanding dealer rental fleets where 30% to 35% of earthmoving transactions now start as rentals.
Some tractor demand was pulled ahead into Q3 to manage Q4 execution risks, and Q4 segment margins will see seasonal pressure alongside an absence of further tariff refunds.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues increased 5% year-over-year to $12.608 billion, and diluted earnings per share was $5.10.
Equipment operations net sales rose 6% year-over-year to $10.999 billion, achieving an operating margin of 14.4%.
Production & Precision Ag net sales fell 6% year-over-year to $3.998 billion with an operating margin of 13.2% and operating profit of $527 million.
Small Ag & Turf net sales increased 12% to $3.383 billion with an operating profit of $622 million and an 18.4% operating margin.
Construction & Forestry net sales rose 18% to $3.618 billion, generating $436 million in operating profit at a 12.1% operating margin, aided by 8 points of price realization.

Dan Pooley, Manager of Investor Communications, projected Small Ag & Turf net sales up approximately 15% with operating margins raised to 14.5%-15.5%.
Dan Pooley, Manager of Investor Communications, guided Construction & Forestry net sales up approximately 20% with operating margins between 10.5% and 11.5% and price realization raised to +3 points.

Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, expects full-year direct tariff expense to be approximately $1.1 billion, while Brent Norwood, CFO, projected direct tariffs of roughly $1 billion in fiscal 2027.

qa.question: What is driving the reduction in expected direct tariff impact to $1.1 billion, and what is the status of the excavator launch and adoption timeline?
qa.answer: Direct tariff expense was lowered from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion because Section 232 import tariff rates fell from roughly 25% to 15% effective June 1, creating a 5-month benefit in 2026 and an additional tailwind in 2027, while the first three Deere-designed excavators launched this spring with more rolling out over three to four years.

qa.question: Will net tariff expense be a headwind or tailwind in fiscal 2027 compared to 2026?
qa.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind in fiscal 2027, as net tariff expense for fiscal 2026 is approximately $750 million ($1.1 billion direct tariffs less $382 million refunds) against an anticipated run rate of roughly $1 billion in 2027.

qa.question: How could mix and higher precision technology adoption influence 2027 results compared to historical 2-3 point mix benefits?
qa.answer: Broader uncertainty in ag inputs, commodities, and recent softness in the EU and Brazil make it too early to quantify net mix impact, which will ultimately depend on final EOP wrap-up and combine order intake.

qa.question: What dynamics drive the implied deceleration in C&F pricing in Q4, and how will expanding dealer rental fleets affect business economics?
qa.answer: Q3 C&F price realization of 8% benefited from lapping a negative 5% comparison in Q3 2025 caused by retail incentives, bringing full-year price guidance to 3%, while 30% to 35% of earthmoving transactions currently begin as rentals.

qa.question: Could the 2028 CAP budget policy change pull forward European equipment demand into 2027 or cause purchasing delays?
qa.answer: Management stated it is too early to determine if the 2028 CAP policy will pull forward or delay demand, pointing instead to stable European dairy and livestock sentiment and current order books of four to five months.

exchanges.question: Can you provide additional color on performance for this quarter, the guidance adjustments, and regional dynamics across segments?
exchanges.answer: Q3 results were driven by factory execution, disciplined cost management, and positive pricing, alongside $110 million in incremental IEPA refunds bringing full-year refunds to $382 million. Direct tariff expense is now expected to be roughly $1.1 billion. PPA net sales guidance was narrowed to down approximately 10% with operating margin between 11% and 12%, while Small Ag & Turf margin guide rose to 14.5%-15.5% and C&F margin guide tightened to 10.5%-11.5%. Full-year net income outlook was raised to $4.75 billion-$5 billion and equipment operating cash flows to $5 billion-$5.5 billion.

exchanges.question: How are you thinking about production versus retail by region for 2027, and what are the pricing expectations given concerns over inflationary costs?
exchanges.answer: For 2026, PPA and Construction & Forestry are underproducing retail demand by a couple of percentage points, driven by shipping plans and caution in South America. On EOP pricing, pricing was rolled out several months ago with a focus on covering inflation across EOP products and the PPA portfolio heading into 2027.

exchanges.question: What is driving the reduction in expected direct tariff impact to $1.1 billion, and what is the status of the excavator launch and adoption timeline?
exchanges.answer: The reduction in run-rate direct tariff expense from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion stems from Section 232 import tariff rates dropping from roughly 25% to 15% effective June 1, providing a 5-month impact in 2026 and an additional tailwind in 2027. For excavators, the first three Deere-designed models launched in the spring with positive initial customer reception, and additional models will roll out over the next three to four years.

exchanges.question: Did something slip between 3Q and 4Q given higher tractor inventory in 3Q, and what is the cadence exiting the year?
exchanges.answer: Shipment plans were largely set and some demand was pulled ahead into Q3 to manage Q4 risk. For Q4, net sales for PPA and C&F are expected to be similar to Q3 levels, but PPA and SAT margins will be lower due to no Q4 refunds and seasonally higher R&D and SA&G expenses.

exchanges.question: How could mix and higher precision technology adoption influence 2027 results compared to historical 2-3 point mix benefits?
exchanges.answer: It is too early to tell how mix will net out given broader uncertainty in ag inputs, commodities, and recent softness in the EU and Brazil. While early order program technology adoption and C&F demand signals are encouraging, full mix impact will depend on how the EOP finishes and where combines land.

exchanges.question: Can you unpack early order program demand variability by region and discuss whether mid-single-digit order intake could finish in the high single digits?
exchanges.answer: Regionally, the U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada. Collective planter and sprayer intake is up mid-single digits, factory-installed See & Spray orders have doubled to about one-third of North American sprayers, and advanced planting technology is on over 40% of planters, though final growth rates will depend on program wrap-up.

exchanges.question: What drove the cadence of mid-single-digit early order intake—was it grain prices, technology, or program tweaks?
exchanges.answer: The cadence has progressed as expected following slight adjustments to provide dealers more choice. Order progress is supported by solid technology take rates, and the company hopes the mid-single-digit increase carries through the year.

exchanges.question: How are 8 Series Tractor orders trending in North America, and how is customer sentiment evolving in Europe amidst heat and input stress?
exchanges.answer: 8R tractor orders are as expected with four to five months of orders on hand and model year 2026 closed, though recent corn prices near $5.05 provide positive sentiment. Europe presents a mixed picture where arable crop producers remain challenged by input costs and weather, while Small Ag & Turf producers benefit from stable dairy and livestock economics.

exchanges.question: How are Construction & Forestry order books shaping up and how much is driven by dealer rental fleet expansion?
exchanges.answer: C&F order trends remain very positive with four to five months of orders on hand versus normal levels of two to three months. Demand is driven by large infrastructure projects, data centers, independent rental demand, and expansion of dealer-owned rental fleets.

exchanges.question: Will net tariff expense be a headwind or tailwind in fiscal 2027 compared to 2026?
exchanges.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind in fiscal 2027. Net tariff exposure for fiscal 2026 is approximately $750 million ($1.1 billion in direct tariffs minus $382 million in refunds), while fiscal 2027 is expected to see a run rate of roughly $1 billion.

exchanges.question: What dynamics drive the implied deceleration in C&F pricing in Q4, and how will expanding dealer rental fleets affect business economics?
exchanges.answer: Q3 C&F pricing of 8% benefited from lapping a negative 5% comparison in Q3 2025 caused by retail incentive programs; full-year C&F pricing is guided to 3%. Regarding rental, 30% to 35% of earthmoving transactions currently begin as rentals, offering dealers a meaningful opportunity to expand fleet investment and driving equipment pull.

exchanges.question: What pricing and merchandising incentives are included in EOPs, and what are the implications of the FTC right-to-repair settlement on lifecycle parts?
exchanges.answer: EOP pricing is set to cover inflation in a measured way across various decision windows as suppliers pass on dynamic tariff and input costs. The FTC agreement formalizes tools Deere already offers—such as Operations Center PRO Service diagnostic tools, digital manuals, and software updates—and supports long-term lifecycle solutions aspirations.

exchanges.question: Could the 2028 CAP budget policy change pull forward European equipment demand into 2027 or cause purchasing delays?
exchanges.answer: It is too early to determine whether the 2028 CAP budget policy will pull forward or delay demand. European order books are currently four to five months out, with dairy and livestock demand stable while arable farmer activity will depend on commodity and input price trends.

exchanges.question: What positioning and decisions are Brazilian and U.S. farmers taking in response to input costs like fertilizer?
exchanges.answer: Farmers are staying resilient and agile by exploring alternative products, application rates, and sourcing rather than drastically reducing application, as they remain focused on maximizing yield. Larger growers also hold multi-year input contracts that help mitigate near-term swings.

exchanges.question: The current year accident year loss ratio improved from 2Q 2025, which I think is a bit different from what many other commercial insurers are reporting. I was hoping you could please talk through the key factors that drove that. Was it lower non-cat property losses mix, changes in loss picks and so on? My second question, just on the reinsurance and ceding commission rate. I think the commission rate has actually been going up for Kinsale over the past couple of years. I was wondering if you expect the same this year after the renewals.
exchanges.answer: Losses for the quarter came in below expectations, as they have for the last few quarters. There's really nothing out of the ordinary. It's just kind of normal variability and mix of business. The loss ratio is a composite of a dozen statutory lines of business. I would just reiterate that our reserves are as conservative as they've ever been in our company's history.

exchanges.question: My first question is on the E&S casualty. Just given that segment is softening a bit, I guess given GWP, I think was up 3% versus up 4% in the first quarter, how much are ROEs compressing in the line, assuming your views on loss trends, high single digits to low double digits haven't changed? For my second question, I guess given the softer market, you've been pretty protective of your commissions or ratios to brokers, I guess how are you guys thinking about broker commissions on a go-forward basis?
exchanges.answer: We manage everything to a 20% ROE or greater. I think most of our product lines are probably running ahead of that. I think we were 24.4% for the quarter. There's always a give and take where we're trying to balance profit and growth. Brokers are critical to our success. Obviously, they're looking to maximize their economics. That makes sense. There's some tension between the wholesalers that we distribute most of our business through and their retail clients in terms of how they split the gross commission. Of course, the customer, the buyer, is keenly focused on lower cost insurance. You're always going to have some tension across the spectrum, if you will. Of course, in a soft market when rates have drifted down, that puts pressure on everybody. I think it's a normal tension in the business.

exchanges.question: Does Kinsale view this 2Q as maybe the trough there, given some larger players are pulling out? Is the view that property pricing can maybe become less negative in 2027, or could maybe Kinsale get back on some of these larger shared placements next year as they continue to pull back? Then maybe just focusing on the 37 growth figure, excluding the large account property. Just what's driving that acceleration? Is it pricing or are you seeing some business starting to return to the admitted market?
exchanges.answer: There's no telling where it's going to go in 2027. There still is pressure from various MGAs in London. A lot of traditional markets are still heavy in the shared layered deals, putting up larger limits, stretch primaries. It's still squeezing and it's still competitive. Our role now is to keep our pricing as close to tactical and meet our return thresholds, and if we shrink because of it is what it is in that division. There's heavy competition in some long-tail lines from London that's starting to creep into some other liability occurrence and long-tail lines. It's depressing pricing across the market for Construction lines of business. We're starting to see some more competition around general casualty type business. There are pockets of opportunity that we can grow, and we're going to lean into those. There is some flow to the admitted market, but it's not pervasive.

exchanges.question: You had mentioned in the press release that there was an increase in inbound accounts. I think that was some new language added, but maybe you could just talk about how much of that increase in inbound accounts is coming from some of the broker engagement that you've been working on versus more competitive pricing. Some carriers have been pointing to maybe some incremental improvement in claims emergence and loss cost trends, even if they're not declaring victory on social inflation by any means, what is your current view of the social inflation and casualty loss trend landscape?
exchanges.answer: It's a little bit of both. We're doing a good job with our idle broker initiative to reengage brokers that have slipped off over the years. We're seeing an increase of flow from them. Our hit ratios have stayed roughly the same, renewal and new business. With the growth in submissions, we're just seeing more accounts bind.

exchanges.question: My question on the property pricing, the property cycle. Any kind of granularity you can provide around what you saw in Q2 versus Q1? I'm thinking of the E&S data seemed to point to incremental softening in Q2. Trying to understand when or if we can get to a point of some kind of equilibrium, and that it might stabilize at this lower level. Any thoughts there would be helpful. You touched on the current accident year number, which was quite good in the quarter. I think you've been, as I read your results, the property has been more profitable than casualty, the mix has been changing here. What should we think about the underlying current accident year loss ratio given the mix shift out of property in the casualty? Should it drift up, or is this kind of level sustainable? One final one, if I might. The buyback, pretty meaningful number this quarter. As you think about it on a go-forward basis, if you're maintaining moderate top-line growth, is that going to be something that you'll continue to lean into? How do you think about the pacing there?
exchanges.answer: Eventually we're going to get to some equilibrium because although catastrophe losses in particular can be intermittent and kind of unpredictable, they do happen. I think being disciplined on how we price that business combined with, just as a reminder, a very disciplined risk management protocol around concentration of business and the like. We're very confident about what we're doing in that space. When it happens, I think we don't have any insight into that. We do have some other property-oriented underwriting divisions that are seeing growth opportunity.

exchanges.question: Maybe just on the product expansion that you mentioned in your prepared remarks, just how's that contributed to growth over the past year or so, and maybe the potential growth uplift going forward on those new products and whatnot?
exchanges.answer: When we roll out new products and new enhancements, we never want to be the market that jumps in feet first into a market and grows like a weed. It's always going to be a crawl, walk, run pace to grow. The new products are creating growth, they are driving submissions, they are driving new premium. It'll be a slow growth. As the market turns, we'll ramp up and go from there.

Gross written premium declined 5.0% compared to Q2 2025, though it rose 3.7% when excluding the Commercial Property Division. Net income grew 31.1% compared to Q2 2025, supported by 19.9% growth in net investment income and a combined ratio of 75.5%.
keyTakeaways: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President, and CEO, emphasized that Kinsale prioritizes profitability over volume during soft market conditions.
Gross written premium fell 5.0% YoY across the company, but grew 3.7% excluding the Commercial Property Division.
Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, stated casualty loss cost trends remain in the mid-single digits with minimal social inflation exposure.
Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President, and CEO, reported that share repurchases remain the primary capital allocation strategy, backed by a new $250 million authorization expansion.

exchanges.answer: The industry environment remains uncertain with volatility in inputs and commodities. EOP signals and tech adoption will drive some mix, but it is too early to tell exactly how it will play out for 2027, though we are encouraged by current signals.

exchanges.question: What variability in demand did you see by region in the early order program, and could the mid-single-digit growth wind up in the high single-digit range?
exchanges.answer: The U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada, though Canada is a limited part of the planter portfolio. We are seeing a doubling of See & Spray on factory-installed sprayer orders and 40% of planters taking advanced technologies, which gives us confidence.

exchanges.question: Was the cadence of the EOP orders being up mid-single digit driven by recent improvements in grain prices or decisions on technology?

exchanges.question: Are 8 Series Tractor orders falling in line with early order programs, and do you expect Europe to react similarly to the U.S. if there is a crop price response?
exchanges.answer: 8R orders are currently as expected, and we are collecting orders for the first quarter. In Europe, it is a mixed picture with arable farmers challenged while dairy and livestock producers benefit from stable cash flows. Overall order pace is as expected and we haven't seen a sudden step-up.

exchanges.question: How are the C&F early order programs shaping up, and how much of that is dealer rental fleet loading?
exchanges.answer: Order trends for C&F have been very positive, with about four to five months of orders on hand. This is driven by large infrastructure projects, data center starts, independent rental channels, and dealer-owned rental fleets.

exchanges.question: Will the net tariff impact be a headwind or tailwind going into 2027?
exchanges.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind going into next year. We will pay about $1.1 billion in direct tariffs this year, less $382 million in refunds, making our net exposure approximately $750 million. Next year, we expect a run rate closer to $1 billion.

exchanges.question: What are the moving dynamics behind C&F pricing guidance, and how are you thinking about growing dealer rental aspirations?
exchanges.answer: Q3 pricing was 8% partly due to easy comps, as Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives. Pricing is going well in C&F. Regarding rental, 30% to 35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental, and we see a meaningful opportunity to further increase our exposure and grow dealer-owned rental fleets.

exchanges.question: Are you doing any merchandising incentives in EOPs, and what implications does the FTC settlement have on your aftermarket business?
exchanges.answer: We are taking a measured approach to inflationary pricing and are committed to covering inflation over time. The FTC agreement formalizes tools like John Deere Operations Center PRO Service, which supports our long-standing principle of allowing customers to maintain their own equipment.

exchanges.question: Could the cap budget policy change in Europe in 2028 pull forward demand into 2027, or delay it?
exchanges.answer: It is too early to tell right now. Our order book is four to five months out, and sentiment will likely be shaped by input costs and commodity prices.

exchanges.question: What are you hearing from Brazilian and U.S. farmers regarding how input costs may affect their crop decisions?
exchanges.answer: Farmers are looking for alternatives in the types and amounts of products they apply, but they remain resilient and focused on driving yield. We are not seeing a huge reduction in intended applications, and farmers are staying nimble with their portfolios.

exchanges.question: How is management thinking about production versus retail setup by region for 2027, and what are the pricing expectations given input inflation?

exchanges.question: Did shipments pull forward into Q3 from Q4, and how should investors bridge performance from Q3 to Q4?

exchanges.question: What has been the cadence of EOP orders being up mid-single digits, and has recent grain price movement impacted order timing?
exchanges.answer: The cadence of EOP orders has progressed as expected following program adjustments that gave dealers more flexibility. High technology take rates remain the primary highlight of the program.

exchanges.question: How are 8 Series tractor orders tracking, and how are European farmers responding to heat stress and input cost pressure compared to North America?
exchanges.answer: 8R tractor order books for model year 2026 are closed and collecting orders for Q1 2027 as expected. In Europe, arable farmers face pressure from elevated input costs and heat stress, while dairy and livestock producers continue to benefit from healthy cash flows.

exchanges.question: How are Construction & Forestry order programs shaping up, and what is the outlook for dealer rental fleet loading?
exchanges.answer: Construction & Forestry order books extend four to five months out, supported by infrastructure, data centers, independent rental, and dealer fleet demand. Modest underproduction in 2026 keeps field inventories clean and sets up potential rental fleet expansion entering 2027.

exchanges.question: Will net tariff impact be a headwind or tailwind in fiscal year 2027 compared to 2026?
exchanges.answer: Net tariff expense will be a headwind in fiscal year 2027, rising to approximately $1.0 billion compared to roughly $750 million in 2026 ($1.1 billion direct tariff expense less $382 million of refunds).

exchanges.question: What is driving C&F pricing dynamics, and how does management view the expansion of dealer rental fleets?
exchanges.answer: Q3 C&F price realization of 8% benefited from easy comparisons against prior-year retail incentives, while full-year C&F price guidance is 3%. Rental accounts for 30% to 35% of earthmoving transactions, presenting a multi-year growth opportunity for Deere and its dealers.

exchanges.question: What are the margin implications of EOP pricing and incentives for next year, and how does the FTC settlement affect the aftermarket parts strategy?
exchanges.answer: Deere takes a disciplined, measured approach to cover cost inflation through regular price adjustments. The FTC agreement formalizes existing repair solutions like Operations Center PRO Service and aligns with Deere's core strategy of supporting customer repair choice.

exchanges.question: Could upcoming European CAP budget policy changes in 2028 pull demand forward into 2027 or delay equipment purchases?
exchanges.answer: It is too early to determine policy impacts on 2027 demand as order intake for Q1 is just beginning. Market direction will depend on arable crop input costs and commodity pricing trends.

exchanges.question: How are Brazilian and U.S. farmers positioning themselves regarding input costs and crop application decisions?
exchanges.answer: Farmers in both regions face elevated input costs but remain focused on yield maximization. Growers are adjusting product types and application strategies while larger producers utilize multi-year input contracts to remain flexible.

qa.question: Can you explain how much of the 9%-11% September quarter growth deceleration versus June is supply constraints versus FX, and what supply constraints beyond advanced SOCs are broadening?
qa.answer: Foreign exchange headwind is around 2.5 percentage points to year-over-year growth rate. Supply constraint impact is expected to increase significantly sequentially from June to September, affecting iPhone, Mac, and iPad. During June, constraints were primarily on Mac, driven by limited flexibility in the supply chain and availability of advanced nodes for SoCs. For September, Tim expects high levels of demand but significantly increased supply constraints with less supply chain flexibility to remedy  it.

qa.question: Does Apple's greater sourcing flexibility for memory aim to ensure supply and mitigate inflation, or primarily to preserve customer value proposition?
qa.answer: Memory costs rose from December to March quarter, expected to rise significantly again in June, and will rise even higher in September. Offsets include carry-in inventory benefits, though benefit will decrease over time, and lower costs on non-memory components. Beyond September, market pricing for memory expected to continue increasing with potential increasing impact on the business. DRAM market has three suppliers; more suppliers could help supply and potentially  pricing.

qa.question: Will you pursue multi-year LTAs with suppliers for supply access at pre-agreed prices, and does pricing strategy protect product gross profit dollars or gross margins?
qa.answer: Prices were raised reluctantly due to 100-year flood of memory pricing with exponential increases. Philosophy looks at units, revenue, and margin together to make business judgment; not a mathematical formula or single dimension. Think about it over long term rather than 90-day clock.

qa.question: Services grew 12% versus guidance, below 10% implied for September. Explain  deceleration drivers and whether App Store headwinds relate to AI reprioritizing user time?
qa.answer: Foreign exchange was main driver of growth rate change from March to June. Other factors: no theatrical F1 release this year versus prior year, and App Store headwinds in mobile gaming. App Store changes in certain countries and court ruling on link-out transactions in US impacted performance. Despite this, App Store set June quarter record. Strong double-digit growth in cloud, video, payment, advertising. Set records in every category.

qa.question: Has demand pull-forward occurred in consumer or enterprise/education markets, and is this factored into forward views?
qa.answer: iPhone has been running 22% growth rate year to date. It's not obvious in the data that pull-forward has occurred. Price increases on iPad and Mac occurred; price elasticity too early to conclude. Channel inventory adjustments take time for consumer response to be understood in weeks ahead.

qa.question: Does AI proliferation at edge open additional addressable market opportunities for Apple beyond current products?
qa.answer: Enormous opportunities for Apple moving forward in AI. Siri AI feedback is excellent. Ability to run percentage of requests on-device is strategic and competitive advantage. Extremely excited about these  opportunities.

App Store changes in certain countries and court ruling on link-out transactions in US impacted performance. Despite this, App Store set June quarter record. Strong double-digit growth in cloud, video, payment, advertising. Set records in every category.

exchanges.question: Has demand pull-forward occurred in consumer or enterprise/education markets, and is this factored into forward views?
exchanges.answer: iPhone has been running 22% growth rate year to date. It's not obvious in the data that pull-forward has occurred. Price increases on iPad and Mac occurred; price elasticity too early to conclude. Channel inventory adjustments take time for consumer response to be understood in weeks ahead.

exchanges.question: Does AI proliferation at edge open additional addressable market opportunities for Apple beyond current products?
exchanges.answer: Enormous opportunities for Apple moving forward in AI. Siri AI feedback is excellent. Ability to run percentage of requests on-device is strategic and competitive advantage. Extremely excited about these opportunities.

exchanges.question: Will Siri AI change Apple's capital intensity given on-device and distributed compute, with some backend requests to first-party and third-party cloud?
exchanges.answer: Uses hybrid model with some third-party cloud and own data centers. Generally OpEx and AI spending growing significantly. Other P&L locations like COGS also have AI expenditures. What Siri AI does on cost side uncertain. Also ability for heavy users to move up iCloud Plans provides recovery option.

exchanges.question: How is competitive landscape changing, particularly with OpenAI or SpaceX potentially building AI-enabled phones that bypass carrier infrastructure?
exchanges.answer: There is so much opportunity for Apple with everything happening in this space. Apple is focused on its plans and very excited about them.

exchanges.question: You mentioned Siri AI won't launch initially in China and Europe. What are updated thoughts on launch timing and hurdles needed in those regions?
exchanges.answer: EU: Working closely with commission; complete desire is to launch everywhere simultaneously. Not been able to do so in EU. Working closely to get to something allowing Siri AI offer there. Will be offered on Mac as not covered by same regulations as iPhone/iPad. China: Last week received approval for original Apple Intelligence features like cleanup. Working through rollout; more work required for Siri AI, at front end of that.

exchanges.question: Walk through sequential gross margin drivers from 48% adjusted in June to 46.5% September guidance, separating FX from commodity costs and memory?
exchanges.answer: More than 100% of 120 bps change from March 49.3% to June 48.1% explained by memory cost changes. Same dynamics for 160 bps change from June 48.1% to September 46.5% midpoint. Partial offsets from carry-in inventory benefits, lower non-memory component costs, favorable mix. FX minimal impact versus memory. Sequential change from March to September really driven by memory.

summary.overview: Apple's fiscal Q3 2026 revenue rose 16% to $109.4B, with iPhone up 22% to $54.3B and Mac up 29% to $10.4B, on Tim Cook's final earnings call as CEO. Kevan Parekh, CFO, guided September-quarter revenue growth to 9%-11% on supply constraints and FX, and gross margin to 47%-48% as memory costs rise. Diluted EPS was $2.02, up 29%, including $0.11 from tariff refunds.
keyTakeaways: Kevan Parekh, CFO, guided September revenue growth to 9%-11%, down from 16% in June, citing a 2.5-point sequential FX headwind and supply constraints that increase significantly across iPhone, Mac and iPad.
Tim Cook, CEO, said the root cause of the constraints is a demand-forecast miss, with advanced-node SoC availability the primary limit and iPhone (22% growth) and Mac (29%) far above expectations.
Cook said Apple 'reluctantly' raised prices amid memory pricing he called a '100-year flood', and has now raised prices on iPad and Mac.
Parekh said services growth slowed from 16% in March to 12% in June, mainly on FX, no F1 theatrical release this year, and App Store softness in mobile gaming.
Cook said Siri AI developer and public beta feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, while China approved the original Apple Intelligence features last week and Siri AI there needs more work.
financialHighlights: Revenue was $109.4B, up 16%, with Products at $78.7B (up 18%) and Services at $30.7B (up 12%).
Company gross margin was 50.1%, up 80bp sequentially, including about 2 points of tariff refund benefit; Parekh said it was 48.1% excluding the refund.
Operating expenses were $19.1B, up 23%, and net income was $29.8B.
Diluted EPS was $2.02, up 29%, including a $0.11 favorable tariff refund impact.
Apple generated $34.4B of operating cash flow and returned $33B, including $25.8B of share repurchases and $4B of dividends and equivalents.

guidance: Parekh guided September-quarter total revenue growth of 9%-11%, with FX a 2.5-point sequential headwind to y/y growth from June.
Parekh expects supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially and to affect iPhone, Mac and iPad, and guided reported iPhone growth of mid-teens.
Parekh expects reported services growth largely similar to June's 12% after removing the negative sequential FX impact of about 2.5 points.
Parekh guided gross margin of 47%-48%, including about 1 point of tariff refund benefit, operating expenses of $19.1B-$19.4B, other income and expense of about $350M and a tax rate of about 16.5%.

Cook expects higher memory costs in September, partly offset by carry-in inventory and lower non-memory costs, with market memory pricing continuing to rise beyond September; Parekh gave no guidance beyond the September quarter.

qa.answer: Parekh said September growth reflects about 2.5 points of FX headwind plus supply constraints that, together, get close to June's total growth rate. Cook said the constraints are 'very significant' with limited flexibility, memory cost rose in June versus March and will rise again in September, and the carry-in inventory benefit shrinks beyond September. Cook said DRAM has three suppliers and Apple is 'evaluating all options'.
qa.read: Answered partially: gave the FX and cost direction but no split of the deceleration between supply and FX.

qa.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter, is there guidance beyond September, and could Apple broaden its silicon providers quickly?
qa.answer: Cook said the root cause is a demand-forecast miss, with iPhone up 22% and Mac up 29%, and September will be a quarter of scrambling on supply. Kevan Parekh, CFO, gave no color beyond September. Cook said it is not a partner or supplier issue and that Apple sources over 100 million components this year from Arizona under its $600B U.S. commitment.
qa.read: Answered partially: declined December guidance and did not say whether providers would be broadened.

qa.question: Is Apple pursuing multi-year LTAs, is pricing aimed at gross profit dollars or margin percentage, and why does services growth of 12% decelerate further?
qa.answer: Cook said Apple reluctantly raised prices and weighs units, revenue and margin without a formula. qa.answer: Cook said iPhone has run about 22% growth year to date and pull-forward is not obvious in the data. He said it is too early to judge price elasticity after the iPad and Mac price increases, and called on-device AI a strategic competitive weapon.
qa.read: Answered partially: pushed back on the premise and named no new markets.

exchanges.question: Procedural: IR asks analysts to limit themselves to two questions and hands to the operator. No analyst question.
exchanges.answer: Asked callers to limit to two questions; no substantive content.

exchanges.question: How much of the roughly 500bp deceleration implied by 9%-11% September guidance is supply constraints versus FX, and what are the supply constraints that are broadening beyond advanced SoCs? Separately, are reported efforts to gain sourcing flexibility on memory about securing supply, mitigating memory inflation, or preserving the customer value proposition?
exchanges.answer: Parekh: September revenue growth of 9%-11% y/y is hit by FX (about 2.5 points sequential headwind to y/y growth from June to September) and supply constraints that increase significantly sequentially, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad; together these get pretty close to the June total company growth rate. Cook: June constraints were primarily Mac, less so iPhone and iPad, driven by availability of advanced nodes for SoCs and less supply chain flexibility than normal; constraints are 'very significant' with limited flexibility to remedy. On memory: paid more in June than March (partly offset by carry-in inventory), expects higher memory cost in September partly offset by carry-in inventory and lower non-memory BOM costs; benefit from carry-in decreases beyond September, and market memory pricing continues to increase beyond September. DRAM has three suppliers, more would help supply and perhaps pricing; 'evaluating all options'.

exchanges.question: What adoption is expected for the Apple Upgrade program across the 2.5 billion-device base, and will it shorten replacement cycles for iPhone, Mac and iPad? Also, what has the iOS 27 public beta taught about Siri AI as an iPhone demand driver this holiday, and about compute costs and recovering them through iCloud+?
exchanges.answer: Apple Upgrade is a leasing plan offered in retail stores, not widely in all channels; Apple residual values are generally much higher than competitors'; uptake still to be seen but early feedback is quite positive. Parekh added it is only available in the U.S. right now. On Siri AI, developer and public beta feedback has been overwhelmingly positive; on compute costs it is early and Cook does not claim a complete plan, but there will be iCloud+ upgrade possibilities for heavy users. Did not address holiday iPhone demand or replacement-cycle impact directly.

exchanges.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter, given the Street at about 8%-9% growth versus about 12% for September; any guidance beyond September? Could Apple broaden its silicon providers (the Arizona fab being built by another company) within a reasonable time to alleviate constraints?
exchanges.answer: Cook: the primary constraint is advanced nodes for SoCs; the root cause is a demand forecast issue, with iPhone (22% growth, also 22% year to date) and Mac (29%) far exceeding expectations; supply has been pulled ahead but there is a limit, and the September quarter will be one of scrambling on supply. Parekh: the 9%-11% reflects supply and FX; no color or guidance beyond the September quarter. On new silicon providers, Cook said this is not a partner or supplier issue and noted Apple sources over 100 million components this year from Arizona as part of the $600 billion U.S. commitment; he did not answer whether providers would be broadened.

exchanges.question: Is Apple pursuing multi-year LTAs with suppliers for supply at pre-agreed prices, and in pricing is the intent to protect product gross profit dollars or gross margin percentage? Separately, why did services growth of 12% come in a bit below guidance, why does September guidance imply a further deceleration (below 10% as reported), and is App Store pressure from AI reprioritizing time a factor?
exchanges.answer: Cook: Apple reluctantly raised prices because of a '100-year flood' on memory pricing with exponential increases; it weighs units, revenue and margin with a long-term view rather than a formula; LTAs not addressed. Parekh: services growth went from 16% in the March quarter to 12% in June, mainly FX, plus no F1 theatrical release this year (favorable in the year-ago June and September quarters) and App Store softness in mobile gaming; June roughly met expectations. Court ruling on U.S. link-out transactions remains in effect and the Supreme Court will hear Apple's appeal. For September, FX is a headwind of about 5 percentage points to y/y growth from March to September quarter, including another 2.5 points sequentially from June; AI reprioritizing time was not addressed.

exchanges.question: Has Apple seen any pull-forward of demand (consumer, enterprise, education) given memory pricing dynamics? Does AI at the edge open additional addressable markets over time?
exchanges.answer: Cook: iPhone has run at about 22% growth year to date and it is not obvious in the data that there is pull-forward. Apple has now raised prices on iPad and Mac and it is too early for a definitive conclusion on price elasticity because channel inventory and consumer response take time; more will be understood in the weeks ahead. On AI, there are enormous opportunities and running some percentage of requests on device is strategic and a competitive weapon; no specific new markets named.

exchanges.question: Will Siri AI change Apple's capital intensity given the mix of on-device, first-party cloud and third-party cloud? Separately, John Ternus is asked for a high-level view on a changing competitive landscape, including AI-device entrants such as OpenAI and SpaceX AI.
exchanges.answer: Cook: Apple uses a hybrid model with some third-party cloud and its own data centers; OpEx and AI spending have grown quite a bit, and COGS also carries AI expenditure. The cost impact of Siri AI is to be seen, with possible iCloud Plan upgrades from heavy use; the balance is uncertain. Ternus said there is so much opportunity in the space and Apple is focused on its plans; he did not address the named competitors or capital intensity.

exchanges.question: What are the hurdles and updated thinking for launching Siri AI in China and Europe? Separately, what drives the gross margin step from 48% (ex-tariff refund) in June to about 46.5% guided for September: FX versus commodity costs?
exchanges.answer: Cook: Apple is working closely with the EU commission and has not been able to launch everything simultaneously there; Siri AI is or will be offered on Mac in the EU since Mac is not covered by the same regulations as iPhone and iPad. In China, approval was received last week to ship the original Apple Intelligence features (such as cleanup), with more work required for Siri AI. Parekh: gross margin fell from 49.3% in March to 48.1% in June ex-tariff refund (120bp), and to the 46.5% midpoint of guidance ex-tariff (160bp); more than 100% of each change is explained by memory cost, partly offset by carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix, with FX minimal.

qa.question: Can you evaluate recent management changes and elevation of  Doug and Troy to co-presidents, and what this means for leadership development and your tenure as CEO?
qa.answer: Marianne is exceptional individual. Board made decision to create two co-presidents to prepare them for more at company. Hasn't changed timetable. Marianne decided she'd rather retire than stay, result of knowing about succession plans. No mystery.

qa.question: How do you judge sustainability of investment banking and markets strength, and how risk-on are the various businesses?
qa.answer: Investment banking fees historically fine but not super peak, had room to come up. Some pull forward happened, large deals  contributed meaningfully. Pipeline quite robust; high-profile activity seems encouraging more activity. Markets elevated for time; equities exceptionally strong this quarter with highly dynamic conditions. Separation between fixed income up 6% and equities up 86% year-over-year.

qa.question: Can you discuss progression toward 15% retail market share target and how higher-for-longer rates impact pace of market share gains?
qa.answer: Wholesale deposit growth strong this quarter and first half, outperforming expectations due to franchise strength, winning deals, and lending environment particularly BFI space and data center stuff. Consumer expecting low single-digit growth, unchanged expectation, balance between  robust net new checking accounts and yield-seeking flows. View that 15% will be outcome of executing strategy across components from primary bank relationships, branch expansion, deepening product-value proposition.

qa.question: Where are we in the investment cycle for branch build-out, AI investments, and banker hires, and how does this play into operating leverage outlook?
qa.answer: Complete continuation of what we've been doing for years. Shouldn't expect any change. Power of franchise is such that able to aggressively invest for future generating returns and solidifying competitive position while delivering exceptional current returns. Would be true delivering 15%, 16%, 17%  returns. When delivering these types, firing on all cylinders.

qa.question: Can you talk about drivers of upward revision to NII ex-Markets from $95 billion to $96.5 billion and cadence in Q3, Q4, and exit rate?
qa.answer: Biggest single factor is deposit balances across wholesale and consumer, overall quantum and mix shift in favor of slightly higher margin. Rates higher than previously guided in short and back end. Sensitivity a little more than EAR suggests due to consumer betas outperformance, disproportionately in front end. Increase as function of higher rates but most is balances overall.

qa.question: Markets NII guided higher even though rate outlook higher. What are drivers, balance sheet mix?
qa.answer: Markets NII actually liability sensitive. Higher rates would expect it down; instead forecast up. Difference is changes in balance sheet composition, expecting lower finance non-interest-bearing assets in second half. One balance sheet unit drives number quite a bit, can overwhelm rate effect. Also increased equity allocation to CIB this quarter moves some equity out of corporate into CIB; markets NII moving out of NII ex-Markets into markets NII, about $150 million not expected to offset on bottom line.
