exchanges.question: Markets NII guided higher even though rate outlook higher. What are drivers, balance sheet mix?
exchanges.answer: Markets NII actually liability sensitive. Higher rates would expect it down; instead forecast up. Difference is changes in balance sheet composition, expecting lower finance non-interest-bearing assets in second half. One balance sheet unit drives number quite a bit, can overwhelm rate effect. Also increased equity allocation to CIB this quarter moves some equity out of corporate into CIB; markets NII moving out of NII ex-Markets into markets NII, about $150 million not expected to offset on bottom line.

exchanges.question: What characteristics are you and board looking for in new CEO, and what makes an exceptional CEO? Should investors think tenure more fixed or rolling retirement date?
exchanges.answer: Timing essentially same, not changed. Want good at management, people, analytical, detailed, culture carrier, curious, heart, grit, soul, work ethic, travel, walk in operating centers with CEOs and prime ministers. Blessed with many great culture carriers. No one has all perfect, some learned, some improve. See it when see it. Two exceptional co-presidents. Flexible mind deal with growing complex world. Fully confident would be fine if hit by truck.

exchanges.question: Your marginal margin based on 77% given. Why is that as good as it gets? Revenue environment as good as it gets?
exchanges.answer: Very healthy, active, exuberant market with very high prices and high volumes; benefit from that. Just don't know how long continues. Could get lot better. How much better? Don't know.

exchanges.question: Troy taking over consumer bank. What gives confidence Troy is right person when doesn't have that experience? (FX trader selling mortgage, credit cards)?
exchanges.answer: Evaluate people on analytics, brain power, EQ, heart, soul, culture carrier, can they walk into operating centers. Exhibited in markets, investment banking. IB extensive operations, back office, technology function where great expertise. Very important people have experience across company. Investment bank only leadership can cause rest of franchise suffer. Need respect for rest of franchise. Great for him, great for company, already excited. Troy actually options trader, not FX.

exchanges.question: Argument we're vastly underestimating AI benefits to efficiency? Could banks operate leaner with different structure while not sacrificing product velocity?
exchanges.answer: Use AI to do better job for clients. Fully expect huge efficiency in certain parts. Analyze all time. Spend quite a bit on it. Lots of MVPs. Whole company working this, almost 1,000 use cases, really important ones 50 across risk, fraud, marketing, hedging, prospecting, note-taking, idea generation, document reading. Just starting. May accelerate what want to get done anyway. Preparing to retrain people. Discrete areas reduced jobs 30% or 40%, most offered jobs elsewhere. Benefit accrues to customer not JPMorgan because others doing same.

exchanges.question: Can you elaborate on what was most exceptional in equities this quarter that may be difficult to sustain?
exchanges.answer: Major IPOs, major index rebalancing, very complicated Korean equity market dynamics, lots of activity in Asia, overall environment dynamic and interesting. Clients extremely active. All the headlines basically driven market. Statistically improbable that particular combination effects repeat itself though could. Volumes NYSE, CME, hedge fund volumes show most taking place daily, not secret.

exchanges.question: Talk about Main Street. Fragility in housing, real estate, rates up. Consumer resilience if rates go up? AI CapEx beyond AI? Commercial lending AI-centric?
exchanges.answer: Decent CapEx and loan growth across franchise; not all appears AI related but reluctant to conclude strongly. AI theme proliferated in so many parts of economy. CapEx about $4 trillion year, AI went $400 billion last year to $700 billion this year, projected little over trillion next year with maybe reduction non-AI CapEx. Hard figure out. Consumer spend fine, robust across income segments, tailwind from tax refunds. Delinquencies lower expected, better across FICO. Economic heterogeneity data doesn't support K-shape narrative. Long expansion, economy surprised upside.

exchanges.question: Why buy back stock at three times tangible book when things good, bad things could happen? Why not more excess capital for rainy day?
exchanges.answer: Buy back less as price goes up, more as price goes down. Had lots excess capital couple years ago, still think use approximately $40 billion, now think deployed over time. World gotten bigger, more complex. Security resiliency initiative, hyperscalers needs huge. Not just AI. Global infrastructure, remilitarization, trade restructuring, government needs enormous. Global deficits almost 4.5% or 5%, very big number competing for same capital. Goal deploy capital at 17% return. Always looking at inorganic. Huge opportunities organic growth every business. Been doing deals this year, most good, couple not particularly good. Open-minded.

exchanges.question: Status of smart cash tool you're working on? When might roll out? Comments on paying more for money over time?
exchanges.answer: Still test case. Banks in different position. Relates to narrow segment accounts where competing for investment and deposit business. Tests coming out; find what can and can't do, learn by doing. Think could be good for customers and us. Not finding ways waste money. You'll see something this year.

exchanges.question: European consumer banking aspirations? What trying to be as consumer bank across major European markets?
exchanges.answer: Weren't going to compete with local banks when talking bricks mortar, brands, capabilities. Digital may changed that. Started Chase UK 4-5 years ago, complete startup, almost 3 million or 2.5 million customers in UK now. Opened Berlin, done much better in Germany than thought, not quite profitable yet. Platform costs money, distribute across more clients, countries, reach break even then profitable. Added investment products in UK, assume add elsewhere, probably credit card. Dream pan-European successful digital bank off JPMorgan strengths. Private bank, huge upscale business. Lots clients cross border. Training, underwriting, research capability.

exchanges.question: You've talked about excesses in underwriting and credit, risk on in capital markets. What seeing in credit underwriting from competitors? Getting crazier?
exchanges.answer: Crazy strong word. Data center underwriting bellwether. Passed on some deals. Key question what happens power supply, tenants, well-discussed. Precise framework govern willing to do. Saw deals where not doing that. Normal, competitive, people eager. Some element relationship lending through data center with startup entity. Mild deterioration credit underwriting standards across spectrum. Assumptions revenue growth, add back expenses, more PIK, more across some players. Weaker covenants, more rollover risk if rates up, interest rate exposure. Credit cycle will be, when there is cycle, how will everybody perform? Not bell curve, some outliers.

exchanges.question: Basel III endgame hopefully codified by year end. Next year tailoring. Could envision regulatory stability period enhancing bank stock valuations?
exchanges.answer: Regulatory stability desirable, relatively nonpartisan. Big reaction to crisis, reaction to reaction, amplitude oscillations decreasing, getting to point have it about right. Banks focused not on complying regulatory constraints but own standards, own risk appetite, be true north. Getting closer to state. Whether that supportive bank stock valuations, leave to you. For banks like us, not convinced major drag or been past. Recent Supreme decision makes flip-flopping less likely. When write legislation, be more clear intent, could have said independent or only replace some. Mickey Bowman and Kevin Warsh taking step back broad range changes, extensive 20 years. Makes safer. No MRAs none related safety soundness, related other issues.

summary.overview: JPMorgan reported fiscal Q2 2026 net income of $16.9B, EPS of $6.14 and ROTCE of 23%, with revenue ex significant items up 15% y/y and expenses up 15% to $27.3B. Corporate and Investment Bank revenue rose 27% to $24.9B on equities up 86% and investment banking fees up 30%. Jeremy Barnum, CFO, raised full-year NII ex-Markets guidance to about $96.5B and expense guidance to about $107.5B.
keyTakeaways: Equities markets revenue rose 86% y/y and IB fees rose 30%, though Jeremy Barnum, CFO, said there was pull forward and that this quarter's equities set of events is hard to imagine repeating.
Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said 'It's getting close to as good as it gets' but that nobody knows how long it lasts.
Dimon said the board named two co-presidents to prepare them to do far more, the CEO timetable is essentially unchanged at several years, plus or minus, and the date is up to the board.
Dimon said AI has almost 1,000 use cases, about 50 really important, with some discrete areas cutting jobs 30% or 40%, and that the benefits will accrue to customers rather than margins.
Dimon said he made a mistake mentioning $20B of buybacks last time, and that the goal is deploying capital at a 17% return, organic growth first.
financialHighlights: Net income was $16.9B and EPS was $6.14, with ROTCE of 23% and revenue ex significant items up 15% y/y.
Expenses were $27.3B, up 15% y/y, and credit costs were $2.5B, with net charge-offs of $2.4B and a net reserve build of $149M.
Standardized CET1 was 14.1%, down 20bp q/q, with standardized RWA up about $103B.
CIB net income was $9.7B on revenue of $24.9B, up 27%, with fixed income markets revenue up 6%.
AWM revenue was $6.9B, up 19%, with a 38% pre-tax margin and $50B of long-term net inflows; CCB revenue was $20.3B, up 8%.
guidance: Barnum guided full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets to about $96.5B, up from $95B, with total NII of about $105.5B and Markets NII of about $9B.
Barnum guided adjusted expense to about $107.5B, raised by $2.5B, with $1.5B booked in the first half and about $1B implied for the second half.
Barnum guided the full-year card net charge-off rate to approximately 3.2%, versus approximately 3.4% last quarter.
Barnum said consumer deposits are still expected to grow low single digits this year, and the board intends to raise the quarterly dividend to $1.65 per share effective Q3.
Barnum said AI token expense was trivial in the first half and is forecast to accelerate meaningfully in the second half, though still trivial for the full year.

qa.question: What should investors take from the co-president appointments, and how sustainable are investment banking and markets activity?
qa.answer: Dimon said the board made two co-presidents to prepare them to do far more and the timetable has not changed. Jeremy Barnum, CFO, said IB fees were not super-peak, with some pull forward and large IPOs contributing, the pipeline is quite robust, and he declined to guide. Barnum said the equities events this quarter are hard to imagine repeating.

qa.question: What drove the upward revision to NII ex-Markets, and why is Markets NII guided higher?
qa.answer: Barnum said NII ex-Markets moved from $95B to $96.5B, driven mainly by deposit balances across wholesale and consumer plus a mix shift toward slightly higher margin, with consumer betas outperforming the model. He said Markets NII rises on lower non-interest-bearing financing assets in the second half, and raising CIB equity allocation shifts about $150M of NII into Markets NII.

qa.question: What is the board looking for in the next CEO, and is Dimon's remaining tenure fixed or rolling?
qa.answer: Dimon said timing is essentially the same and up to the board, repeating 'several years, plus or minus'. He listed attributes including analytics, culture, grit and work ethic, said no one has all of them, and named COO Jen Piepszak and Mary Erdoes as exceptional alongside the co-presidents.
qa.read: Answered partially: did not say whether the date is fixed or rolling.

qa.question: Is negative operating leverage the right framing with revenue up 15%, and what gives confidence in Troy running consumer?
qa.answer: Barnum said the capital markets complex outperformed first-half expectations by $6.5B, with $1.5B of additional expense booked. qa.answer: Dimon said some discrete areas cut jobs 30% or 40% with most offered jobs elsewhere, and the benefits will accrue to customers, not ROE rising to 50%. Barnum cited major IPOs, index rebalancing and the Korean equity market as equities drivers, calling a repeat statistically improbable.

whatChanged.toneShift: Last quarter's call centered on private credit risk, Basel III and a held $105B expense guide; this quarter centers on management succession, record markets activity and raised guidance, with Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, saying 'It's getting close to as good as it gets'.

risksMentioned: Jeremy Barnum, CFO, said consumer yield-seeking deposit flows are a possible risk to the low-single-digit consumer deposit growth outlook.
Barnum said deposit rate-paid convexity has not shown up yet but must kick in at some point, and a 7% rate environment would not be great.
Dimon said competitors show mild deterioration in credit underwriting, including more PIK, weaker covenants and rollover risk, and that a credit cycle will come with outliers.
Dimon said market risk capital of $80B or more versus a largest quarterly loss of $1.4B reflects double counts in capital rules, and that G-SIB calibration should be fixed back to 2015.
Barnum said the short-term wholesale funding change disproportionately burdens banks like JPM and Bank of America versus former investment bank competitors.

exchanges.question: What should investors take from the recent management changes (Doug and Troy elevated to co-presidents) and does it imply anything for Dimon's tenure as CEO? Separately, how sustainable is the very high investment banking and markets activity, and how risk-on is the firm?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: the board made two co-presidents to prepare them to do far more; it has not changed the timetable; Marianne chose to retire rather than stay. Barnum: investment banking fees were fine but not super-peak, with some pull forward and large IPOs/ECM deals contributing, though the pipeline is quite robust and the activity may be begetting more; he declined to guide. In markets, the particular equities set of events this quarter is hard to imagine repeating; the market is extremely risk on and JPM is a taker of that, balancing client support with caution.

exchanges.question: How is progress toward the 15% retail deposit market share goal, and how might higher-for-longer rates affect the pace? Separately, where are we in the investment cycle (branches, AI, bankers) and what does it mean for medium-term operating leverage?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: wholesale deposit growth was strong in the first half and outperformed expectations (franchise strength plus lending, including BFI and data center activity); consumer deposits still expected to grow low single digits this year, unchanged, with strong net new checking accounts but yield-seeking flows a possible risk; the 15% is an outcome of executing the strategy, with no change to the aspiration. Dimon: expenses are a complete continuation of what has been done for years, no change expected. Barnum: the firm will always invest and returns speak for themselves; no stated end point to the investment cycle or operating leverage figure.

exchanges.question: What drove the upward revision to NII ex-Markets and what is the cadence in Q3 and Q4 and the exit rate? Why is markets NII guided higher even though rate expectations are higher?
exchanges.answer: NII ex-Markets was revised from $95 billion to $96.5 billion for the full year, implying a higher exit run rate if the forward curve plays out; the biggest driver is deposit balances across wholesale and consumer, plus mix shift toward slightly higher margin, with higher short- and long-end rates a smaller part and consumer betas outperforming the model. Markets NII is liability sensitive and would have fallen on higher rates, but is forecast up due to lower non-interest-bearing financing assets in the second half. Raising CIB equity allocation moves about $150 million of NII from ex-Markets into markets NII, which would not be offset on the bottom line.

exchanges.question: What characteristics are Dimon and the board looking for in the next CEO? Should investors view Dimon's remaining tenure as fixed or rolling, given that Marianne's departure may read as an extension?
exchanges.answer: Dimon said the timing is essentially the same and up to the board; he listed management, people skills, analytics, detail, culture, curiosity, heart, grit, work ethic and the ability to deal with CEOs and prime ministers, noting no one has all of them and he has two exceptional co-presidents, COO Jen Piepszak and Mary Erdoes running AWM. Asked what no change in timing means, he said whatever he said last time stands: several years, plus or minus, up to the board. He did not say whether the date is fixed or rolling.

exchanges.question: Year-to-date adjusted operating leverage is negative; over the intermediate term can expense growth slow and operating leverage become likely given AI and technology? Separately, any update on regulatory proposals, including the G-SIB surcharge and Basel III?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: forever increasing operating leverage is a crazy notion; AI has gives and takes and cannot be projected, but growth might slow in 2027 or 2028; benefits of AI will accrue to customers, not margins. On regulation, Dimon said regulators should do the numbers properly: remove double counts in operational risk and market risk capital (market risk capital is $80 billion or more versus a largest quarterly loss of $1.4 billion), fix G-SIB calibration back to 2015 and short-term wholesale funding. Barnum: the short-term wholesale funding change disproportionately burdens banks like JPM and Bank of America versus former investment bank competitors.

exchanges.question: Is this as good as it gets, or are we earlier in the cycle given AI, defense spending and supply chains? Is there a tipping point where deposit volumes and betas change if rates rise a certain amount?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: it is getting close to as good as it gets, but nobody knows how long it lasts. Barnum: the tipping point is unknown; deposit rate-paid convexity (negative for consumer) has not shown up yet but must kick in at some point; stress tests model an acceleration in rate paid, and one should not be naive about higher rates since a 7% rate environment would not be great if the deposit franchise had to be repurchased. Dimon added the firm assumes some of that.

exchanges.question: Is negative operating leverage the right framing when revenue grew 15% and dollars are positive, given high marginal returns on incremental revenue? Separately, what gives confidence Troy, a trader, can run the consumer business?
exchanges.answer: Dimon agreed operating leverage in dollars was positive and a rapid revenue increase drives big operating leverage. Barnum: expense guidance was raised by $2.5 billion; the first-half capital markets complex outperformed expectations by $6.5 billion with $1.5 billion of additional expense booked, implicitly adding $1 billion for the second half. Dimon said the market is healthy, active and exuberant and he does not know how long it lasts; on Troy, he cited analytics, EQ, culture, and experience in investment banking operations and that big banks run only by investment bankers can suffer. Barnum corrected that Troy was an options trader.

exchanges.question: Are we underestimating AI's efficiency potential, as with Block cutting 40% of its workforce, and could banks operate with a much leaner structure? On equities, what was most exceptional this quarter and hard to sustain?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: AI will be used to do a better job for clients with huge efficiency in parts of the company; almost 1,000 use cases, about 50 really important; some discrete areas cut jobs 30% or 40% with most offered jobs elsewhere; benefits will accrue to customers, not ROE rising to 50%. Barnum: equities drivers were obvious and heavily reported: major IPOs, index rebalancing, complicated dynamics in the Korean equity market and Asia activity; repeating that combination seems statistically improbable though it could happen. Dimon noted volumes are visible daily.

exchanges.question: What are you seeing on the consumer and Main Street side, and is capex broadening beyond AI? Why buy back stock at three times tangible book rather than hold more excess capital, and what about M&A?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: some capex and loan growth does not appear AI related, though AI is proliferating widely; consumer spend is robust across income segments with a tax-refund tailwind, delinquencies lower than expected across FICO scores, little support for a K-shape narrative; consumer credit comes down to the labor market, which has been resilient. Dimon: capex is about $4 trillion a year, AI went from $400 billion last year to $700 billion this year, and a little over a trillion is projected next year. On buybacks, Barnum said they buy back less as the price rises; Dimon said he made a mistake mentioning $20 billion last time, it could be far more or nothing, buybacks are an investment decision, the goal is deploying capital at a 17% return, organic growth first, and they remain open to inorganic opportunities (adjacencies, data) with no specifics; Chase UK is being built.

exchanges.question: What is the status and rollout timing of the smart cash tool, and what did the comment about paying more for money mean? What are the aspirations for European consumer banking?
exchanges.answer: Dimon: smart cash is still a test case affecting a narrow segment of accounts where JPM competes for investment and deposit business; tests are coming and something will be seen this year. In Europe, JPM started Chase UK four or five years ago and has about 2.5 million to 3 million customers in the U.K.; Germany (Berlin) is doing better than expected but not yet profitable; investment products added in the U.K. and likely elsewhere, probably credit card; the aspiration is a pan-European digital bank.

exchanges.question: What are you seeing in competitors' credit underwriting; is it getting crazier? Separately, could regulation enter a period of stability, including Basel III endgame and tailoring, that supports bank valuations?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: crazy is too strong, but JPM passed on some data center deals and sees normal competitive pressure while flexing for important clients and holding the line otherwise. Dimon: only a very mild deterioration across revenue-growth assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants and rollover risk, in some players more than others; a credit cycle will come with outliers. On regulation, Barnum said stability is desirable and nonpartisan, and he is not convinced regulation is a major drag on valuations for banks like JPM; Dimon wants regulators to focus on real safety and soundness and said resolution recovery does not work.

exchanges.question: Besides revenue-related expense, are other expense categories such as tech or marketing being pulled forward? How nimble can the CIB capital allocation be, is it at peak, and are there internal limits?
exchanges.answer: Barnum: some of that is going on, with ups and downs including marketing he will not disclose; token (AI model) expense is trivial in the first half, forecast to accelerate meaningfully in the second half but still trivial for the full year and not a driver of the outlook revision. He would not discuss internal limit management: capital allocation responds to client demand plus passive effects (market risk capital rises with volatility, prime RWA with equity appreciation), the firm has a ton of excess capital, and the system is flush with capital but less so with liquidity, calling for liquidity regulation adjustment. Dimon said risk standards have not changed.

summary.overview: Lilly's fiscal Q2 2026 revenue grew 48% versus Q2 2025, with MOUNJARO plus ZEPBOUND at $14.9B, up $6.3B, and non-GAAP EPS of $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges. Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised full-year revenue guidance to $85B-$87B, a $2.5B increase at the midpoint, and non-GAAP performance margin to 49%-50.5%. US price fell 3%, and the US Foundayo launch drew questions on pace.
keyTakeaways: Ilya Yuffa, President, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities, said Foundayo volume in the last week of July almost doubled versus a month earlier, with about one in four new starts on Foundayo, and US prescribers rose from 8,000 to 36,000.
Ilya Yuffa said the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge launched July 1, with about 80% of people treated on injectables and 60%-70% new to treatment.
Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, said Lilly expects to submit retatrutide by Q1 next year under a BLA pathway, after gathering a little more CMC data.
Montarce said US price is expected to decline as medical exceptions fade with CVS access from Q4, with volume growth more than offsetting it, and this is embedded in the guide.
Patrik Jonsson, President, Lilly International, said Lilly's international incretin share is about 55% in a market up 74%, and Foundayo's major ex-US launches come at the beginning of 2027.
financialHighlights: Gross margin was 86.3% of revenue, up about 1.3 points, and non-GAAP performance margin was 54.8%, up nine points.
Marketing, selling and administrative expenses rose 25% and R&D rose 14%, with more than 40 active phase III programs.
US revenue rose 33% with price down 3%, or down 9% excluding rebate and discount estimate changes; Europe rose 55%, China 93% and rest of world 136% in constant currency.
Oncology, immunology and neuroscience medicines grew 121%, with Jaypirca up 56% and Ebglyss sales more than doubling.
Lilly returned $1.5B in dividends and $1.6B in share repurchases.

guidance: Montarce guided FY2026 revenue to $85B-$87B, with the low end raised by $3B and the high end by $2B.
Montarce guided non-GAAP performance margin to 49%-50.5%, up 2 points at both ends, and non-GAAP EPS to $35.50-$36.50, after the $3.03 Q2 acquired IPR&D charge.
Ricks expects US regulatory action for Foundayo in Type 2 diabetes later this year, with approvals in additional markets later this year and a global rollout in all major markets in 2027.

Dan Skovronsky, Chief Scientific and Product Officer, expects the retatrutide BLA submission in Q1 2027, EU approval of insulin efsitora alfa in the coming months, and lebrikizumab every-12-weeks data in 2027.

Montarce expects H2 growth to be more driven by OUS penetration, because Q2 included one-off prior-period US rebate and discount adjustments and the 2025 base had a bolus of new-country MOUNJARO launches.

Patrik Jonsson, President, Lilly International, said Lilly's combined incretin share held steady in the UAE with a second oral entering, next launches are Mexico and Saudi, most launches come in 2027, and Novo's figure is noisy sell-in data including inventory build.

exchanges.question: How does Lilly see its consumer-facing position expanding, including more aesthetic-driven approaches, and how similar are the US and international self-pay markets?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Yuffa: obesity treatment is still at mid-single-digit utilization, access is improving with Bridge and state Medicaid going live or committing next year, obesity TRxs are about 3 million, and about 55% of ZEPBOUND prescriptions are self-pay; Lilly is expanding LillyDirect and consumer awareness. Jonsson: obesity outside the US is still mainly out of pocket, Lilly has launched versions of LillyDirect outside the US, regulations differ so models will differ, and the common aim is reaching patients with safe and authentic Lilly medicines. The aesthetic-driven angle was not addressed.

exchanges.question: Why has the US Foundayo launch curve been slower than anticipated and when will it inflect? Outside the US, what are the competitive dynamics with Novo's oral pill, including share in the UAE where Novo said it reached 50% share within three weeks?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Yuffa: three focus areas (physician education, access and affordability, consumer awareness); CVS added Foundayo in June, Bridge launched July 1, full DTC campaign started; in the last week of July volume almost doubled versus a month earlier and about one in four new starts are on Foundayo. Jonsson: UAE launch was early May with a strong start, patients are mostly incretin-naive, Lilly's combined incretin share held steady with a second oral entering, next launches are Mexico and Saudi with most launches in 2027, supply is ready with no gating; the Novo figure is early, noisy sell-in data that includes inventory build.

exchanges.question: What are the requirements and milestones to get retatrutide accepted as a BLA, and would this pathway apply to subsequent incretins?
exchanges.answer: Lilly believes retatrutide is a biologic application (amino acid count rule, analogous to a protein). The first court decision was mixed and litigation is active; Lilly hopes to reach a conclusion with the FDA supporting a BLA. Lilly has the clinical data needed but must gather a little more on CMC, is in communication with the agency, and expects to submit by Q1 next year. The question about subsequent incretins was not addressed.

exchanges.question: What are the learnings and surprises from the Medicare obesity (Bridge) rollout, the ramp curve, and orals versus injectables?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Early days but a significant inflection over the last few weeks for both ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO. Prior authorization and approval process is working well, criteria are clear, and LillyDirect can fulfil Bridge. Roughly 80% of people getting treatment are on injectables, and about 60%-70% are new people who had no prior access.

exchanges.question: Do you need a commercial strategy to protect against retatrutide that is apparently available today, or will formal approval solve that? Does retatrutide's higher efficacy open indications beyond those of tirzepatide?
exchanges.answer: On the commercial point, people await authentic retatrutide and will vote with their feet once it is on the market; no specific strategy was described. On development, high-dose weight loss opens more opportunities: knee osteoarthritis pain reduced by 75% (TRIUMPH-4 and TRIUMPH-1), an ongoing MASH/MASLD study, additional indications under internal evaluation, and a chronic lower back pain study reading out sometime next year.

exchanges.question: What is the post-Verzenio strategy in breast cancer, given the SERD and oral PI3K, and is an all-oral combination on the table?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: Lilly believes it has the best medicines for the three key targets (estrogen receptor, CDK4/6, PI3K alpha) and plans to combine them. INLURIYO (imlunestrant) has EMBER-4 in adjuvant reading out next year. The phase III program for tersolisib (PI3K inhibitor) is about to begin, initially with existing endocrine therapies and over time combined with INLURIYO, with investigators' choice of CDK4/6, largely Verzenio. Lilly is excited about an all-oral combination down the road.

exchanges.question: Guidance appears to imply a revenue deceleration in the back half versus Q2 despite Bridge and Foundayo access ramping. Is something missing on price, or is the guide conservative?
exchanges.answer: The guide was upgraded by $2.5 billion. Q2 and recent quarters included one-off prior-period adjustments to US rebate and discount estimates that are not expected to continue in H2. The 2025 base had a bolus of MOUNJARO launches in new countries in H2, which will not repeat, and growth is expected to be more driven by OUS penetration; dollar growth is still expected to be significant. Q3 Europe holiday seasonality and Q4 US Type 2 diabetes seasonality are factored in. He did not say whether the guide is conservative.

exchanges.question: Which regions are driving the strongest OUS growth, and what is being seen in India with generic semaglutide launching and capacity constraints?
exchanges.answer: MOUNJARO is performing very strongly nearly everywhere; China NRDL gave category leadership after 16 months, with significant growth in Korea, the UK, Mexico and Germany, and share in many markets similar to or above the US. In India and Brazil, MOUNJARO TRx continue to grow after generic semaglutide launched, in Canada tirzepatide TRx grow at the pace of the total market, and generic companies face significant supply constraints that Lilly will monitor.

exchanges.question: How extensive is the Foundayo sampling program and is it dampening IQVIA prescription data? Can you quantify the expansion in the US prescriber base?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Lilly is using every promotional lever; sampling covers the first 30 days of the first dose, similar to a typical oral small molecule, extensively across prescribers, with full supply. Prescribers rose from 8,000 at the last earnings call to 36,000 now. He did not address whether sampling depresses IQVIA data.

exchanges.question: Net price per obesity prescription looks well above cash and other benchmarks. How sustainable is that, with medical exceptions and CVS back on formulary, and is it what drives favourable rebate adjustments each quarter?
exchanges.answer: Channel prices are transparent: LillyDirect $299 to $449, Bridge $245, plus commercial. Medical exception and script size are drivers; CVS access, starting in Q4, removes the need for medical exceptions, which he called a short-term thing. He expects price to go down, this is embedded in the guide and reset expectations, and volume growth will more than offset it. No net price figure was given.

exchanges.question: Are psychiatry and vaccines areas Lilly can scale and are they high priority, or are the assets one-offs driven by the science?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: Both areas share immense unmet need, which is the through line of internal and BD work; the deals were struck at prices allowing discipline and long-term value creation, and are not that different from other deals this year. He declined to forward look on building more in infectious disease and psychiatry because Lilly will be opportunistic.

exchanges.question: Which one or two pipeline assets outside obesity should the street pay more attention to?
exchanges.answer: Cardiovascular: PCSK9 gene editing and oral and injectable Lp(a) drugs. Neuroscience: psychiatry expansion, sleep-wake disorders with Centessa, and addiction and major depressive disorder possibly addressable with incretin science. Oncology: probably the richest period of readouts ever, including Kelonia in vivo CAR T for multiple myeloma and AJ1-11095. Immunology: progress with the drug (transcript says empagliflozin) and combination ideas in IBD and psoriatic disease. Without incretins the pipeline would still be strong and large.

exchanges.question: UAE Foundayo sales of $31 million were close to half of the $67 million in the US; what is the ex-US obesity potential, and will Foundayo be better reimbursed than tirzepatide for diabetes ex-US?
exchanges.answer: Encouraged by the UAE start but very early days with a lot of noise and an initial inventory build. Most patients are naive to incretins and there is a need for an oral in obesity and Type 2 diabetes; the major OUS rollout and launches happen at the beginning of 2027. Lilly is probably slightly better positioned with an oral for Type 2 reimbursement given three head-to-head trials, but OUS reimbursement takes time and the focus at launch will be chronic weight management.

summary.overview: Chipotle's fiscal Q2 2026 revenue rose 9.3% to $3.3B, with comparable restaurant sales up 2.2% including a 1% transaction comp, versus 0.5% in Q1. Restaurant level margin was 25.2%, down 220bp, and adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat y/y. Adam Rymer, CFO, guided full-year comps to the low single digits and Q3 comps to around plus 1%, assuming a roughly 200bp Cyclospora-related softness persists.
keyTakeaways: Adam Rymer, CFO, said traffic improved through Q2 and into early July, then softened by about 200bp in the second half of July around the industry Cyclospora issue.
Scott Boatwright, CEO, said Chipotle is not involved in the Cyclospora conversation and is affected on sales only, since the implicated products are not on the menu.
Boatwright said HEAP gives two to four hours of labor efficiency, will be in 2,000 restaurants by year-end, and should cover the whole portfolio sometime in 2027.
Boatwright said the affordability scores were better in Q2 than in probably the past couple of years, and the younger and lower-income cohorts improved the most, per Rymer.
Boatwright said a frictionless in-restaurant rewards pilot begins in August, since only about 20% of in-restaurant transactions scan versus nearly 90% of digital.
financialHighlights: Revenue was $3.3B, up 9.3%, with comparable restaurant sales up 2.2% and pricing impact of about 1.6%.
Restaurant level margin was 25.2%, down 220bp y/y, with cost of sales at 29.7% (up about 80bp), labor at 25.0% (up about 30bp) and other operating costs at 14.9% (up about 90bp).
Digital sales were $1.3B, or 38.3% of sales versus 35.5% a year ago.
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat y/y, with non-GAAP G&A of $176M.
Chipotle repurchased $631M of stock at an average $32.55, ended with $800M of cash, restricted cash and investments and no debt, and had $1.7B of authorization remaining after an additional $1.3B.

Rymer guided Q3 menu pricing to the mid 2% range and full-year pricing to the high end of 1%-2%, with price matching inflation from Q4.
Rymer guided Q3 cost of sales to just under 30%, labor to the mid 25% range, other operating costs to the mid 15% range and marketing to the low 3% range.

qa.question: More color on the low-single-digit comp guide, including Q3 and the recent softening.
qa.answer: Rymer said Q2 traffic improved through the quarter and into the first half of July, then softened by about 200bp in the second half of July. He said Q3 is the toughest lap and comps are expected around plus 1% if the impact continues. Scott Boatwright, CEO, said Chipotle is not involved in the Cyclospora conversation.

qa.question: Where does confidence in momentum into 2027 come from, given tough comparisons, a recent slowdown and 1%-2% comps?
qa.answer: Boatwright said Q2 transaction growth was early days of Recipe for Growth, with proof points in guest satisfaction, food quality and operational consistency. He said menu innovation, rewards engagement, brand communication and group occasions will build through H2 2026 and into 2027.
qa.read: Answered partially: no quantified evidence for 2027.

qa.question: Has the incremental capex and sales uplift from the restaurant remodel or refresh program been sized?
qa.answer: Boatwright said Chipotle has never done an aesthetic remodel and is stage-gating a refresh at several locations at roughly $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant. He said he has nothing to report yet.
qa.read: Answered partially: gave the cost range but no results.

qa.question: With a new CMO, how will the brand be positioned given For Real has gone stale, and will value be highlighted more?
qa.answer: Boatwright said the new work is the next evolution of For Real, with more on fresh preparation and ingredients, and value framed as extraordinary value from best ingredients, not price points or discounts. First elements are visible later this quarter.
qa.read: Answered partially: pushed back on the stale premise and gave no specifics.

qa.question: What could be better in promoting loyalty in restaurant, and do non-loyalty transactions over-index to lower-income guests?
qa.answer: Boatwright said the non-loyalty 20% of in-store transactions are broad-based, not lower-income, and could see meaningful lift if enrolled. He said an August one-stop pay pilot will award points on payment and allow enrollment without relying on the restaurant team.

qa.question: Are the new menu items center-of-the-plate or sides, and any more detail?
qa.answer: Boatwright said the culinary team is working on center-of-the-plate items, beverage, sides and desserts. He said some big ideas could be on the calendar in the back half of 2026 but certainly in 2027.
qa.read: Answered partially: no specific items named.

exchanges.question: Does the lift from bringing LTOs back from the pantry (e.g. Chicken al Pastor) still build each time? Are there changes in value perception, and is the industry underpricing issue reflected?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle Honey Chicken performed better the second time, as do many LTOs, though there is a point of diminishing returns (perhaps the fifth or sixth time). Innovation and menu work is 4x what it was a couple of years ago. The brand tracker showed solid progress on value perception across all income groups and age cohorts, and affordability scores were better in Q2 than in probably the past couple of years; value is also convenience, execution and innovation, including the high-protein menu.

exchanges.question: Pushback is that Chipotle is doing and spending a lot for 1%-2% comps; where does confidence in momentum into 2027 come from, given tough comparisons and a recent slowdown, with guidance raised to low single digits?
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth was early days of Recipe for Growth, especially menu innovation. Early proof points in guest satisfaction, food quality and operational consistency show it is on track, and additional drivers (menu innovation, deeper rewards engagement, stronger brand communication, group occasions) are showing green shoots and will build through H2 2026 and into 2027. New digital and brand leaders have not yet had their ideas shown; no quantified evidence given.

exchanges.question: More color on the low-single-digit positive comp guide, including Q3 and the recent softening and its cadence.
exchanges.answer: Q2 traffic improved through the quarter and momentum continued into the first half of July, then softened by about 200 basis points in the second half of July, around the industry Cyclospora issue. Q3 is the toughest lap and comps are expected around plus 1%, assuming the roughly 200 basis point impact continues. Boatwright: Chipotle is not involved in the Cyclospora conversation (affected on sales only); the implicated products are not on the menu and lettuces are sourced in California.

exchanges.question: Has the incremental capex and sales uplift from the restaurant remodel/refresh program (about 1,000-1,500 stores) been sized, and have you considered partners in other international markets rather than owning and operating?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle has never done an aesthetic remodel; this year it is stage-gating a refresh program at several locations, at roughly $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant, to test returns, with nothing to report yet. For international, Alshaya (Middle East), Alsea (Latin America) and SPC (Southeast Asia) are partner-operated or JV, built slowly; Western Europe remains owned and operated and the rest of the world partner-operated.

exchanges.question: Digital sales grew 18% including unit growth; was there a catalyst that unlocked this, and is it linked to loyalty and payment at the register?
exchanges.answer: It is all linked. Last year's Summer of Extras showed where Chipotle can win in digital, informing the rewards relaunch a couple of months ago (less app friction, more flexible earning and redemption); this year's Summer of Extras and an emerging trend add to it. Arlie Sisson is taking a holistic approach to digital and there is more work to do.

exchanges.question: Will HEAP labor efficiency be reinvested into labor on the production line, and could it drive traffic and customer satisfaction?
exchanges.answer: Yes. HEAP gives about two to four hours of efficiency depending on volume, left in the restaurant to get prep done in the morning and deploy labor on the line during peak, which shows up in transactions, Max 15 throughput, total sales and better taste scores. HEAP will be in 2,000 restaurants by year-end and hopes to cover the whole portfolio sometime in 2027; all new restaurants come with HEAP standard.

exchanges.question: Why is 350 company-operated openings per year the right level versus the prior ceiling of 400, and what is the gating factor to accelerating beyond 350?
exchanges.answer: Given US white space and the ability to develop ready-now leaders, one restaurant per day is meaningful growth; beyond 350 there may be diminishing returns or risk to fracture the base, and the team is comfortable with 350. Incremental growth comes from company-owned Western Europe and partner-operated markets, which ramp quickly: the Middle East partnership with Alshaya began a couple of years ago and is already at 15 restaurants across three or four countries, with meaningful acceleration in 2027.

exchanges.question: With a new CMO, how will the brand be positioned, given the For Real campaign has gone stale; will value and ingredient quality be highlighted more?
exchanges.answer: For Real was extraordinary and served the company for many years; Fernando Machado's work is the next evolution rather than a 180 pivot. Expect more on fresh in-restaurant preparation, ingredients and the brand's opportunity to cultivate a better world, with creative ambition to break through. Value will be highlighted as extraordinary value from best ingredients, fresh, in abundance, at speed and an approachable price point, not price points or discounts.

exchanges.question: Is the Q3 comp guide of about 1% an underlying trend of about 3% less a sustained roughly 200 basis point Cyclospora headwind? And where is Max 15 throughput system-wide excluding HEAP?
exchanges.answer: Yes, the 1% guide (and expense guidance) assumes the impact continues through the rest of the quarter, and it is very difficult to predict how long it lasts. HEAP restaurants do two or three more entrees in Max 15; overall in-store is in the low 20 range, digital (almost 40% of sales) mid-teen, and combined low to mid-30s per restaurant per day.

exchanges.question: What is working and what could be better in promoting loyalty in restaurant, and do the in-store transactions without loyalty over-index to lower-income guests?
exchanges.answer: No, the non-loyalty 20% of in-store transactions are more broad-based and could see meaningful lift if enrolled. Today's process (phone, loyalty app, card) is clunky; in August a one-stop pay pilot will award rewards points on payment and allow enrollment, without relying on the restaurant team so throughput is not hurt. More work remains to educate consumers in restaurant.

exchanges.question: Are the new menu items coming in the months ahead center-of-the-plate or sides, and any more detail?
exchanges.answer: The expanded culinary team is working on real new news, not just pantry items: center-of-the-plate items, beverage, sides and desserts. Some big ideas have been stage-gated and could be on the calendar in the back half of 2026, but certainly in 2027. No specific items named.

exchanges.question: Update on Q2 and Q3-to-date trends by age and income, particularly the younger and lower-to-middle-income cohorts, and frequency differences.
exchanges.answer: Rymer: the younger and lower-income cohorts, previously most pressured, have improved the most, with broad-based trends from Q1 into Q2 driven by menu innovation (Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce), promotions (Matchday BOGO) and rewards. Boatwright: highest year-over-year gains in wallet share last quarter since 2024, with share taken in each month of 2026 across all income cohorts and age groups. No Q3-to-date cohort data was given.

exchanges.question: How is the margin outlook beyond Q3, given last quarter's comment on the gap between pricing and inflation narrowing near year end?
exchanges.answer: The gap between price and inflation was widest in H1 (pricing around 1% versus inflation low to mid 3%) and is easing in H2 with the rolling pricing approach. In Q3, inflation is expected closer to 3% and pricing in the mid 2% range, and from Q4 forward the two should match.

exchanges.question: Did the World Cup create regional divergences or a benefit? And what has been learned from the rolling pricing approach that gives comfort to land at the high end of the 1%-2% range?
exchanges.answer: World Cup impact was very small: about 300 restaurants within roughly 10 miles of stadiums saw a 50 to 100 basis point comp benefit during the tournament, but the impact on the overall quarter was less than five basis points. Rolling market-by-market pricing measures resistance precisely and adjusts for inflation; the earlier dislocation was just timing and the approach will continue.

exchanges.question: How much do LTOs contribute to frequency uplift, and do high-protein LTOs attract new guests or existing guests?
exchanges.answer: Rymer: no LTO-specific figures, but Honey Chicken and Chicken al Pastor raise transactions, from most frequent guests coming more often and new guests; typically hundreds of basis points of transaction lift, mostly sustained through the promotion, with stickiness after; a multi-year AUV lever. Boatwright: protein LTOs bring in new customers and raise lifetime value; expect a couple more center-of-the-plate items in H2, sides innovation and a bigger push into beverage.

qa.question: Accident  year loss ratio improved from Q2 2025 unlike many other commercial insurers. What drove that improvement—was it lower non-cat property losses, changes in loss picks, or other factors?
qa.answer: Losses came in below expectations as they have for several quarters, reflecting normal variability and business mix. Loss ratio is composite of a dozen statutory lines. Reserves are as conservative as company history. On commissions: second quarter provides good indication of forward trajectory; slight uptick in commission rate expected going forward; AI activities may provide efficiency gains on operating side; second quarter expense ratio should be good measure going forward.

qa.question: Given E&S casualty softening and GWP up only 3% versus 4% in Q1, how much are ROEs compressing given your mid-to-high single digit loss trend views? How are you thinking about broker commissions going forward?
qa.answer: Management ROE target is 20% or greater; most product lines running ahead of that; company annualized 24.4% for quarter. On commissions: brokers critical to success and seeking to maximize economics; tension between wholesalers and retail clients on commission split; soft market rate declines pressure all parties. Kinsale offers best customer service in industry with strongest quote ratio and response time, plus broadest risk appetite. Outside Commercial Property, business growing  well.

qa.question: How much of the increase in inbound accounts comes from broker engagement versus competitive pricing? What is current view on social inflation and casualty loss trend landscape?
qa.answer: Increase in inbound accounts from both broker engagement and pricing; idle broker initiative reengaging brokers, hit ratios staying roughly same. Confidence in business model despite slower growth in Commercial Property. Casualty loss cost trends mid-single digits varying by line; company less exposed to social inflation due to smaller accounts and lower limits; short tail lines performing especially well. Company being conservative  releasing IBNR in longer tail occurrence business.

qa.question: What granularity on property pricing Q2 versus Q1? When can property pricing stabilize? Given mix shift from property to casualty, should accident year loss ratio drift up or is current level sustainable?
qa.answer: Eventually reach equilibrium; catastrophe losses intermittent and unpredictable but do happen; disciplined pricing and risk management protocol essential. Specialized property areas like Agribusiness seeing growth; small business property more stable than large shared deals; some competition in Inland Marine; people reaching floor on property pricing with pressure from London.  Accident year loss ratio hard to predict; could drift up; losses coming below expectations; feel good about loss ratio bookings and very good about IBNR reserve conservatism as positive for future performance.

qa.question: How have new products and enhancements contributed to growth, and what is potential uplift going forward?
qa.answer: Never want to jump in feet first and grow like weed; always crawl, walk, run pace. New products creating growth, driving submissions and new premium. Growth will be slow, ramping up as market turns.

summary.overview: Kinsale's fiscal Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS was $5.54, up 15.9% from $4.78, with annualized operating ROE of 24.4% and a combined ratio of 75.5%. Gross written premium fell 5% and was up 3.7% excluding the Commercial Property Division, while net earned premium rose 8.9%. Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, announced an additional $250 million buyback authorization and described a Commercial Property market where Kinsale is writing shrinking volume.
keyTakeaways: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, said Commercial Property is a buyer's market and Kinsale is writing a shrinking volume of business there.

Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said London MGAs and traditional markets are putting up larger limits on shared and layered property deals, and long-tail London competition is depressing Construction pricing.
Kehoe said Kinsale manages everything to a 20% ROE or greater, with Q2 operating ROE at 24.4%.

Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, said reserves are as conservative as they have ever been, with the Q2 combined ratio including 4.5 points of favorable prior year development.
Kehoe said Kinsale will keep leaning into buybacks while growth is limited, with an additional $250 million authorization bringing the total to $337 million.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS was $5.54 versus $4.78 in Q2 2025, up 15.9%, while net income rose 31.1% and net operating earnings rose 13.3%.
Combined ratio was 75.5%, including 4.5 points of favorable prior year reserve development (3.9 last year) and 1.3 points of cat losses.
Expense ratio was 21.7% versus 20.7% in Q2 2025, with the other underwriting expense ratio at 10.3% versus 10.6%.
Net investment income rose 19.9%, and float was $3.4B versus $3.1B at the end of 2025.
Net written premium fell 1.4% while net earned premium rose 8.9%; new business submissions rose 6%, or 8% excluding Commercial Property.
guidance: Kehoe said Commercial Property Division y/y comparisons should be modestly easier in Q3 and Q4, because 60% of its premium was written in the first half of last year.
Kehoe announced an additional $250 million buyback authorization, bringing the current authorization to $337 million.
Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said a slight uptick in ceding commissions is possible after the June 1 treaty renewals, and the Q2 expense ratio should be a good measure going forward.
Allibhai said the current accident year loss ratio could drift up over time given the mix shift, although losses are currently below expectations.
Winston said nine new products or enhancements have rolled out this year, five more launch imminently and another 10 are in the pipeline.

Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said treaties renewed June 1 so only one month of new-treaty effect is in Q2, a slight uptick in commissions is possible, and Q2 is a good indicator going forward.

qa.answer: Kehoe said Kinsale manages everything to a 20% ROE or greater, most lines probably run ahead of that, and Q2 operating ROE was 24.4%. He gave no commission plan and called the wholesaler-retailer commission split a normal tension in a soft market.
qa.read: Answered partially: ROE answered, commissions not.

qa.question: Is Q2 the trough in Commercial Property, and what is driving the 3.7% growth ex Commercial Property?
qa.answer: Winston said there is no telling where it goes in 2027, pressure continues from London MGAs, and Kinsale will keep pricing tactical and accept shrinking in that division. He said London long-tail competition is creeping into other liability occurrence lines, and some flow to the admitted market is not pervasive.
qa.read: Answered partially: declined to call a trough.

qa.question: How much of the increase in inbound accounts is broker engagement versus pricing, and what is the view on casualty loss trends?
qa.answer: Winston said it is a bit of both, with the idle broker initiative re-engaging brokers. Allibhai said casualty loss cost trend is probably mid-single digits, and Kehoe said Kinsale is slowing IBNR release in longer-tail occurrence business while letting it flow out faster in short-tail lines.

qa.question: When might property pricing stabilize, could the accident year loss ratio drift up, and how will buyback pacing look?

Allibhai: the loss ratio could drift up over time, but losses are below expectations. Kehoe on buyback: will keep leaning in; first $100 million authorization exhausted, then $250 million with about $80 million left, plus the new $250 million; growth would be the first priority when it accelerates; small dividend also paid.

exchanges.question: How have new products contributed to growth over the past year, and what is the potential growth uplift going forward?
exchanges.answer: Winston: Kinsale does not jump in feet first; the pace is crawl, walk, run. New products are driving submissions and new premium, but growth will be slow, and Kinsale will ramp up as the market turns. No quantification of past contribution or future uplift was given.

qa.question: How is Deere thinking about production versus retail by region for 2027? Given early order programs up mid-single digit, what are pricing expectations for 2027 given inflationary cost concerns?
qa.answer: Modest underproduction planned for PPA and C&F, couple percentage points  each; production plans set for full year. South America caution drives underproduction. C&F underproduction reflects continuous growth pace and four-to-five-month order position. EOP pricing rolled out to cover inflation across portfolio; focus remains on inflation coverage across PPA products as rolling toward 2027.

qa.question: Tariff expense down to $1.1 billion from $1.2 billion expected—is this due to Ag Equipment tariff relief in July or refunds? Can you explain what drove the change? Any updates on excavator launch timing and broader adoption outlook?
qa.answer: $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion driven by Section 232 tariff changes—imported goods rate dropped from  25% to 15%, effective June 1, driving five months of impact for FY 2026. Expect tailwind for FY 2027. Excavator launch occurred spring with three models now in market; positive customer feedback so far; full portfolio to roll out spring through next three-to-four years, early days with very positive reception.

qa.question: Did inventory or shipment demand slip between Q3 and Q4? Inventory-to-sales ratios show tractor inventory built in Q3. Is South America demand offset driving caution? Help understand cadence exiting year.
qa.answer: Nothing to be concerned about on inventory; shipment plans largely set for year with orders on hand. Pulled ahead  some demand in Q3 to manage risk in Q4. Factories hitting forecasts; retail pace continuing historical averages with expectations to move inventory. PPA and C&F expect similar net sales Q4 as Q3, but margins down due to no refund benefit and seasonal R&D/SA&G hits in Q4.

qa.question: Unpack early order program comments. What variability by region? Mid-single digit growth could wind up high single digits. Comment on moving pieces?
qa.answer: U.S. trending slightly better than Canada. Customers continue wanting latest technologies in planting/spraying. Best signals are mid-single digit increases in orders and doubling of See & Spray on factory sprayers and 40% of planters taking advanced technology. Confidence heading in right direction as  customers maximize everything going into 2027.

qa.question: Given EOP open for a while, what drove mid-single digit cadence of orders? Recent grain price improvement or technology decision factors?
qa.answer: Cadence as expected; made tweaks to EOP this year for dealer choice. Pleasantly surprised by tech take rates; hopeful mid-single digit increase extends through year.

qa.question: Comments on 8 Series Tractor orders aligning with EOP? Europe experiencing heat stress and input costs—how diverse are reactions? Will Europe react similarly to U.S. if crop price  response?
qa.answer: 8R orders as expected; four-to-five months out, MY2026 basically closed. Encouraged by recent commodity price changes; corn futures at $5.05 good signal for growers. Brazil three-month order book changed industry guide per circumstances. Too early for 2027. Move financing at single-digit rates hopefully drives momentum. Europe mixed: solid Small Ag & Turf but PPA exposed; arable challenged; Small Ag & Turf benefiting from dairy/livestock cash flows stable.

summary.overview: Deere's fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues rose 5% to $12.608B, with equipment operations net sales up 6% to $10.999B at a 14.4% operating margin and net income of $1.379B, or $5.10 per diluted share. Dan Pooley, Manager, Investor Communications, raised FY2026 net income guidance to $4.75B-$5B and equipment operations cash flow to $5B-$5.5B. Brent Norwood, CFO, said 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle, and Deanna Kovar said MY2027 planter and sprayer early orders are up mid-single digits.
keyTakeaways: Brent Norwood, CFO, said Deere continues to believe 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle, with Deanna Kovar, President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, expecting a measured recovery rather than a sharp rebound in 2027.

Kovar said MY2027 planter and sprayer early orders are up mid-single digits versus last year's completed programs, with See & Spray factory-installed orders doubling and 40% of planters taking the most advanced technologies.

Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, said FY2026 direct tariff expense falls to about $1.1B from $1.2B excluding refunds, mainly on Section 232 changes cutting the rate on imported goods from roughly 25% to 15%.
Norwood said net tariffs will be a headwind in 2027, with a run rate closer to around $1B versus roughly $750M net this year.
Seibert said Construction & Forestry has four to five months of orders on hand versus the typical two to three, driven by infrastructure, data center starts and rental channels.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues were $12.608B, up 5%, with equipment operations net sales of $10.999B, up 6%, and a 14.4% operating margin.
Net income attributable to Deere was $1.379B, or $5.10 per diluted share, with $110M of incremental tariff refunds recognized in Q3 and $382M year to date.
Production & Precision Ag net sales fell 6% to $3.998B with a 13.2% operating margin, while Small Ag & Turf rose 12% to $3.383B at 18.4%.
Construction & Forestry net sales rose 18% to $3.618B at a 12.1% operating margin, with price up 8 points.
Financial Services net income was $219M.
guidance: Pooley guided FY2026 net income to $4.75B-$5B and equipment operations operating cash flow to $5B-$5.5B, with Financial Services net income of $870M.

Pooley guided Production & Precision Ag net sales down approximately 10% with an 11%-12% margin, Small Ag & Turf up approximately 15% with a 14.5%-15.5% margin, and Construction & Forestry up approximately 20% with a 10.5%-11.5% margin.
Pooley guided U.S. and Canada large ag industry sales down 15%-20%, South America down 15%-20%, Europe approximately flat, and U.S. and Canada construction equipment up 5%-10%.

Norwood expects Q4 net sales for Production & Precision Ag and Construction & Forestry similar to Q3, with no refund benefit and margins for PPA and Small Ag & Turf a little lower on seasonally higher R&D and SA&G.
Seibert said direct tariff expense is approximately $1.1B excluding refunds, with no further refunds assumed in the outlook.

qa.question: With roughly $800M of net tariff impact this year, is net tariff impact a headwind, tailwind or neutral for 2027?
qa.answer: Norwood said net tariffs will be a headwind next year: about $1.1B of direct tariffs less $382M of refunds is roughly $750M net this year, and the 2027 run rate is closer to around $1B. He said there will be a bit of a step up in tariff expense versus this year.

qa.question: How could mix, including higher technology take rates, affect 2027 compared with the 2- to 3-point mix benefit discussed in prior years?
qa.answer: Seibert said it is too early to tell, especially in South America where things can turn quickly, citing input and commodity volatility, Black Sea disruptions and softness in the E.U. and Brazil. He said early order program signals will drive mix depending on how they wrap up.

qa.question: What regional variability is behind the early order program, and could mid-single-digit growth end up high single digits?
qa.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Ag & Turf, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
qa.answer: Kovar said the programs are still open with a couple of weeks left on sprayers and a little longer on planters, and the U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada. She said time will tell whether mid-single digits turns more positive, citing See & Spray factory orders doubling and 40% of planters taking the most advanced technologies.
qa.read: Answered partially: would not call the final range.

qa.question: Why does C&F guidance imply roughly 50bp of positive price in Q4 versus 8% in Q3, and does Deere want to grow dealer rental?
qa.answer: Seibert said Q3 price of 8% was partly easy comps, since Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives, and Q4 has nothing outsized. Norwood said 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental and dealer-owned fleets could boost inventory fill next year.
qa.read: Answered partially: did not reconcile the 50bp implied Q4 figure.

qa.question: What are the pricing expectations for 2027 given the early order program is up mid-single digits?
qa.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Ag & Turf, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
qa.answer: Kovar said early order program pricing was rolled out several months ago and the focus is covering inflation into 2027. Seibert said PPA and C&F are each modestly underproducing in 2026 by a couple of percentage points.

qa.question: Could the 2028 EU CAP policy change pull demand forward into 2027, and is there a directional forecast for Europe in 2027?
qa.answer: Seibert said it is too early to tell, order books run four to five months out and Q1 orders are just starting. He gave no pull-forward view and no 2027 forecast.

exchanges.answer: Seibert: PPA and C&F are both modestly underproducing in 2026, call it a couple of percentage points each; shipping plans are set for the full year, South America drives more caution, and C&F orders are four to five months out. Kovar: EOP pricing was rolled out several months ago and the focus remains on covering inflation across EOP products and the PPA portfolio into 2027. No specific 2027 price percentage given.

exchanges.question: What drove the tariff expectation falling to $1.1 billion, roughly $100 million lower than previously expected: July tariff relief or expected refunds? Also, how is the Deere-designed excavator launch trending and when does broader adoption come?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: the FY2026 annual run rate moves from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion excluding refunds, mainly from Section 232 changes cutting the rate on imported goods from roughly 25% to 15%, especially for European imports; effective 1st June, so only five of 12 months are in this year, and 2027 gets a further tailwind. Norwood: first Deere-designed excavator models launched earlier this spring, three models in the market, feedback very positive, more models rolling out over the next three to four years, early days.

exchanges.question: Did anything slip or pull forward between 3Q and 4Q, given tractor inventory-to-sales appears to have built in 3Q ahead of the industry? What is the cadence exiting the year?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: do not read too much into Q3; shipment plans were set for the year and some demand was pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk, with nothing to be concerned about on inventory. Kovar: factories are hitting forecasts and sold-ahead positions and retail pace in the Americas are on trend with historical averages. Norwood: Q4 net sales similar to Q3 for PPA and C&F; no refund benefit in Q4; PPA and SAT margins come in a little because of seasonally higher R&D and SA&G in Q4.

exchanges.question: How could mix, including higher technology take rates in C&F and precision ag early orders, affect 2027, compared with the 2- to 3-point mix benefit discussed in prior years?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: the industry environment is still uncertain (input and commodity volatility, Black Sea shipment disruptions, softness in the E.U. and Brazil), and it is too early to tell on mix, especially in South America where things can turn quickly. C&F fundamentals are good, EOP signals including tech adoption will drive mix depending on how they wrap up, and management is encouraged. No mix point figure given.

exchanges.question: What variability by region is behind the early order program, which came in better than expected, and could the mid-single-digit growth wind up in the high single-digit range as the programs close?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Ag & Turf, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
exchanges.answer: Kovar: the programs are still open with a couple of weeks left on sprayers and a little longer on planters; the U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada (a very limited part of planter portfolio); time will tell whether mid-single digits turns more positive. The best signal is technology take rates, with See & Spray factory-installed orders doubling and 40% of planters taking the most advanced technologies.

exchanges.question: What is driving the cadence of early order programs being up mid-single digit: improved grain prices, or technology decisions?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Ag & Turf, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
exchanges.answer: Kovar: would not read much into cadence, which has been as expected; tweaks were made to the early order program this year to give dealers more choice; pleasantly surprised by technology take rates; hopeful the mid-single-digit increase extends well into the year.

exchanges.question: What are 8 Series tractor orders showing in North America? How should Europe be viewed given heat and input cost stress, and would it react like the U.S. to a crop price response?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: 8R orders are as expected, orders run four to five months out and the model year 2026 shipment schedule is basically closed; encouraged by commodity prices, with corn futures about $5.05. In Brazil Deere takes a three-month order book, has Q4 orders on hand and has changed its industry guide; it is too early to tell for 2027, and the financing program at single-digit rates may help. Europe is mixed: arable farmers more challenged, Small Ag & Turf supported by dairy and livestock cash flows; overall order pace as expected with no step-up in the last day or two.

exchanges.question: How are the C&F order programs shaping up, and how much is dealer rental fleet loading?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: C&F order trends are very positive, with about four to five months of orders on hand versus the typical two to three months, which is a little more than wanted. Drivers are large infrastructure projects, data center starts, the independent rental channel and dealer-owned rental fleets; modest underproduction in 2026 sets up an opportunity in 2027. No split of rental fleet loading was quantified.

exchanges.question: Comparing 2026 and 2027, with roughly an $800 million net tariff impact this year, is net tariff impact a headwind, tailwind or neutral for 2027?
exchanges.answer: Norwood: net tariffs will be a headwind next year. About $1.1 billion of direct tariffs this year less $382 million of refunds is approximately $750-ish of net exposure; 2027 run rate is closer to right around $1 billion, so a step up in tariff expense versus this year.

exchanges.question: Why does C&F guidance imply roughly 50 basis points of positive price in Q4 versus +8% in Q3? Does Deere want to grow dealer rental, and how would that change the economics?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: the C&F price guide went 2.5%, 3%, 2.5% and is now back at the full-year guide; Q3 was 8% partly on easy comps, since Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives; Q4 has nothing outsized and pricing is going well. Norwood: sees opportunity to increase rental exposure; 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental; dealer-owned fleets are growing and could help boost inventory fill next year.

exchanges.question: On EOP pricing covering inflation, what about merchandising incentives and the direction of margins into next year? What does the FTC settlement on right to repair mean for the aftermarket and lifecycle solutions business?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: taking measured inflationary price, committed to cover inflation over time, nothing outsized; pricing is set at several points in the year; suppliers pass on tariffs and oil moves. No comment on incentives or directional margin backlog. Norwood: Deere has always supported customers repairing their own equipment, the agreement formalizes tools like Operations Center PRO Service (diagnostics, digital manuals, software updates), and it will support lifecycle solutions long term; no figure given.

exchanges.question: Could the 2028 EU CAP policy change pull demand forward into 2027 or delay European purchases? Any directional forecast for Europe in 2027?
exchanges.answer: Seibert: too early to tell. Order books run four to five months out and Q1 orders are just starting; arable sentiment depends on input costs and commodity prices; dairy and livestock look fairly stable. No pull-forward or delay view and no 2027 forecast.

exchanges.question: How are Brazilian and U.S. farmers positioning on input costs and how will that affect crop and purchase decisions?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Ag & Turf, PPA, Sales and Marketing, Americas and Australia
exchanges.answer: Kovar: input uncertainty is global and fertilizer affects Brazilian and U.S. farmers differently; farmers are looking for alternatives in products, amounts and sourcing, remain resilient, and are not cutting intended application much, still focused on yield. Larger farmers have multiple years of inputs contracted and are considering changes.

summary.overview: Apple posted fiscal Q3 2026 revenue of $109.4B, up 16% YoY, led by iPhone (+22%) and Mac (+29%), while Services slowed to 12% from 16%. Kevan Parekh, CFO, guided September-quarter growth to 9%-11%, citing FX and worsening advanced-node SoC supply constraints, and memory costs more than explained the gross margin decline.
keyTakeaways: Tim Cook, CEO, blamed SoC supply constraints on a demand forecast miss and said Apple will be "scrambling" on supply this quarter.
Parekh said a ~2.5 point FX headwind plus a significant sequential rise in supply constraints explain the ~500bp guided deceleration.
Cook said Apple "reluctantly" raised iPad and Mac prices on memory costs and that it is too early to judge elasticity.
Siri AI cannot yet launch on EU iPhone and iPad, and China has approved only original Apple Intelligence features, per Cook.
financialHighlights: Revenue was $109.4B (+16%), with Products $78.7B (+18%), Services $30.7B (+12%) and iPad down 6% to $6.2B.
Gross margin was 50.1% including a ~2 point tariff refund benefit, or 48.1% ex-refund versus 49.3% in March.
Diluted EPS rose 29% to $2.02, including $0.11 from tariff refunds, while operating expenses rose 23% to $19.1B on R&D.
Operating cash flow was $34.4B and shareholder returns were $33B, including $25.8B of buybacks.
guidance: Kevan Parekh, CFO, guided September-quarter revenue growth of 9%-11%, with iPhone up mid-teens, and gave nothing beyond September.
Parekh expects Services growth similar to June's 12% after removing a ~2.5 point negative FX impact.
Parekh guided gross margin of 47%-48% including ~1 point of tariff refunds (46.5% ex-refund), opex of $19.1B-$19.4B and a ~16.5% tax rate.
Tim Cook, CEO, expects memory costs to rise further in September, with the carry-in inventory offset shrinking afterward.

qa.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter, and could Apple broaden silicon suppliers?
qa.answer: Cook said the cause is a demand forecast miss, not a supplier issue, citing over 100 million components from Arizona this year; Kevan Parekh, CFO, gave no color beyond September.
qa.read: Declined to quantify; pushed back on the supplier premise.

qa.question: Does pricing protect gross profit dollars or margin, and why did Services slow to 12%?
qa.answer: Parekh named FX as the main driver, plus the year-ago F1 release, mobile gaming softness and the U.S. link-out ruling, with FX a ~5 point Services headwind from March to September; Tim Cook, CEO, said pricing weighs units, revenue and margin long term.

qa.question: What drives the gross margin walk to the ~46.5% ex-refund midpoint, and where is Siri AI in China and Europe?
qa.answer: Parekh said memory more than explains both the 120bp fall to 48.1% and the 160bp step to 46.5%, with FX minimal; Tim Cook, CEO, said Siri AI is or will be on Mac in the EU but not iPhone or iPad.

qa.question: Has demand been pulled forward ahead of memory-driven price increases?
qa.answer: Cook said pull-forward is not obvious given iPhone's 22% year-to-date growth, and elasticity on iPad and Mac price increases will be clearer in the weeks ahead.

unanswered.how: Kevan Parekh, CFO, said Apple is "not providing any color" beyond September.

unanswered.how: Tim Cook, CEO, called the cost balance uncertain; John Ternus, Incoming CEO, did not comment on competitors.

unanswered.how: Tim Cook, CEO, said uptake remains to be seen, with no figures.
