summary.overview: JPMorgan earned $16.9B, or $6.14 per share, with a 23% ROTCE, on revenue up 15% year-on-year excluding significant items, led by CIB revenue of $24.9B (+27%), investment banking fees up 30% and equities revenue up 86%. Jeremy Barnum, CFO, raised full-year NII ex-Markets guidance to about $96.5B from $95B and adjusted expense to about $107.5B from $105B. Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said the environment is "getting close to as good as it gets".
keyTakeaways: Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said naming Doug and Troy co-presidents and Marianne Lake's retirement left his succession timetable unchanged at "several years or a few years, plus or minus".
Jeremy Barnum, CFO, tied the $2.5B expense raise to a $6.5B first-half capital markets beat, with $1.5B of expense booked and about $1B implied for the second half.
Barnum called the equities drivers (major IPOs, index rebalancing, Korean market dynamics) statistically improbable to repeat and said investment banking saw some pull-forward.
Barnum said the roughly $40B of excess capital will now be deployed over time at a 17% return target; Dimon called his earlier $20B buyback remark a mistake.
financialHighlights: Net income $16.9B, EPS $6.14 and ROTCE 23%, including significant items; expenses $27.3B, up 15%.
Credit costs $2.5B ($2.4B net charge-offs, $149M reserve build); CET1 14.1%, down 20 bps on about $103B of RWA growth.
CCB net income $5.3B on revenue of $20.3B (+8%); CIB net income $9.7B on revenue of $24.9B (+27%).
AWM net income $2B on revenue of $6.9B (+19%), with $50B of long-term net inflows and AUM of $5.1T (+18%).
guidance: Jeremy Barnum, CFO, raised NII ex-Markets to about $96.5B from $95B on deposit balances and mix; total NII about $105.5B with markets NII about $9B, including roughly $150M shifted by the CIB equity allocation.
Barnum raised adjusted expense to about $107.5B from $105B, mostly volume and revenue-related.
Barnum lowered the card net charge-off rate to about 3.2% from 3.4%; the board intends to raise the dividend to $1.65 in the third quarter.
Barnum kept consumer deposit growth at low single digits and the 15% retail share aspiration; Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO, said expense growth might slow in 2027 or 2028.
risksMentioned: Barnum said the equities combination is hard to imagine repeating and investment banking had pull-forward.
Barnum does not know when deposit rate-paid convexity kicks in; yield-seeking flows remain a risk under a hawkish rate path.
Dimon described mild underwriting deterioration (aggressive assumptions, add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants) concentrated in some players.
Barnum said the short-term wholesale funding G-SIB change disproportionately burdens JPMorgan, and liquidity is less flush at the margin.

qa.question: What drove the NII ex-Markets revision, and why is liability-sensitive markets NII guided higher?
qa.answer: NII ex-Markets rises from $95B to $96.5B with a higher implied exit rate; deposit balances and mix are the main driver, and sensitivity is probably above the EAR as consumer betas beat the model. Markets NII rose on fewer financed non-interest-bearing assets plus roughly $150M moved in from the CIB equity allocation.

qa.question: Challenged the negative operating leverage framing given 15% revenue growth, asked why this is as good as it gets, and why Troy should run the consumer bank.
qa.answer: Dimon agreed operating leverage was positive in dollars; Barnum said the $2.5B expense raise follows a $6.5B first-half capital markets beat. Dimon said the market could get better but he does not know by how much or for how long; Troy has shown analytics, EQ and culture across markets and banking.

qa.question: How resilient is the consumer, is CapEx broadening beyond AI, and why buy back stock at three times tangible book?
qa.answer: Decent CapEx and loan growth beyond obvious AI; Dimon sized AI CapEx rising from $400B to $700B this year and a little over $1T next year; consumer spend is fine and delinquencies a little lower than expected. The $40B of excess capital will be deployed over time; Dimon said he "made a mistake last time mentioning $20 billion".

qa.question: Is the market underestimating AI efficiency, and could banks run far leaner as Block did after cutting 40% of staff?
qa.answer: Almost 1,000 use cases, about 50 really important; discrete areas have cut jobs 30%-40% with most people re-placed, and more is expected; but the benefit accrues to customers and ROE will not go to 50% and stay there.

exchanges.question: Asked Jamie to comment on the recent management changes elevating Doug and Troy to co-presidents, what it means for leadership development and for his tenure as CEO from the board's perspective. Follow-up to Jeremy: how sustainable is the far-higher-than-expected investment banking and markets activity, and how risk-on are the various businesses?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: Marianne is an exceptional leader; the board decided to appoint two co-presidents to prepare them to do far more at the company, which has not changed the timetable; when Marianne learned of the plans she chose to retire rather than stay, and there is no mystery. Jeremy bifurcated the second question: investment banking fees were fine by historical standards but not at peak, there was clearly some pull-forward and large high-profile IPOs and capital raisings contributed meaningfully, yet the pipeline is quite robust and the high-profile activity seems to be begetting more activity, though he will not guide. In markets, revenues have been elevated for some time alongside much more financial resource deployment for clients; the particular set of things that happened in equities this quarter is hard to imagine being repeated, though the backdrop is supportive. On risk-on, the market is extremely risk-on and JPMorgan is a taker of that, trying to balance supporting clients with being appropriately cautious in an environment with complicated dynamics.

exchanges.question: On the strong CCB deposit growth, how is progress toward the 15% retail deposit market share aspiration, and how might higher-for-longer rates affect the pace of share gains? Follow-up: what returns is JPMorgan getting from the branch build-out, AI investments and banker hiring, where is it in the investment cycle, and what does that mean for medium-term operating leverage?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: wholesale deposit growth was quite strong this quarter and for the first half, outperforming expectations of a fine but less strong year than last year, helped by franchise share gains and by loans creating deposits in the lending environment (BFI space, data centers). Consumer deposit expectations of low single-digit growth this year are unchanged, balancing very robust net new checking account growth against yield-seeking flows, which remain a factor and a bit of a risk given the more hawkish rate environment. There is no change to the 15% share aspiration, which he views as a natural long-term outcome of executing the strategy (primary bank relationships, branch expansion, deepening the product value proposition). Jamie: expenses are a complete continuation of what the firm has done for years and no change should be expected; Jeremy added the firm will always invest, the returns speak for themselves, and the franchise can invest aggressively for the future while delivering exceptional current returns, which would hold even at 15%, 16% or 17% returns.

exchanges.question: What drove the upward revision to NII ex-Markets, and what is the cadence through the third and fourth quarters and the exit rate into next year? Follow-up: why is markets NII guided higher when the rate outlook is also higher, given it is liability sensitive?
exchanges.answer: NII ex-Markets guidance rises from $95 billion to $96.5 billion for the full year; the implied second half suggests a higher exit run rate in the central case, assuming the yield curve follows the forwards and deposit and other drivers match current expectations. The biggest single driver is deposit balances across wholesale and consumer, both the overall quantum and a mix shift toward slightly higher margin; rates are a little higher at both the short and long end, and actual sensitivity is probably a bit more than the EAR suggests because consumer betas have outperformed the model, disproportionately in the front end, but most of the increase is balances. Markets NII is liability sensitive all else equal and would have been expected to fall on higher rates, but the forecast rose because of balance sheet composition, with lower amounts of financed non-interest-bearing assets expected in the second half, which at these rate levels can overwhelm the rate effect. Separately, the equity allocation to the CIB was increased this quarter, moving roughly $150 million of NII from NII ex-Markets into markets NII, a rare case where a markets NII change is not offset in the bottom line, though it is left pocket, right pocket for the company.

exchanges.question: What characteristics are Jamie and the board looking for in the next CEO, and should investors read Marianne's departure as an extension of Jamie's tenure, with a fixed remaining tenure or a rolling retirement date and longer stay as executive chair? Follow-up: what does no change in timing mean?
exchanges.answer: The timing is essentially the same and entirely up to the board; this is a natural change in how the firm goes about succession. The desired qualities include being good at management and people, analytical, detailed, a culture carrier, curious, with heart, grit, soul and work ethic, able to travel and to walk operating centers as well as meet CEOs and prime ministers; no one has all of them perfectly, and the firm is blessed with many culture carriers including two exceptional co-presidents, Jen Piepszak as Chief Operating Officer and Mary Erdoes continuing to run Asset & Wealth Management, across 300,000 employees, 50,000 in branches and 150,000 in operating and call centers. He is fully confident the firm would be fine if he were hit by a truck. On timing: exactly what was said last time, several years or a few years plus or minus, and totally up to the board, not him.

exchanges.question: Year-to-date adjusted operating leverage has been negative despite a strong revenue environment; with the benefits of AI and technology, is there a point over the next few years when expense growth slows and operating leverage becomes more likely? Follow-up: any update on potential adjustments to regulatory proposals such as the G-SIB surcharge and elements of Basel III?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: with great returns and margins that rose this quarter, the notion of forever increasing operating leverage is a crazy notion and part of why banks failed 20 years ago; AI will have gives and takes and cannot be projected, though there might be a slowdown in expense growth maybe in 2027 or 2028; the firm will spend more on marketing when deposit ROI justifies it, some expenses are really investments with good returns, and the ultimate beneficiary of AI will be customers in a competitive market, otherwise margins would be 80% today from 20 years of computerization. On regulation, four obvious changes: remove the double count in operational risk capital, remove the double count in market risk capital (the firm holds $80 billion or more of market risk capital versus a biggest-ever quarterly loss of $1.4 billion and a CCAR market loss of about $14 billion or $15 billion), adjust the G-SIB as intended going back to 2015, and make short-term wholesale funding treatment fair to everybody; regulators should do the numbers the right way and add conservatism explicitly, and he would happily hold 10% more capital if asked rather than have numbers falsely done. Jeremy: the short-term wholesale funding change, by removing RWA from the denominator of its contribution to the G-SIB score, disproportionately burdens banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America that combine markets, banking and consumer businesses relative to former investment bank competitors, damaging banks' ability to serve Main Street; policymakers should state that outcome if they want it rather than let it happen by accident, as laid out in the firm's comment letter.

exchanges.question: With trading, investment banking, lending and credit all firing, is this as good as it gets, or is there an argument the cycle is earlier given AI, higher global defense spending and supply chain shifts? Follow-up: is there a rate tipping point where deposit behavior changes meaningfully in volumes and betas, which have been better than expected so far?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: it is getting close to as good as it gets and the firm does not know how long it will last. Jeremy: the short answer on deposits is they do not really know; at the start of this rate cycle he would have expected the negative convexity in consumer deposit rate paid to be showing by now and it is not, but common sense says it kicks in at some point. Stress testing considers a true regime change with meaningfully higher inflation and a more aggressive Fed and asks when rate paid accelerates; one should not be naive about higher rates, because taking the current EAR (even though the empirical EAR is probably higher than reported) and ignoring convexity could make a 7% rate environment look great when it would not if the firm had to massively repurchase the deposit franchise. Jamie added the firm does assume some of that; it is in the models and part of the discipline, and the open questions are when it happens and the competitive dynamics of the deposit franchise.

exchanges.question: Challenged the negative operating leverage framing, noting it was positive in dollars with 15% revenue growth and that marginal margins on incremental revenue far exceed the 25% overall margin, and asked why Jamie said this is as good as it gets. Follow-up: with Troy taking over the consumer bank despite no consumer experience (characterised as an FX trader now selling mortgages, cards and deposits), what gives confidence he is the right person?
exchanges.answer: Jamie agreed operating leverage was definitely positive in dollars and that a rapid revenue increase drives a big increase in operating leverage. Jeremy pieced it together: the firm revised this year's expense guidance up by $2.5 billion; consensus built off fourth-quarter guidance implied meaningful negative operating leverage because NII was still working through headwinds while inflation and investment drove expenses; since then the capital markets complex outperformed then-expectations by $6.5 billion in the first half with $1.5 billion of additional associated expense booked, so $1.5 billion of the $2.5 billion increase is already booked and about $1 billion is implicitly added for the second half, from which no strong conclusions about revenue expectations should be drawn; returns, which are exceptional, are what matter. Jamie: similar dynamics exist in Asset & Wealth Management, card spend and elsewhere; on as good as it gets, the market is very healthy, active and exuberant with very high prices and volumes, it could get better but he does not know by how much or for how long. On Troy: people are evaluated on analytics, brainpower, EQ, heart and culture; he has shown that in markets and investment banking, which include extensive operations, back office and technology functions; cross-company experience is important because investment-bank-only leaders can let the rest of the franchise suffer; he is excited and has always visited branches. Jeremy corrected that Troy was an options trader, not an FX trader.

exchanges.question: Is the market vastly underestimating AI's efficiency potential, and could banks, like Block after cutting 40% of its workforce, operate with a much leaner, more agile structure over time? Follow-up: what was most exceptional in equities this quarter by product or geography that may be hard to sustain?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: not a sensitive topic; the firm will use AI to do a better job for clients and fully expects huge efficiency in certain parts of the company; there are almost 1,000 use cases today of which about 50 are really important, across risk, fraud, marketing, hedging, prospecting, note-taking, idea generation and document reading, and it is just starting. The firm is preparing to retrain people, has had discrete areas where it reduced jobs by 30% or 40% with most people offered jobs elsewhere, expects more of that, and notes AI will also reach smaller competitors through Fiserv, FIS and other fintechs; it is a big topic at the July offsite and the firm will report back, but the benefit accrues to customers rather than JPMorgan, and one cannot assume ROE goes to 50% and stays there. Jeremy on equities: nothing beyond the heavily reported obvious drivers, including major IPOs, major index rebalancing, very complicated dynamics in the Korean equity market, a lot of activity in Asia and extremely active clients; it could repeat but statistically that particular combination seems improbable. Jamie added this is visible daily in NYSE and CME volumes, hedge fund volumes and margin loans.

exchanges.question: What is JPMorgan seeing on Main Street given perceived fragility in housing and the risk of higher rates, how resilient is the consumer, and is CapEx and commercial lending broadening beyond AI? Follow-up: why buy back stock at three times tangible book rather than hold more excess capital for a rainy day, and what about potential M&A in asset management or fintech?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: there is decent CapEx and loan growth across the franchise, some of which does not superficially appear AI-related, but he is reluctant to conclude that because AI demand shows up in non-obvious places such as plumbers and electricians for data centers; CHIPS Act CapEx is rolling off and being replaced by direct AI spend. Jamie: CapEx is about $4 trillion a year, AI went from $400 billion last year to $700 billion this year and is projected at a little over a trillion next year, with maybe a little reduction in non-AI CapEx. On the consumer, spend is fine and robust across income segments with a tax refund tailwind, delinquencies are a little lower than expected across FICO scores, recent Fed heterogeneity data does not support the K-shape narrative, a cohort with negative real wage growth is a watch area, and consumer credit performance comes down to a surprisingly resilient labor market. On capital, Jeremy agreed the firm buys back less as the price rises; excess capital is still approximately $40 billion and the firm now thinks it will deploy over time given a bigger, more complex world (security resiliency, hyperscalers, global infrastructure, remilitarization, trade restructuring, government needs with global deficits of almost 4.5% or 5%), it will not tell the market what it will do, and buying back stock is an investment decision rather than returning money to shareholders. Jamie: he made a mistake last time mentioning $20 billion and could do far more or nothing; the goal is to deploy capital at a 17% return, mainly through hard organic growth in every business (including Europe, where share has doubled in areas with room for more, U.S. branches, cards and the Apple business); inorganic options are always considered but never as a substitute for fixing organic weakness; competition includes Goldman Sachs, Stripe, PayPal, Cash App, Block, Chime, SoFi and Revolut; the firm did a bunch of deals this year, most good and a couple not, remains open-minded on adjacencies and data, has skunk works underway, and hopes Chase UK becomes a great European digital bank over time.

exchanges.question: What is the status of the smart cash tool, when and to whom will it roll out, and what did Jamie mean about having to pay more for money over time? Follow-up: how would Jamie sum up JPMorgan's European consumer banking aspirations across the major markets?
exchanges.answer: The tool relates to how the velocity of money will change in a new world; it is still a test case aimed at a narrow segment of accounts where the firm competes for both investment and deposit business, certain tests will come out and the firm will learn what it can and cannot do, and it could be good for customers and for the firm; something will be seen this year. On Europe, the firm never tried to compete in bricks and mortar against local banks, but digital changed that: Chase UK started about 4 or 5 years ago as a complete startup and now has almost 3 million or 2.5 million UK customers, Berlin has opened and Germany is doing much better than expected though not yet profitable, and the platform cost spreads across more clients and countries toward break-even and profitability. Investment products have been added in the UK and will be added elsewhere, probably with credit card; the dream is a pan-European successful digital bank built off JPMorgan Chase's private bank, cross-border clients, underwriting and research strengths, and he has high hopes while being patient, kind of.

exchanges.question: Having flagged excesses in underwriting late last year and risk-on capital markets, what is JPMorgan seeing in competitors' credit underwriting, is it getting crazier, and what is the outlook? Follow-up: with Basel III endgame possibly codified by year-end and tailoring next year, could the industry enter a period of regulatory stability that enhances bank valuations?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: crazy is a strong word; data center underwriting is a bellwether, where the key risks are power supply and tenants, the firm has a precise framework and has passed on some deals; it is competitive and eager, with some relationship lending to startup data center builders, but these are normal pressures, and the firm flexes for important clients while holding the line on its own risk appetite with an appropriately skeptical view. Jamie: the firm described a very mild deterioration, not a huge one, across a spectrum including aggressive revenue growth assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants and more rollover and interest rate risk, concentrated in some players rather than across the board; when the credit cycle comes, performance will not be a bell curve and there will be outliers as in the financial crisis. On regulation, Jeremy said stability is desirable and nonpartisan, the amplitude of post-crisis oscillations may be decreasing toward getting it about right, banks should be guided by their own standards with regulation as a backstop, and he is not convinced regulation is a major drag on valuations for banks like JPMorgan. Jamie: a Supreme Court decision allowing a president to remove officials more easily makes flip-flopping less likely, legislation should be clearer about intent, he welcomes Mickey Bowman and Kevin Warsh reviewing 20 years of changes, a true safety-and-soundness focus would leave JPMorgan with no MRAs, SVB and First Republic were disclosed interest rate risk failures, resolution and recovery does not work, the discount window should be viewed differently, and the system can be made much safer.

exchanges.question: Beyond the volume and revenue-related line, is JPMorgan also raising other expense buckets such as bankers, tech or marketing, or pulling forward spend given the environment? Follow-up: on the increased CIB capital allocation, how nimble can the firm be, is this peak allocation, are internal limits being approached, and is there room to keep allocating balance sheet?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: there are some ups and downs in other categories, including marketing strategy he does not want to disclose, but the big driver is volume and revenue-related expense; token expense is a trivial number for the first half and for the full year, though meaningful acceleration is forecast for the second half, it was budgeted and is not a driver of the outlook revision, and it becomes an important question for next year and beyond, where the firm's infrastructure positions it to use the right model for the right purpose (not a cutting-edge expensive model to summarise analyst reports) and open source where appropriate, yielding more capacity, efficiency, better revenue or competitiveness. He will not discuss internal limit management; capital allocation is not like giving a hedge fund a pot of capital but the opposite, responding to client demand, alongside passive effects such as higher volatility raising market risk capital and equity market appreciation raising prime RWA; the firm has a ton of excess capital, its primary goal is to deploy it organically, and it has plenty of capital to serve CIB clients within its risk appetite and return hurdles, subject to other financial resource constraints. The system is flush with capital but at the margin less flush with liquidity, and shrinking the Fed balance sheet requires reducing bank demand for reserves and adjusting liquidity regulation, the next item on the advocacy agenda. Jamie: risk standards have not changed, and if some clients self-select elsewhere that is fine.

summary.overview: Lilly's Q2 revenue grew 48% year over year, with MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND contributing $14.9B (+$6.3B) and non-GAAP EPS of $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges, versus $6.31 a year ago. Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised full-year revenue guidance to $85B-$87B from $82B-$85B and the performance margin range to 49%-50.5%. Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, said that while Lilly is pleased with progress, "we're not satisfied".
keyTakeaways: Ilya Yuffa, President of Lilly USA, said U.S. Foundayo volume almost doubled in the last week of July versus a month earlier, with about one in four new starts and prescribers up from about 8,000 to 36,000.
Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, said retatrutide's BLA classification is in active litigation with the FDA, with submission expected by Q1 2027 once more CMC data are gathered.
The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program launched July 1 for 20 million eligible Americans at $50 a month; Yuffa said around 80% of early patients are on injectables and 60%-70% are new to treatment.
Lucas Montarce, CFO, said ZEPBOUND net price will go down "for sure" as CVS access resumes in Q4, embedded in the guide and more than offset by volume.
financialHighlights: Revenue up 48%; U.S. revenue up 33% on volume, with U.S. price down 3% (down 9% excluding rebate estimate changes).
Constant-currency growth of 55% in Europe (including a $250M Jardiance milestone), 30% in Japan, 93% in China and 136% in rest of world.
Gross margin 86.3%, up about 1.3 points; marketing, selling and administrative up 25%; R&D up 14% with more than 40 phase III programs.
Non-GAAP performance margin 54.8%, up nine points; Ebglyss sales more than doubled and Jaypirca grew 56%.
guidance: Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised full-year revenue to $85B-$87B from $82B-$85B, a $2.5B midpoint increase, with second-half growth significant in dollars but slower in percentage terms.
Montarce raised the non-GAAP performance margin to 49%-50.5% from 47%-48.5% and set non-GAAP EPS at $35.50-$36.50, up $2.78 at the midpoint before the $3.03 Q2 acquired IPR&D charge.
Montarce said prior-period rebate adjustments will not recur in the second half, which also carries Europe Q3 and U.S. Type 2 diabetes Q4 seasonality.

Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, expects Foundayo U.S. Type 2 diabetes action later this year; Patrik Jonsson, President of Lilly International, expects the major OUS rollout at the beginning of 2027; Dan Skovronsky, Chief Scientific and Product Officer, expects the retatrutide submission in Q1 2027.
risksMentioned: Foundayo's U.S. launch curve was slower than anticipated, and the inflection claim rests on a few weeks of data.
ZEPBOUND net price is expected to fall from Q4 as CVS access resumes and medical exceptions fade, per Montarce.
Retatrutide's BLA pathway is disputed with the FDA, with a mixed first court decision, per Ricks.
Novo Nordisk's oral is scaling in the U.K., Germany and the UAE and generic semaglutide has launched in India and Brazil, per Jonsson.

qa.question: Why has the U.S. Foundayo launch been slower than anticipated, when will it inflect, and how is the ex-U.S. race against Novo's oral shaping up?

qa.answer: CVS added Foundayo in June, Bridge launched July 1 and full DTC began; in the last week of July volume almost doubled with about one in four new starts on Foundayo. Patrik Jonsson, President of Lilly International: the UAE launch started strongly and Lilly held incretin share despite a second oral; Mexico and Saudi Arabia are next, most launches in 2027.

qa.question: What milestones remain for retatrutide under the BLA pathway, and will the classification apply to later incretins?
qa.answer: Lilly holds retatrutide is a biologic under the amino acid count rule; the first court decision was mixed and litigation is active. All clinical data are in hand, more CMC data must be gathered, and submission is expected by Q1 next year.
qa.read: Answered partially; later incretins not addressed.

qa.question: Guidance implies a second-half deceleration despite Bridge and Foundayo access; is price being missed or is the team conservative?
qa.answer: The guide rose $2.5B; recent quarters included one-off rebate adjustments that will not continue, the 2025 base had a bolus of new-country MOUNJARO launches that will not repeat, and Europe Q3 and U.S. Type 2 diabetes Q4 seasonality are factored in; second-half dollar growth is still significant.

CVS access resumes in Q4, medical exceptions are "maybe a short-term thing", and price is expected to go down for sure, embedded in the guide.

exchanges.question: How does Lilly envision expanding its increasingly deep consumer-facing position in obesity and where is the consumer market heading; how unique or similar is the U.S. self-pay market versus the international self-pay market?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: U.S. and global obesity treatment is still only mid-single-digit utilization, so significant patient opportunity remains; access is improving with the Bridge program and state Medicaid coverage going live or committed for next year; Q2 obesity TRx reached about 3 million, driven by injectable and oral new patients, with about 55% of ZEPBOUND prescriptions self-pay; Lilly is investing in consumer awareness and expanding LillyDirect. Patrik: obesity outside the U.S. is still mainly out of pocket; Lilly is rapidly replicating U.S. consumer-activation practices and has launched versions of LillyDirect OUS, with models varying by local regulation and a common focus on patients receiving safe, authentic Lilly medicines.

exchanges.question: The U.S. Foundayo launch curve has been slower than anticipated: what are the contributing factors and when should an inflection be expected? Ex-U.S., how are competitive dynamics and the launch trajectory shaping up now that Novo Nordisk is scaling its oral in the U.K., Germany and the UAE, where Novo claims 50% share within three weeks?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Lilly is focused on three fronts (physician education, access and affordability, consumer awareness) and leading indicators are positive with week-to-week prescription growth; in the last 30 days CVS added Foundayo in June, Bridge launched July 1 and the full DTC campaign began; in the last week of July volume almost doubled versus a month earlier and about one in four new starts are on Foundayo, so an inflection is now visible and growth is expected over the coming quarters. Patrik: the UAE launch in early May started strongly, orals are expanding the market and most patients are incretin-naive and titrating up; Lilly's combined incretin share held steady despite a second oral entering; Mexico and Saudi Arabia launch next with most launches in 2027, with no gating from supply; the early data are noisy and often reflect sell-in with inventory build.

exchanges.question: What are the requirements and milestones ahead for retatrutide to be accepted under the BLA pathway given the dispute with the FDA, and will BLA classification be unique to retatrutide or apply to subsequent incretins?
exchanges.answer: Lilly's position is that retatrutide is a biologic under both the amino acid count rule and as analogous to a protein; the first court decision was mixed and litigation is active, but Lilly hopes to reach a conclusion with the FDA supporting a BLA. All clinical data needed for submission are in hand but more CMC data must be gathered; Lilly is in communication with the agency and will update investors on filing status, with submission expected by Q1 next year. He called it a super exciting data package with unprecedented efficacy and a large lead over any triple-acting competitor.

exchanges.question: What are the early learnings and surprises from the Medicare obesity (GLP-1 Bridge) rollout, and what does the initial ramp look like for orals versus injectables?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Bridge expands access to about 35% more Americans; it is early but a pretty significant inflection point is visible, and Lilly is working closely with CMS to educate physicians, pharmacies and consumers on criteria and prior authorization, which is working well; LillyDirect has been enabled to fulfil Bridge prescriptions. Both ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO have inflected over the last few weeks, partly from Bridge; around 80% of people getting treatment are on injectables, and approximately 60%-70% are new patients who did not previously have access.

exchanges.question: Does retatrutide need a commercial strategy to protect against the unapproved product apparently available today, or will formal approval solve that; and with its higher efficacy, are there additional indications beyond tirzepatide's base that retatrutide can address?
exchanges.answer: People are eagerly awaiting authentic retatrutide and Lilly fully expects them to vote with their feet for the guaranteed product once it is on the market. Transformative weight loss at the high dose opens additional opportunities: knee osteoarthritis pain was reduced by an unprecedented 75% in TRIUMPH-4 and TRIUMPH-1; a MASH/MASLD study is ongoing where the glucagon mechanism may offer unique advantages; several additional indications are being evaluated internally; a chronic lower back pain study reads out sometime next year. Retatrutide can work at the high end with bariatric-surgery-like weight loss and at the low end with a single titration step.

exchanges.question: What is the post-Verzenio strategy in breast cancer given the oral SERD and oral PI3K assets, and is an all-oral combination on the table?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: The three most important targets in breast cancer are the estrogen receptor, CDK4/6 and PI3 kinase alpha; Lilly believes it has the best medicine for each and plans to combine them all. INLURIYO's adjuvant EMBER-4 trial reads out next year, a major moment for that medicine. Lilly is on the precipice of starting the phase III program for tersolisib (PI3K inhibitor), initially combined with existing endocrine therapies and investigator's choice of CDK4/6 (largely Verzenio), and over time combined with INLURIYO as an all-oral combination across settings.

exchanges.question: Guidance seems to imply a second-half revenue deceleration versus Q2 despite the Medicare Bridge ramp and Foundayo commercial access coming online; is something being missed on price, or is the team being conservative?
exchanges.answer: The full-year guide was raised by $2.5 billion. Recent quarters including Q2 included one-off prior-period adjustments to U.S. rebate and discount estimates that are not expected to continue in the second half. The 2025 base period included the bolus of MOUNJARO launches in new OUS countries, which will not repeat, and future OUS growth is driven by penetration rather than new countries; in dollars rather than percentage, significant growth is still expected in the second half. Seasonality is also factored in: Europe in Q3 from vacation holidays and U.S. Type 2 diabetes in Q4.

exchanges.question: Which specific regions are driving the most OUS MOUNJARO growth, and what is Lilly seeing in India where generic semaglutide is launching amid reported capacity constraints?
exchanges.answer: MOUNJARO continues to perform very strongly more or less everywhere with market leadership across many markets; key drivers are China, where NRDL listing delivered category leadership after 16 months, plus Korea, the U.K., Mexico and Germany, with share in many markets similar to or above U.S. levels. In India and Brazil MOUNJARO TRx continued to grow after generic semaglutide launched, driven by superiority data as the first line of defense; in Canada tirzepatide TRx is growing at the same pace as the total market. Generic companies are showing significant supply constraints, which Lilly is monitoring closely.

exchanges.question: How extensive is the Foundayo sampling program and is it dampening the weekly IQVIA prescription data; is the U.S. prescriber base expanding and can that be quantified?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Every promotional lever is active; sampling covers the first 30 days of the first dose, similar to a typical oral small molecule in retail, is extensive across the prescriber base and fully supplied. The prescriber count has grown from about 8,000 at the last earnings call to 36,000, with continued week-on-week progress in adoption, awareness and perception of the Foundayo profile; Lilly feels good about inflection ahead as access and consumer awareness increase.

exchanges.question: ZEPBOUND net price appears to be about $580 per prescription, well above the cash price; how sustainable is the medical-exception-driven delta now that CVS is back on formulary, and is this what drives the favourable rebate adjustments quarter after quarter?
exchanges.answer: ZEPBOUND pricing is transparent across channels: LillyDirect direct-to-patient from $299 to $449, the Bridge program at $245, and the commercial price. Medical exceptions are one driver, and script size in the commercial segment is another, so price per pack is significantly lower than the per-prescription figure. After CVS moved to a one-of-one formulary last year patients had three options (switch to the competitor, go to the cash market, or use the medical exception process); CVS access resumes starting in Q4, medical exceptions are maybe a short-term thing and the goal is open access. Price is expected to go down for sure as a result, which is embedded in the guide and will be more than offset by volume growth.

exchanges.question: Lilly surprised investors by getting back into psychiatry and doing vaccine deals: are these areas Lilly can scale and a high priority, or are the assets more one-off and science-driven?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: What the two areas share is immense remaining unmet need, which is the through line of all internal and business development work; Lilly acquired technology and medicines it believes can be really impactful at prices that keep it disciplined and create long-term shareholder value, not unlike the other deals done year to date. He would not forward-look on whether Lilly builds further in infectious disease and psychiatry specifically, saying it will be opportunistic based on what is available, but is very excited about both areas and the assets purchased.

exchanges.question: Which one or two non-obesity pipeline assets is management most excited about that the street should be paying more attention to?
exchanges.answer: Cardiovascular: PCSK9 gene editing for ASCVD plus oral and injectable Lp(a)-lowering drugs, which are huge opportunities. Neuroscience: psychiatry, sleep-wake disorders via Centessa, and diseases like addiction and major depressive disorder that may be addressable with incretin science. Oncology: probably the richest readout period in Lilly's history, including Kelonia's in vivo CAR T for multiple myeloma and the AJ1-11095 JAK inhibitor. Immunology: still early days for the atopic dermatitis franchise (transcribed as empagliflozin) with new indications coming, plus combination ideas in IBD and psoriatic diseases; he called it the strongest pipeline Lilly has ever had, even excluding incretins.

exchanges.question: Foundayo sales of $31 million in the UAE alone were close to half the $67 million generated in the U.S., suggesting explosive ex-U.S. potential: how does Lilly see its ex-U.S. obesity potential, and will ex-U.S. governments reimburse Foundayo for diabetes better than tirzepatide given it can be offered much cheaper?
exchanges.answer: Lilly is encouraged by the UAE start but it is very early days with a lot of noise in the data and an initial inventory build alongside real demand; the learning so far is a clear need for an oral in both obesity and Type 2 diabetes, with the majority of patients incretin-naive. The major OUS rollout happens at the beginning of 2027. On Type 2 diabetes reimbursement, Lilly is probably slightly better positioned with an oral and three head-to-head orforglipron trials offering an appealing value proposition, but OUS reimbursement always takes time, so launch focus will be chronic weight management, building on U.S. and UAE experience.

summary.overview: Chipotle's Q2 revenue rose 9.3% to $3.3B on comparable sales of +2.2% (transactions +1%, pricing about 1.6%), with restaurant-level margin down 220 bps to 25.2% and adjusted EPS flat at $0.33. Adam Rymer, CFO, raised the full-year comp outlook to low single digits from about flat but guided Q3 to around +1% after comps softened about 200 bps in late July around an industry Cyclospora issue. Scott Boatwright, CEO, said Chipotle is not involved in that issue.
keyTakeaways: Adam Rymer, CFO, said traffic improved through Q2 and the first half of July before softening about 200 bps; the Q3 guide of around +1% assumes that headwind persists, implying roughly +3% underlying.

Scott Boatwright, CEO, said HEAP is in more than 1,000 restaurants, adding 2 to 3 entrees in the peak 15 minutes and 2 to 4 hours of daily labor efficiency, with 2,000 restaurants targeted by year-end.
Boatwright said 350 company-operated openings a year is the right pace, with incremental growth from Western Europe and partners; Alshaya already runs 15 restaurants.
Rymer said the pricing-inflation gap (about 1% versus low-to-mid 3% in the first half) narrows in Q3 and closes from Q4; Boatwright cited the highest wallet share gains since 2024.
financialHighlights: Revenue $3.3B, up 9.3%; comps +2.2% with transactions +1% and pricing about 1.6%; digital sales $1.3B, or 38.3% of sales versus 35.5%.
Restaurant-level margin 25.2%, down 220 bps: cost of sales 29.7% (+80 bps on beef and freight), labor 25% (+30 bps), other operating costs 14.9% (+90 bps), marketing 3%.
Adjusted diluted EPS $0.33, flat; non-GAAP G&A $176M; 101 openings including 80 Chipotlanes.
$631M repurchased at an average $32.55 (over $1.3B year to date), with $1.7B of authorization remaining; $800M of cash and no debt.
guidance: Adam Rymer, CFO, raised full-year comps to low single digits from about flat and guided Q3 comps to around +1%, assuming the roughly 200 bps Cyclospora-related softening continues against the toughest lap of the year.

Rymer expects Q3 pricing in the mid 2% range (full year near the high end of 1%-2%), cost of sales just under 30%, labor in the mid 25% range, other operating costs in the mid 15% range and marketing in the low 3% range.
Rymer guided Q3 non-GAAP G&A to around $180M, depreciation around 3% of sales and a 24%-26% tax rate, with pricing and inflation expected to match from Q4.

Scott Boatwright, CEO, expects approximately 350 openings in 2026 (about 80% Chipotlanes), HEAP in about 2,000 restaurants by year-end, a frictionless rewards pilot in August and a national catering launch in 2027.
risksMentioned: The industry Cyclospora issue cut comps about 200 bps in late July; Rymer called its duration "very difficult to predict".
Q3 is the toughest comparison of the year, per Rymer.
Beef and freight inflation and sequentially higher avocado prices, with first-half pricing of about 1% against inflation in the low-to-mid 3% range.
Investor pushback, raised by David Palmer of Evercore ISI, that heavy spending is yielding only 1%-2% comps.

qa.question: What is behind the low single-digit comp guide, the recent softening and the cadence from here?
qa.answer: Traffic improved through Q2 and the first half of July, then comps softened about 200 bps around the industry Cyclospora issue; Q3 is guided to around +1% assuming that continues. Scott Boatwright, CEO, said the implicated products are not on Chipotle's menu and its lettuce is sourced in California.

qa.question: Does the +1% Q3 guide with a 200 bps headwind imply about +3% underlying, and where is Max 15 throughput without HEAP?
qa.answer: Correct; the guide assumes the impact persists through the quarter. HEAP restaurants do two or three more entrees in Max 15; system in-store Max 15 is in the low 20s, digital adds mid-teens, for a combined low-to-mid 30s per restaurant per day.

qa.question: How does the margin outlook beyond Q3 look as the pricing-inflation gap narrows?
qa.answer: The gap was widest in the first half, with pricing around 1% and inflation in the low-to-mid 3% range; in Q3 inflation should be about 3% versus pricing in the mid 2% range, and from Q4 pricing and inflation are expected to match.

qa.question: Has Chipotle sized remodel capex and any sales uplift, and will it use partners in other international markets?
qa.answer: Chipotle has never done an aesthetic remodel; it is stage-gating a test at $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant across several geographies with nothing to report yet. Alshaya, Alsea and SPC operate as partners or JVs, while Chipotle owns Western Europe.
qa.read: Answered partially; no uplift or timeline.

unanswered.how: Adam Rymer, CFO, said no specific LTO lifts are disclosed, offering only that LTOs typically deliver hundreds of basis points.

unanswered.how: Scott Boatwright, CEO: "I have nothing to report today, unfortunately, but I'll tell you that work is in flight."

unanswered.how: Boatwright cited green shoots; the digital and brand plans were called industry changing but not shared.

exchanges.question: When LTOs are brought back from the pantry (e.g. Chicken al Pastor), is the lift still as good or better than the prior run given mixed card data? And is value perception changing given generous portions and having underpriced the industry for so long?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle Honey Chicken performed better the second time around, as do many LTOs, though there is likely a point of diminishing returns around the fifth or sixth run; menu innovation has been ramped to 4x what it was a couple of years ago, with new items coming in the months ahead alongside returning favorites. The brand tracker showed solid progress on value perception across all income groups and age cohorts, and Q2 affordability scores were the best in probably the past couple of years. Value is about convenience, execution and menu innovation, not just discounting; the high-protein menu at an approachable price point is contributing and Chipotle believes it should own the protein category.

exchanges.question: Investors push back that Chipotle is doing and spending a lot to get only 1%-2% same-store sales growth; with tough comparisons and a recent slowdown, what gives management confidence that momentum picks up into 2027?
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflected the early days of the Recipe for Growth strategy, particularly menu innovation, while investments in HEAP, throughput and hospitality are producing early proof points in guest satisfaction, food quality and operational consistency. Additional drivers (menu innovation, deeper rewards engagement, stronger brand communication, expanded group occasions) are showing green shoots and will build and layer through the second half of 2026 and into 2027. Early thinking from Arlie Sisson on digital commerce and Fernando Machado on culturally relevant branding was described as really innovative and industry changing but not shared on the call.

exchanges.question: Can you give more color on the positive low single-digit 2026 comp guide, including Q3 and the recent softening, where the trend was before the industry challenges, and the cadence from here?
exchanges.answer: Traffic improved throughout Q2 and momentum continued into the first half of July; in the second half of July comps softened by about 200 basis points around the industry Cyclospora issue. Q3 comps are expected at around plus 1%, assuming the roughly 200 basis point impact continues since its duration is hard to predict, against the toughest lap of the year; year-to-date performance plus the Q3 set-up and Q4 plans drove the raise to low single digits for the full year. Scott added that Chipotle is affected on sales but not involved in the Cyclospora issue: the implicated products are not on its menu and its lettuces are sourced in California.

exchanges.question: Has Chipotle sized the incremental capex for the store refresh program (three investment levels across roughly 1,000-1,500 North American stores) and is there any early read on sales uplift and timeline? Would Chipotle use partners rather than owning restaurants in other international markets?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle has never done an aesthetic remodel in its history; this year it is stage-gating a remodel/refresh test at several locations across several geographies at $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant to gauge consumer perception and return, with nothing to report yet and management optimistic but patient. Internationally, partnerships are being built slowly and strategically: Alshaya in the Middle East, Alsea in Latin America and SPC in Southeast Asia, through partner-operated and/or JV structures. Chipotle will continue to own and operate Western Europe and grow from that base, with the rest of the world partner-operated.

exchanges.question: Digital sales grew about 18% year over year including unit growth; was there a catalyst that unlocked this roughly four quarters ago, and is it linked to the loyalty and payment changes at the register?
exchanges.answer: It is all linked: last year's Summer of Extras showed where Chipotle has the right to win in digital and what does not work for the brand, which informed the rewards relaunch a couple of months ago that removed friction and added flexibility in earning and redeeming; this year's Summer of Extras has accelerated digital revenue, helped by being right place, right time on an emerging trend. Arlie is taking a holistic approach to digital, it is early days, and the digital commerce innovation she brings over the coming weeks and months is expected to be game changing.

exchanges.question: Should all of the HEAP labor efficiency be expected to be reinvested into the production line, and could it help drive positive traffic and front-line customer satisfaction?
exchanges.answer: Yes: HEAP yields about two to four hours of labor efficiency depending on volume, which is left in the restaurant to complete morning prep and deploy crew on the line during peak; this is translating into transaction gains in Max 15 and total sales plus better taste-of-food scores. Rollout is as aggressive as possible, reaching 2,000 restaurants by year-end with the entire portfolio hopefully completed sometime in 2027, and all new restaurants come standard with HEAP.

exchanges.question: Why is 350 company-operated openings per year the right level versus the prior ceiling of 400, and what is the gating factor to accelerating above 350?
exchanges.answer: Given U.S. white space and the ability to develop ready-now leaders, one restaurant per day is meaningful growth the organization can support without losing its opening edge; beyond 350 there could be diminishing returns in opening quality or a risk of fracturing the base. Incremental growth comes from global expansion, both company-owned Western Europe and partner-operated markets that will ramp quickly: Alshaya is already at 15 restaurants across three or four countries after a couple of years with meaningful acceleration planned for 2027, so Chipotle can still target the total growth number discussed historically.

exchanges.question: With a new Chief Brand Officer, how should the brand be positioned given the long-running For Real campaign feels stale, and will value and in-restaurant food preparation versus limited-service competitors be highlighted more prominently?
exchanges.answer: For Real was extraordinary and served the brand for many years; Fernando's work is not a 180 pivot but the next evolution, showing more of how food is prepared fresh in-restaurant, more on ingredient usage and more on cultivating a better world, with creative ambition that breaks through the sea of sameness on television. Value will be highlighted, but as the extraordinary value of the best ingredients prepared fresh daily at abundance and speed for an approachable price point, rather than price points or discounts.

exchanges.question: Does the roughly 1% Q3 comp guide with a 200 basis point Cyclospora impact imply an underlying trend of about plus 3% with the headwind assumed to persist for the rest of the quarter? And where is system Max 15 throughput for restaurants without HEAP?
exchanges.answer: Correct: the 1% guide assumes the impact continues through the rest of the quarter and the expense-line guidance was built on it; duration is very difficult to predict. HEAP restaurants do about two or three more entrees in Max 15; system-wide in-store Max 15 is in the low 20s, digital (almost 40% of sales) adds somewhere in the mid-teens, so combined Max 15 is in the low to mid-30s per restaurant per day.

exchanges.question: Can you elaborate on efforts to promote the loyalty program in-restaurant, what is working and what could improve? And do the roughly 80% of in-store transactions without loyalty correlate with lower-income guests?
exchanges.answer: No, the non-loyalty in-store transactions are broad-based rather than lower-income skewed, and converting them could deliver a meaningful lift. The current experience (opening the app, then paying by card) is clunky, so in August Curt and team will launch a one-stop pay where paying earns rewards points and guests can ask to be enrolled, executed behind the scenes without relying on restaurant teams or hurting throughput; more consumer education on the program in-restaurant is still needed.

exchanges.question: Can you elaborate on the new menu items coming in the months ahead: are they center-of-the-plate items or sides?
exchanges.answer: The culinary team has been expanded to drive thoughtful innovation that is new news rather than just pantry items; the focus is center-of-the-plate items, with teams also working on beverage, sides and desserts. Some really big ideas, glimpsed on social media in recent months, are moving through the stage-gate process and could appear on the calendar in the back half of 2026 but certainly in 2027.

exchanges.question: What were the Q2 trends by age and income cohort, are younger and lower-to-middle income guests improving relative to higher-income guests or showing frequency differences, and is there anything to call out in Q3 to date?
exchanges.answer: The younger and lower-income cohorts that were under the most pressure have improved the most; the Q1-to-Q2 improvement was broad-based but outsized in those two groups, driven by menu innovation (Chipotle Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce), in-restaurant promotions such as the Matchday BOGO celebrating World Cup fans, and the rewards program. Scott added that Chipotle saw its highest year-over-year wallet share gains last quarter since 2024 and has taken share in each month of 2026 across all income cohorts and age groups.

exchanges.question: How is management thinking about the margin outlook beyond Q3, specifically the gap between pricing and inflation that was expected to narrow near year-end?
exchanges.answer: The price-inflation gap was widest in the first half, when pricing was around 1% and inflation in the low to mid 3% range, and it is easing in the second half under the rolling pricing strategy. In Q3 inflation should be closer to about 3% with pricing in the mid 2% range, so the gap is largely closed; from Q4 forward pricing and inflation are expected to match, removing the dislocation going forward.

exchanges.question: Were there regional or market divergences indicating a World Cup benefit in recent months? And what was learned from the methodical pricing rollout that gave comfort to trend toward the high end of the initial 1%-2% guide?
exchanges.answer: About 300 restaurants within roughly 10 miles of World Cup stadiums saw a comp benefit of 50 to 100 basis points during the tournament, but the overall quarterly impact was less than five basis points. The rolling market-by-market pricing process is working well: it lets Chipotle measure resistance precisely, adjust if needed and respond to inflation; reads on resistance and consumer feedback supported continuing to push forward, the strategy will continue, and the first-half dislocation was purely a timing effect.

exchanges.question: What is the LTO contribution to the frequency and traffic uplift versus historical benchmarks given the stepped-up cadence? And do guests gravitating to high-protein LTOs tend to be existing customers or a new cohort?
exchanges.answer: No specific LTO lifts are disclosed, but Chipotle Honey Chicken and Chicken al Pastor increased transactions from the most frequent guests visiting more often and from new guests; LTOs typically deliver hundreds of basis points of transaction lift, most of which sustains through the promotion, and post-promotion stickiness is measured; management views this as a multi-year AUV lever rather than a short spike. Scott added that LTOs bring in first-time customers, a guest who tries an LTO sees materially higher lifetime value, and existing customers come more often; the back half brings a couple more center-of-the-plate items, sides innovation and a more meaningful push into beverage, where Chipotle sees significant opportunity.

summary.overview: Kinsale's Q2 diluted operating EPS rose 15.9% to $5.54 with a 24.4% annualized operating ROE and a 75.5% combined ratio, even as gross written premium fell 5% because the Commercial Property Division shrank in what Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, called a buyer's market. Excluding that division, gross written premium grew 3.7%, and the board added $250M to the buyback authorization, bringing it to $337M.
keyTakeaways: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, said the Commercial Property "crisis is over and rates are coming down pretty dramatically", so Kinsale is writing a shrinking volume there and prioritizing profitability over growth.

Combined pricing fell 5.9%, versus 3.3% in Q1, and Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said London competition in long-tail lines is creeping into other liability lines and depressing Construction pricing.

Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, said losses came in below expectations and reserves are as conservative as ever, though the accident year loss ratio could drift up as mix shifts toward casualty.
Kehoe called Kinsale shares "a very good value" and said buybacks remain the principal capital allocation lever until growth accelerates.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS $5.54 versus $4.78; net income up 31.1%, net operating earnings up 13.3%; annualized operating ROE 24.4%.
Gross written premium down 5%, net written premium down 1.4%, net earned premium up 8.9%; ex Commercial Property, gross written premium up 3.7% (4.8% for the first half).

Combined ratio 75.5%, including 4.5 points of favorable prior year development (3.9 last year) and 1.3 points of cat losses; expense ratio 21.7% versus 20.7% on higher net commissions from higher reinsurance retentions.
Net investment income up 19.9%; float $3.4B versus $3.1B at year-end; new money yields around 5.25%; submissions up 6% (8% ex Commercial Property).
guidance: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, expects the gross written premium comparison to get modestly easier in Q3 and Q4 because 60% of Commercial Property premium was written in the first half of last year.

Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said the 21.7% Q2 expense ratio is a good measure going forward, with a slight uptick possible in net commissions from the June 1 reinsurance renewal, potentially offset by AI efficiency gains.
Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said five more product offerings launch imminently with 10 in the pipeline, after nine so far this year.
Kehoe said everything is managed to a 20% ROE or greater; Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, put casualty loss cost trend at mid-single digits.
risksMentioned: Commercial Property rate declines with no telling where pricing goes in 2027, per Winston, under pressure from London MGAs and large shared and layered deals.
London competition spreading into liability occurrence lines, Construction and general casualty, per Winston.
Broker commission tension in a soft market and some flow to the admitted market, which Winston called not pervasive.
The accident year loss ratio could drift up as mix shifts from property to casualty, per Allibhai.

qa.question: What drove the accident year loss ratio improvement versus peers, and will the ceding commission rate keep rising after renewals?
qa.answer: Losses came in below expectations as in recent quarters, with normal variability across a dozen statutory lines and reserves as conservative as ever. Bryan Petrucelli, CFO: the Q2 expense ratio is a good indication going forward, with a slight uptick possible since only one month of the June 1 treaty is reflected.

qa.question: Is Q2 the trough for commercial property, and what drives the 3.7% ex-property growth?
qa.answer: There is no telling where property goes in 2027; London MGA pressure continues and Kinsale will keep pricing tactical and accept shrinking there. Long-tail competition from London is creeping into other liability lines and depressing Construction pricing; admitted-market flow exists but is not pervasive.

qa.question: Is the rise in inbound accounts from broker engagement or pricing, and what is the view on social inflation and casualty loss trend?
qa.answer: A bit of both: the idle broker initiative is increasing flow while hit ratios are roughly unchanged. Allibhai put casualty loss cost trend at mid-single digits with favorable losses across the board; Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, said Kinsale has slowed IBNR releases in longer-tail occurrence business.

qa.question: How did property pricing move Q2 versus Q1, should the accident year loss ratio drift up with mix, and how will buybacks be paced?
qa.answer: Equilibrium will come because catastrophes happen, but there is no insight on timing; Winston said Agribusiness and small business property are more stable and pricing is nearing a floor. Allibhai said the loss ratio could drift up but current bookings look good. Buybacks continue: roughly $80M remained on the prior $250M plus the new $250M.

whatChanged.toneShift: Q1 had "no good news to report" on property but stressed "lots of ways to grow"; Q2 declared the property crisis over with rates falling dramatically, leaned harder on buybacks and reserve conservatism, and Stuart Winston warned against growth from compromised margins.

exchanges.question: What drove the improvement in the current accident year loss ratio versus 2Q 2025, which differs from what other commercial insurers are reporting (lower non-cat property losses, mix, changes in loss picks)? Second, the ceding commission rate has been rising for a couple of years; is the same expected this year after the reinsurance renewals?
exchanges.answer: Allibhai said losses came in below expectations as they have for the last few quarters, with nothing out of the ordinary, just normal variability and mix across a composite of a dozen statutory lines, and reserves are as conservative as they have ever been. Petrucelli said the second quarter is a good indication of the expense ratio going forward, with a slight uptick possible in the net commission ratio; reinsurance treaties renewed June 1st so only one month of the new treaty is reflected, and AI-driven efficiency gains on the operating side could offset, so in aggregate the Q2 expense ratio is a good measure going forward.

exchanges.question: With E&S casualty softening and GWP up about 3% versus 4% in Q1, how much are ROEs compressing in that line assuming loss trend views of high single digits to low double digits are unchanged? Second, how is Kinsale thinking about broker commissions going forward, given brokers push for higher commissions in soft markets and appear to be placing more business on the admitted side?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe said everything is managed to a 20% ROE or greater, most product lines are probably running ahead of that, and the company produced 24.4% for the quarter, with a constant give and take between profit and growth. On brokers, he said there is normal tension between wholesalers and retailers over splitting the gross commission, which a soft market intensifies, but Kinsale offers the best customer service, quote ratio, response time and broadest risk appetite in the industry and continues to grow outside the Commercial Property Division, which is going through a unique correction.

exchanges.question: Is 2Q the trough for commercial property given larger players are pulling out, and could pricing become less negative in 2027 or Kinsale return to larger shared placements? Second, what is driving the 3.7% ex-property growth figure, is business returning to the admitted market, and what would need to change for that number to inflect?
exchanges.answer: Winston said there is no telling where property goes in 2027; pressure continues from MGAs in London and traditional markets remain heavy in shared and layered deals with larger limits and stretch primaries, so Kinsale will keep pricing tactical, meet return thresholds and accept shrinking in that division. On ex-property growth, heavy competition in long-tail lines from London is creeping into other liability occurrence lines and depressing Construction pricing, with more competition emerging in general casualty, but there are pockets of opportunity to lean into. There is some flow to the admitted market but it is not pervasive.

exchanges.question: How much of the increase in inbound accounts cited in the press release comes from broker engagement versus more competitive pricing? Second, what is the current view of social inflation and casualty loss cost trend, and was the favorable accident year variability entirely in short-tail property?
exchanges.answer: Winston said it is a bit of both: the idle broker initiative to reengage lapsed brokers is increasing flow, hit ratios on renewal and new business are roughly unchanged, and more submissions mean more accounts bind. Kehoe added the language was included to show confidence in the model, since the Commercial Property crisis is over and rates are coming down dramatically but the underlying business is still working well. Allibhai put casualty loss cost trend at probably mid-single digits varying by line, said smaller accounts and lower limits leave Kinsale less exposed to social inflation, and said favorable losses are across the board with short-tail lines performing especially well. Kehoe added that for a couple of years the company has slowed the release of IBNR in longer-tail occurrence business while letting it flow out more quickly in short-tail lines.

exchanges.question: What granularity can be given on property pricing in Q2 versus Q1, and when might pricing reach equilibrium? Second, with the mix shifting from property to casualty, should the underlying current accident year loss ratio drift up or is the level sustainable? Third, how should the pacing of buybacks be thought about going forward if top-line growth remains moderate?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe said equilibrium will eventually come because catastrophe losses do happen, but the company has no insight into when; other property divisions are seeing growth. Winston cited Agribusiness Property and small business property as more stable than large shared and layered deals over the last year and a half to two years, noted a little more competition in Inland Marine across its five product buckets, and said people are starting to reach the floor on property pricing though London pressure persists. Allibhai said the accident year loss ratio could drift up over time but losses are coming in below expectations and they feel good about current bookings, and Kehoe added IBNR conservatism is a positive indicator. On buybacks, Kehoe said they will continue to lean in: the first $100 million authorization was exhausted a little over a year ago, roughly $80 million remains on the subsequent $250 million, plus the new $250 million; buybacks are the principal capital allocation strategy alongside a small dividend, with growth becoming first priority again when it accelerates.

exchanges.question: How has product expansion contributed to growth over the past year, and what is the potential growth uplift from the new products going forward?
exchanges.answer: Winston said Kinsale never wants to jump into a new market feet first and grow like a weed; new products follow a crawl, walk, run pace. They are creating growth and driving submissions and new premium, but growth will be slow, ramping up as the market turns.

summary.overview: Deere's fiscal Q3 net sales and revenues rose 5% to $12.608B, with a 14.4% equipment operations margin and net income of $1.379B, or $5.10 per diluted share, helped by $110M of incremental IEPA tariff refunds. Dan Pooley, Manager of Investor Communications, presented a raised fiscal 2026 net income guide of $4.75B-$5B, and Brent Norwood, CFO, reiterated that 2026 is the bottom of the ag cycle with a measured 2027 recovery.
keyTakeaways: Brent Norwood, CFO, said net tariffs become a headwind in fiscal 2027: about $750M net this year ($1.1B direct less $382M refunds) versus a run rate of about $1B next year.

Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, said model year 2027 planter and sprayer early orders are up mid-single digits, with See & Spray adoption nearly doubling to about one-third of North American sprayers on order.

Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, said Construction & Forestry holds four to five months of orders, more than the two to three Deere typically wants, with PPA and C&F each underproducing retail by a couple of points.
Kovar said South America demand is softer, with the industry cut to down 15%-20%, while used model-year 2023 and 2024 high horsepower tractors are down nearly 40% from a year ago.
financialHighlights: Equipment net sales up 6% to $10.999B; net income $1.379B, EPS $5.10; equipment operations margin 14.4%.
Production & Precision Ag sales down 6% to $3.998B at a 13.2% margin; Small Ag & Turf sales up 12% to $3.383B at an 18.4% margin.
Construction & Forestry sales up 18% to $3.618B at a 12.1% margin, including 8 points of price lapping about 5% negative price a year ago.
Financial Services net income $219M; IEPA refunds $110M in Q3 and $382M year to date.

Pooley guided PPA sales down about 10% (from down 5%-10%) at an 11%-12% margin, SAT up about 15% at a 14.5%-15.5% margin (from 13.5%-15%), and C&F up about 20% at a 10.5%-11.5% margin.

qa.question: Is the roughly $800M net tariff impact this year a headwind, tailwind or neutral going into 2027?
qa.answer: A headwind: about $1.1B of direct tariffs less $382M of refunds gives net exposure of approximately $750M this year, while the 2027 run rate is expected right around $1B.

qa.question: Did something slip from Q4 into Q3, and was tractor inventory built in Q3 ahead of the industry?
qa.answer: Not to read too much into Q3; some demand was pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk and nothing on inventory is concerning. Norwood said Q4 PPA and C&F sales should be similar to Q3 without the refund benefit and with seasonally high R&D and SA&G, so margins come in a little.
qa.read: Answered directly; disputed the inventory premise.

qa.question: Is the tariff estimate cut to $1.1B from relief or refunds, and how is the excavator launch trending?
qa.answer: Mainly Section 232 changes cutting the rate on imported goods from roughly 25% to 15% effective June 1, so only five of 12 months benefit this year with a further 2027 tailwind. Norwood: three Deere-designed excavator models are in market, with more over three to four years.

qa.question: Why does C&F guidance imply only about 50 bps of Q4 price after +8% in Q3, and how large should dealer rental fleets get?
qa.answer: The C&F price guide went 2.5% to 3% to 2.5% and back to 3%; Q3's 8% partly reflected about 5% negative price in Q3 2025. Norwood said 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental and dealers want to expand fleets, with no target size.
qa.read: Answered partially; declined to size rental fleets.
