summary.overview: Deere reported fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues of $12.608 billion, up 5% year-over-year, and net income attributable to Deere of $1.379 billion, or $5.10 per diluted share. Management narrowed or raised most FY2026 guidance items and lowered direct tariff expense to about $1.1 billion, while Production & Precision Ag sales are now guided down about 10%.
keyTakeaways: Dan Pooley, Manager, Investor Communications, said equipment operations delivered a 14.4% operating margin.
Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, said Q3 shipments were pulled ahead "to kind of manage some risk here in Q4."
Brent Norwood, CFO, said net tariff expense will be a headwind in 2027, with a run rate closer to about $1 billion.
Chris Seibert said C&F has about four to five months of orders on hand, versus the typical two to three months.
Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, said the programs are up mid-single digits and technology take rates were a pleasant surprise.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues $12.608 billion, up 5% year-over-year; equipment operations net sales $10.999 billion, up 6%.
Production & Precision Ag net sales $3.998 billion, down 6%; operating profit $527 million at a 13.2% margin.
Small Ag & Turf net sales $3.383 billion, up 12%; operating profit $622 million at an 18.4% margin.
Construction & Forestry net sales $3.618 billion, up 18%, with price up 8 points; operating profit $436 million at a 12.1% margin.
Q3 IEPA tariff refunds recognized were $110 million; Worldwide Financial Services net income was $219 million, higher year-over-year.

guidance: Net income attributable to Deere FY2026: $4.75 billion to $5 billion, up from $4.5 billion to $5 billion in Q2 (Dan Pooley).
Financial Services net income FY2026: $870 million, up from $860 million in Q2 (Dan Pooley).
Equipment operations operating cash flow FY2026: $5 billion to $5.5 billion, up from $4.5 billion to $5.5 billion (Dan Pooley).
Production & Precision Ag net sales FY2026: down approximately 10%, versus down 5% to 10% in Q2 (Dan Pooley).
Small Ag & Turf operating margin FY2026: 14.5% to 15.5%, up from 13.5% to 15% (Dan Pooley).
Direct tariff expense excluding IEPA refunds FY2026: approximately $1.1 billion, down from $1.2 billion (Chris Seibert); total refunds recognized $382 million.
Brent Norwood, CFO, expects PPA and C&F Q4 net sales similar to Q3, and PPA and SAT Q4 margins lower on seasonal R&D and SA&G.

qa.question: Is the $1.1 billion tariff expectation, about $100 million lower than originally anticipated, due to tariff relief or expected refunds? What is the status of the excavator launch?
qa.answer: The FY2026 run rate fell from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion, excluding refunds, mainly from Section 232 changes that cut the rate on imported goods from roughly 25% to 15%, affecting imports from Europe effective 1 June, so five of 12 months are affected; a FY2027 tailwind is expected. Brent Norwood said the first Deere-designed excavator models launched earlier this spring, with three models in market and shipments underway.

qa.question: Is the net tariff impact about $800 million this year, and will it be a headwind or tailwind in 2027?
qa.answer: Net tariff expense will be a headwind in 2027. Deere pays about $1.1 billion in direct tariffs this year less $382 million of refunds, so net exposure is about $750 million; the 2027 run rate is expected closer to right around $1 billion.

qa.question: What drives the implied C&F pricing for Q4 versus +8% in Q3, and how large does Deere want its dealer rental fleets to grow?
qa.answer: C&F pricing was 2.5% at the start of the year, then 3%, then 2.5%, and is now back to the full-year guide. Q3's 8% benefited from easy comps, as Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives; Q4 has no outsized comps. Norwood said 30% to 35% of earthmoving transactions start as rental and dealer-owned rental fleets are growing.

qa.question: Did timing slip between Q3 and Q4, and why did tractor inventory appear to build in Q3 ahead of the industry, given South America?
qa.answer: Seibert said shipment plans are set for the year and orders are on hand, though some demand was pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk. Deanna Kovar said North America entered 2027 slowly on tractor shipments. Norwood said PPA and C&F Q4 net sales should be similar to Q3, with no refund benefit in Q4 margins.

qa.question: What merchandising incentives and pricing trends are in EOPs, and what are the implications of the FTC settlement on right to repair and aftermarket business?
qa.answer: Chris Seibert said Deere is taking inflationary price with a measured approach and is committed to covering inflation over time. Norwood said Deere has always supported customers' ability to repair their own equipment, and the agreement formalizes existing tools such as Operations Center PRO Service.
qa.read: Partial; no pricing or aftermarket figures given.

exchanges.question: How are production versus retail expected to set up by region for 2027, and what are pricing expectations for 2027 given the early order program and inflation concerns?
exchanges.answer: PPA and C&F are underproducing retail modestly in 2026, about a couple of percentage points each; shipping plans are set for the full year, with more caution in South America. C&F order position is four to five months out, leading to minor underproduction. Kovar said EOP pricing was rolled out several months ago, with focus on covering inflation across EOP and PPA portfolios as they roll toward 2027.

exchanges.question: Is the $1.1 billion tariff expectation, about $100 million lower than originally anticipated, due to tariff relief or expected refunds? And what is the status of the excavator launch?
exchanges.answer: Previous annual run rate for FY2026 was $1.2 billion, now $1.1 billion, excluding refund impacts. The decrease is mainly from Section 232 tariff changes: rate on imported goods dropped from roughly 25% to 15%, affecting imports from Europe, effective 1 June, so five of 12 months are affected. Expect a tailwind for FY2027. Brent Norwood said the first Deere-designed excavator models launched earlier this spring, with three models in market, shipments underway, and more models rolling out over the next three to four years.

exchanges.question: Did timing slip between Q3 and Q4, and why did tractor inventory appear to build in Q3 ahead of the industry, given South America?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said not to read too much into Q3 changes; shipment plans are set for the year and orders are on hand, though some demand was pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk. Kovar said factories are hitting forecasts, retail is on trend with historical averages, and North America entered 2027 slowly on tractor shipments. Norwood said PPA and C&F net sales in Q4 should be similar to Q3, Q4 margins will not get the refund benefit, and PPA and SAT margins will be lower on a seasonal high of R&D and SA&G in Q4.

exchanges.question: How could mix contribute in 2027, given technology sales in C&F and early order take rates, versus the previously cited 2 to 3 point mix benefit?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said it is too early to tell given uncertainty in inputs, commodities, shipment disruptions and softness in the EU and Brazil. Management is focused on controllables such as inventory management. Construction fundamentals are good and could have a mix impact depending on growth. EOP signals and tech adoption will drive mix depending on how programs wrap up.

exchanges.question: What regional variability in early order program demand was seen, and could mid-single-digit growth end up high single digit?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, Production & Precision Ag
exchanges.answer: Kovar said the programs still have a few weeks to run for sprayers and longer for planters; the U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada, which is a limited part of the planter portfolio. Mid-single-digit growth is a strong signal, and time will tell whether it turns more positive. Technology take rates, including See & Spray factory orders doubling and 40% of planters taking advanced technologies, give confidence.

exchanges.question: Was the cadence of EOP order growth affected by recent grain price improvements or technology decisions?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, Production & Precision Ag
exchanges.answer: Kovar said the cadence was as expected and not to read much into it. Changes to the early order program this year gave dealers more choice, and orders came through as expected. Technology take rates were a pleasant surprise. Management hopes the mid-single-digit increase extends well into the year.

exchanges.question: What are 8R tractor orders trending like, and how is Europe reacting to crop price improvements compared with North America?
exchanges.answer: 8R orders are as expected; the model year 2026 shipment schedule is basically closed and orders are being collected for the first quarter. Corn futures were about $5.05, a good signal for growers. Brazil typically takes a three-month order book, and Q4 orders are on hand. Financing at single-digit rates may help in 2027. Europe is mixed: arable farmers are more challenged, while dairy and livestock cash flows are relatively strong and stable. Overall order pace is as expected.

exchanges.question: How are C&F early order programs shaping up, and how much is dealer rental fleet loading?
exchanges.answer: C&F order trends are very positive, with about four to five months of orders on hand, more than the typical two to three months. Drivers include large infrastructure projects, data center starts, independent rental channel participation, and dealer-owned rental fleet opportunity. Under-production sets up a little opportunity for 2027.

exchanges.question: Is the net tariff impact about $800 million this year, and will it be a headwind or tailwind in 2027?
exchanges.answer: Net tariff expense will be a headwind in 2027. Deere will pay about $1.1 billion in direct tariffs this year less $382 million of refunds, so net exposure is approximately $750 million. The 2027 run rate is expected to be closer to right around $1 billion.

exchanges.question: What drives the implied C&F pricing for Q4 versus +8% in Q3, and how large does Deere want its dealer rental fleets to grow?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said C&F pricing was 2.5% at start of year, then 3%, then 2.5%, now back to full-year guide. Q3 at 8% benefited from easy comps, as Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price due to incentives. Q4 has no outsized comps. Norwood said there is an opportunity to increase rental exposure; 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as rental, and dealer-owned rental fleets are growing, potentially helping inventory fill next year.

exchanges.question: What merchandising incentives and pricing trends are in EOPs and what do backlogs imply for margins, plus implications of the FTC settlement on right to repair and aftermarket business?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said Deere is taking inflationary price in a challenging environment, with a measured approach and nothing outsized, and is committed to covering inflation over time. Pricing decisions occur at several points in the year. Tariffs also affect supplier pass-through. Norwood said Deere has always supported customers' ability to repair their own equipment; the agreement formalizes existing tools such as Operations Center PRO Service and is expected to support lifecycle solutions over the long term.

exchanges.question: Could the EU capital budget policy change in 2028 pull demand forward into 2027 or delay purchases in Europe, and what is the directional 2027 Europe view?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell. Order books are typically four to five months out, and collection has just started for Q1. Arable farmers' 2027 demand depends on input costs and commodity trends. Dairy and livestock look fairly stable. It is too early to say whether the policy will pull demand forward or delay it.

exchanges.question: What are Brazilian and U.S. farmers doing in response to input costs, and how are they affecting crop and purchase decisions?
exchanges.responderTitle: President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, Production & Precision Ag
exchanges.answer: Fertilizer impact differs for Brazilian and U.S. farmers. Markets are reacting and farmers are seeking alternatives in products, application amounts, and sourcing. Farmers remain resilient and are not sharply reducing intended application. Larger farmers have multiple years of inputs contracted and are considering changes. Farmers remain focused on yield.

summary.overview: Chipotle grew Q2 revenue 9.3% to $3.3B on a 2.2% comp, including a 1% transaction comp, while restaurant-level margin fell 220bps to 25.2% and adjusted EPS was flat at $0.33. Adam Rymer, CFO, guided the full-year comp to a low single-digit range, up from about flat, but expects Q3 comps around +1% as a roughly 200bp industry Cyclospora headwind weighs on late-July sales.
keyTakeaways: Adam Rymer, CFO, said traffic improved through Q2 and early July before softening about 200bps in the second half of July around the industry Cyclospora issue.
Scott Boatwright, CEO, said Chipotle is not involved in Cyclospora and the implicated products are not on its menu, but its sales are impacted.
Digital sales reached $1.3B, or 38.3% of sales, versus 35.5% a year ago, which Boatwright tied to the April rewards relaunch and the protein trend.
HEAP equipment is in more than 1,000 restaurants, adding 2-3 entrees in peak 15 minutes, and Boatwright targets about 2,000 by year-end.
Buybacks totaled $631M in Q2 at an average $32.55, with $1.3B of added authorization and $1.7B remaining.
financialHighlights: Revenue rose 9.3% YoY to $3.3B, with menu price contributing about 1.6%.
Restaurant-level margin was 25.2%, down 220bps, as cost of sales rose about 80bps to 29.7% and other operating costs rose about 90bps to 14.9%.
Labor was 25% of sales (up about 30bps) and marketing was 3% (up about 30bps).
Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.33, flat YoY; non-GAAP G&A was $176M.
Cash, restricted cash and investments were $800M, down $1.3B YoY, with no debt and a $500M revolver.
guidance: Adam Rymer, CFO, guides FY2026 comps to a low single-digit range and Q3 comps to around +1%, assuming the roughly 200bp Cyclospora headwind persists.
Rymer expects Q3 menu price impact in the mid 2% range and FY pricing near the high end of 1%-2%, with price matching inflation from Q4 onward.
Rymer guides Q3 cost of sales just under 30%, labor in the mid 25% range, other operating costs in the mid 15% range and marketing in the low 3% range.
Rymer guides Q3 non-GAAP G&A to about $180M and the FY underlying tax rate to 24%-26%.
Scott Boatwright, CEO, targets about 350 openings in 2026 (about 80% with Chipotlanes) and a national catering/Build-Your-Own launch in 2027.

qa.question: Asked about the FY comp guide, Q3 trajectory and recent softening.
qa.answer: Traffic improved through Q2 and the first half of July, then softened about 200bps in late July; Q3 comp is expected around +1% assuming that impact continues, against the toughest lap; Boatwright said Chipotle is not involved in Cyclospora and sources lettuce in California.

qa.question: Asked whether Q3 guide is an underlying ~3% less 200bps, and for system Max 15 throughput.
qa.answer: Confirmed yes; HEAP stores do 2-3 more entrees in Max 15, with system in-store in the low 20s, digital mid-teens and combined low-to-mid 30s.

qa.question: Asked about margins beyond Q3 and the price-versus-inflation gap.
qa.answer: The gap was widest in 1H with pricing about 1% versus inflation in the low-to-mid 3%; Q3 is about 3% inflation versus mid 2% pricing, and price and inflation should match from Q4.

qa.question: Asked about World Cup benefit and pricing learnings.
qa.answer: About 300 restaurants within roughly 10 miles of stadiums saw a 50-100bp comp benefit, but total quarter impact was under 5bps; market-by-market pricing showed favorable resistance, allowing the push toward the high end.

qa.question: Asked about remodel program sizing and returns, and international ownership model.
qa.answer: Testing remodels at $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant with no returns to report yet; Western Europe will be company-owned and the rest of the world partner-operated or via JVs.

qa.question: Asked why 350 company openings per year versus a prior 400 ceiling.
qa.answer: One restaurant a day is supportable given leader development, and going beyond 350 risks diminishing returns; Alshaya has 15 restaurants in three or four countries with acceleration expected in 2027.

unanswered.question: Asked what gives confidence comp momentum builds into 2027 given heavy spending for 1-2% comps.
unanswered.how: Boatwright cited general drivers and declined to share specifics of new CDO and CBO ideas.

unanswered.question: Asked for LTO contribution to frequency and traffic.
unanswered.how: Rymer disclosed no specific LTO lifts, saying only they typically deliver hundreds of bps of transaction lift.

unanswered.question: Asked for cohort trends by age and income in Q2 and Q3-to-date.
unanswered.how: Rymer said younger and lower-income cohorts improved most but gave no figures or Q3-to-date detail.

exchanges.question: Do repeat pantry LTOs still deliver equal or better lift each time? And are value perceptions changing given generous portions and underpricing industry?
exchanges.answer: Honey Chicken performed better second time, as do many LTOs; likely diminishing returns around fifth or sixth time. Menu innovation ramped 4x vs a couple years ago, new items coming. Brand tracker showed value perception progress across all income and age cohorts; Q2 affordability scores best in probably a couple of years. Value includes convenience, execution, innovation; high-protein menu helping.

exchanges.question: Pushback that Chipotle spends a lot for 1-2% comps; what gives confidence momentum builds into 2027?
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflects early Recipe for Growth, especially menu innovation; investments in HEAP, throughput, hospitality showing proof points in guest satisfaction and food quality. Further drivers: rewards, brand communication, group occasions, which will build through 2H26 into 2027. Declined to share specifics of new CDO and CBO ideas, calling them industry changing.

exchanges.question: Color on low single-digit FY comp guide, Q3 trajectory and recent softening.
exchanges.answer: Traffic improved through Q2 and into first half of July; second half of July softened ~200bps around industry Cyclospora issue. Q3 comp expected around +1%, assuming the ~200bp impact continues; Q3 is toughest lap. Boatwright: Chipotle not involved in Cyclospora, implicated products not on its menu, lettuce sourced in California, but sales impacted.

exchanges.question: Sizing, sales uplift and timeline of store refresh program; and considering partners rather than owning in other international markets?
exchanges.answer: Never done an aesthetic remodel; stage-gating test at several locations with $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant investment levels; nothing to report on returns yet. Will own and operate Western Europe; rest of world partner-operated (Alshaya Middle East, Alsea Latin America, SPC Southeast Asia), via partner-operated and/or JVs.

exchanges.question: Digital sales grew ~18%; what catalyst unlocked it, and is it linked to loyalty/register changes?
exchanges.answer: All linked. Last year's Summer of Extras taught what works; informed April rewards relaunch removing app friction and adding earn/redeem flexibility; plus capitalizing on emerging (protein) trend. CDO Arlie taking holistic look; early days.

exchanges.question: Will HEAP labor savings be reinvested in production line and drive traffic/satisfaction?
exchanges.answer: Yes; HEAP gives ~2-4 hours efficiency depending on volume, kept in restaurant for prep and peak line deployment. Seeing transaction lift, Max 15 and total sales gains, better taste scores. 2,000 restaurants by year-end; entire portfolio hoped complete sometime in 2027; new restaurants standard with HEAP.

exchanges.question: Why is 350 company openings/year right vs prior 400 ceiling, and what limits accelerating?
exchanges.answer: One restaurant per day is meaningful and supportable given leader development; beyond 350 risk diminishing returns or fracturing base. Incremental growth from Western Europe company-owned and partner-operated; Alshaya at 15 restaurants across three or four countries with meaningful acceleration for 2027. Still can target historical total growth number.

exchanges.question: With new CMO, where will brand positioning go given For Real campaign seems stale; emphasis on value or ingredient quality vs competitors?
exchanges.answer: Not a 180 pivot but next evolution of For Real: more on fresh in-restaurant prep, ingredients, cultivating a better world, breaking through sea of sameness. Value highlighted via ingredients, abundance, speed and approachable price, not price points or discounts.

exchanges.question: Is Q3 ~1% guide an underlying ~3% less 200bp Cyclospora headwind? And what is system Max 15 throughput ex HEAP?
exchanges.answer: Yes, correct; expense guidance based on 1% assuming impact continues all quarter. HEAP stores do 2-3 more entrees in Max 15; overall in-store low 20s, digital mid-teens, combined low-to-mid 30s per restaurant per day.

exchanges.question: Elaborate on in-restaurant loyalty efforts; do non-loyalty in-store transactions over-index to lower-income guests?
exchanges.answer: No, broad-based, not lower-income skewed. Current experience clunky; in August Curt's team launches one-stop pay earning points on payment with option to enroll, executed behind the scenes without burdening crews or throughput. More consumer education needed.

exchanges.question: Are upcoming new menu items center of plate or sides?
exchanges.answer: Expanded culinary team; pursuing center-of-plate items plus beverage, sides and desserts. Big ideas in stage-gate could appear back half 2026, certainly 2027.

exchanges.question: Update on trends by age and income in Q2 and Q3-to-date; are pressured cohorts improving?
exchanges.answer: Younger and lower-income cohorts improved most, though gains broad-based Q1 into Q2, driven by Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce, Matchday BOGO, rewards. Boatwright: highest YoY wallet share gains last quarter since 2024; took share every month of 2026 across all cohorts.

exchanges.question: Margin outlook beyond Q3; update on price vs inflation gap.
exchanges.answer: Gap widest in 1H (pricing ~1% vs inflation low-to-mid 3%). Q3 inflation ~3% vs pricing mid 2%. From Q4 forward expect price and inflation to match, eliminating dislocation.

exchanges.question: Any World Cup benefit regionally? And learnings from methodical pricing and why trending to high end of 1-2%?
exchanges.answer: ~300 restaurants within ~10 miles of stadiums saw 50-100bps comp benefit during tournament; total quarter impact under 5bps. Rolling market-by-market pricing lets them measure resistance precisely and adjust to inflation; favorable resistance reads allowed pushing forward; will continue strategy, dislocation was timing.

exchanges.question: LTO contribution to frequency/traffic; and do high-protein offerings attract new or existing guests?
exchanges.answer: No specific LTO lifts disclosed; LTOs typically deliver hundreds of bps of transaction lift, mostly sustained through promotion, from frequent guests and new guests; seen as multi-year AUV lever. Boatwright: LTOs bring new customers and materially raise lifetime value; more center-of-plate items, sides and beverage innovation in 2H.

summary.overview: Deere reported fiscal Q3 2026 net income of $1.379B ($5.10 per diluted share) on net sales and revenues of $12.608B, up 5%, with equipment operations margin of 14.4%. Brent Norwood, CFO, said the company continues to believe 2026 is the bottom of the ag equipment cycle, and full-year net income guidance was raised to $4.75B-$5B. Direct tariff expense is now expected at about $1.1B, down from $1.2B.
keyTakeaways: Brent Norwood, CFO, said: "we continue to believe that 2026 represents the bottom of the ag equipment cycle."
Construction & Forestry net sales rose 18% to $3.618B with price up 8 points, while Production & Precision Ag net sales fell 6% to $3.998B.

Direct tariff expense is now about $1.1B versus $1.2B before, mainly because the Section 232 import rate fell from roughly 25% to 15% effective June 1, per Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations.

Early order programs for model year 2027 are up mid-single digits, with See & Spray take rates doubling on factory-installed sprayer orders and 40% of planters taking advanced technology, per Deanna Kovar, President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division.
Brent Norwood said Q4 net sales for PPA and C&F should be similar to Q3, with no refund benefit in Q4.
financialHighlights: Net income was $1.379B, or $5.10 per diluted share, on net sales and revenues of $12.608B, up 5%.
Equipment operations net sales were $10.999B, up 6%, at a 14.4% operating margin.
Small Ag & Turf net sales rose 12% to $3.383B with operating profit of $622M, an 18.4% margin.
PPA operating profit was $527M, a 13.2% margin, on net sales down 6%, with price +2.5 points and currency +1.5 points.
IEEPA tariff refunds were $110M in Q3 and $382M for fiscal 2026 to date, and Financial Services net income was $219M.
guidance: Dan Pooley, Manager, Investor Communications, guided FY2026 net income to $4.75B-$5B, up from $4.5B-$5B last quarter.
Pooley guided PPA net sales down about 10% (prior range down 5%-10%) with margin of 11%-12% (prior 11%-13%).
Pooley guided Small Ag & Turf net sales up about 15% with margin of 14.5%-15.5% (prior 13.5%-15%), and C&F net sales up about 20% with margin of 10.5%-11.5% (prior 10%-12%).
Pooley guided equipment operations cash flow to $5B-$5.5B (prior $4.5B-$5.5B) and Financial Services net income to $870M (prior $860M).
Brent Norwood, CFO, expects the 2027 direct tariff run rate near $1B.

qa.question: Is the net tariff impact in 2027 a headwind, tailwind or neutral versus about $800M this year?
qa.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind: about $1.1B direct less $382M of refunds leaves roughly $750M net this year, against a 2027 run rate near $1B.

qa.question: Did anything slip between Q3 and Q4, given tractor inventory built in Q3, and what is the cadence exiting the year?
qa.answer: Seibert said not to read much into Q3, as shipment plans were set and some demand was pulled ahead. Brent Norwood, CFO, said Q4 PPA and C&F net sales should be similar to Q3, with no refund benefit and seasonally higher R&D and SA&G lowering PPA and SAT margins.

qa.question: Why does C&F guidance imply about 50 bps of price in Q4 versus +8% in Q3, and how large should dealer rental grow?
qa.answer: Q3 had easy comps, as Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives, and Q4 has nothing outsized. Norwood said 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as rental, and dealer fleet expansion could lift inventory fill next year.
qa.read: Answered partially; no target fleet size or economics given.

qa.question: What drove the tariff cut to $1.1B, and how is the Deere-designed excavator launch going?
qa.answer: The run rate moved from $1.2B to $1.1B excluding refunds, with five of 12 months benefiting this year and a further tailwind in 2027. Norwood said three Deere-designed excavator models launched this spring with very positive feedback, and more models follow over three to four years.

qa.question: How do production and retail compare by region for 2027, and what are 2027 pricing expectations?
qa.answer: PPA and C&F are each underproducing retail by about a couple of percentage points in 2026. Deanna Kovar said EOP pricing was set months ago and the focus is covering inflation into 2027.

qa.question: How are C&F order programs shaping up, and how much is dealer rental fleet loading?
qa.answer: C&F has four to five months of orders on hand versus a typical two to three, driven by infrastructure, data center starts and rental channels.
qa.read: Answered partially; rental share not quantified.

exchanges.question: How are production versus retail by region shaping up for 2027 given the EOP up mid-single digits, and what are 2027 pricing expectations given inflation concerns?
exchanges.answer: PPA and C&F are each modestly underproducing retail in 2026, by about a couple of percentage points, due to South America caution and C&F orders four to five months out. Kovar said EOP pricing was set months ago and the focus is covering inflation across EOP products and the PPA portfolio into 2027.

exchanges.question: What drove the tariff expectation change to $1.1 billion, and what is the status of the new Deere-designed excavator launch and adoption?
exchanges.answer: Tariff run rate moved from $1.2 billion to $1.1 billion, excluding refunds, mainly from Section 232 changes: import rate dropped from roughly 25% to 15%, effective June 1, so five of 12 months benefit this year, with a further tailwind in 2027. Norwood said three Deere-designed excavator models launched this spring, feedback is very positive, and more models roll out over three to four years.

exchanges.question: Did anything slip between Q3 and Q4, given tractor inventory built in Q3 ahead of the industry, and what is the cadence exiting the year?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said not to read much into Q3; shipment plans were set and some demand was pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk. Kovar said sold-ahead and retail pace are on historical trend. Norwood said Q4 net sales for PPA and C&F should be similar to Q3, with no refund benefit in Q4 and seasonally higher R&D and SA&G lowering PPA and SAT margins.

exchanges.question: How might mix from higher technology take rates affect 2027, versus the 2-3 point mix benefit cited in past years?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said it is too early to tell given uncertainty in inputs, commodities, Black Sea disruptions, softness in the EU and Brazil, and construction growth. EOP tech adoption and how programs wrap up will drive mix, but he is encouraged by the signals. No mix figure was given.

exchanges.question: What regional variability did you see in the EOP, and could mid-single-digit growth reach high single digits as programs close?
exchanges.answer: The U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada, which is a very limited part of planter sales. Time will tell if it improves as EOPs close. Best signals are the technology take rates: See & Spray doubling on factory-installed sprayer orders and 40% of planters taking advanced technology.

exchanges.question: Was the cadence of EOP orders affected by recent grain price improvement or technology decisions, given orders were already up a month and a half ago?
exchanges.answer: She would not read much into cadence, which came as expected. Deere tweaked the program to give dealers more choice, and technology take rates were a pleasant surprise. They hope the mid-single-digit increase extends.

exchanges.question: How are 8 Series tractor orders trending, and would Europe respond to a crop price response like North America?
exchanges.answer: 8R orders are as expected, with orders four to five months out and the model year 2026 shipment schedule closed. Corn futures are about $5.05, a good signal. Brazil takes a three-month order book and Q4 orders are in hand; the Move financing program at single-digit rates may help 2027. Europe is mixed: arable is challenged while dairy and livestock are stable. Order pace is as expected with no recent step-up.

exchanges.question: How are C&F order programs shaping up, and how much is dealer rental fleet loading?
exchanges.answer: C&F order trends are very positive, with four to five months of orders on hand versus a typical two to three months. Drivers are infrastructure, data center starts, independent rental channel and dealer-owned rental fleets. Underproduction in 2026 gives an opportunity into 2027. No rental share was quantified.

exchanges.question: Is net tariff impact for 2027 versus roughly $800 million this year a headwind, tailwind or neutral?
exchanges.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind. This year is about $1.1 billion direct less $382 million refunds, roughly $750 million net. Next year's run rate is expected near $1 billion, so tariff expense steps up.

exchanges.question: Why does C&F guidance imply about 50 bps of price in Q4 versus +8% in Q3, and how big do you want dealer rental to grow and how does it change the economics?
exchanges.answer: Q3 had easy comps, since Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives; Q4 has nothing outsized and pricing is going well. Norwood said 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as rental, dealer fleets have grown and some want to expand, which could boost inventory fill next year. No target size or economics were given.

exchanges.question: Are there merchandising incentives and what do EOP pricing trends imply for 2027 margins; and what does the FTC settlement on right to repair mean for aftermarket and lifecycle parts?
exchanges.answer: Seibert said pricing is measured and committed to covering inflation, with nothing outsized; no incentive or margin direction given. Norwood said Deere has always supported repair choice, the agreement formalizes tools like Operations Center PRO Service, and it will support the lifecycle solutions business long term. He did not address the $2-3 billion figure.

exchanges.question: Will the 2028 EU CAP policy change pull demand forward into 2027 or delay purchases, and any directional 2027 view for Europe?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell whether policy pulls demand forward or delays it. Orders are four to five months out and Q1 orders are just starting. Arable sentiment depends on inputs and commodity prices; dairy and livestock look stable.

exchanges.question: How are Brazilian and U.S. farmers positioning on input costs and how does it affect crop and purchase decisions?
exchanges.answer: Input price uncertainty exists everywhere and fertilizer impact differs by country. Farmers are seeking alternatives in products, amounts and sourcing but are not sharply cutting intended application and remain focused on yield. Larger farmers have multiple years of inputs contracted and are considering changes.

summary.overview: Kinsale reported Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS of $5.54, up 15.9% from $4.78, with a 75.5% combined ratio and 24.4% annualized operating ROE, while gross written premium fell 5% as the Commercial Property Division shrank. Excluding that division, GWP grew 3.7% in Q2 and 4.8% in 1H. Executives framed the quarter around holding profitability over growth in a softening E&S market and stepping up share buybacks.
keyTakeaways: Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, called commercial property a buyer's market where Kinsale is writing a shrinking volume of business.
GWP declined 5% overall but rose 3.7% excluding the Commercial Property Division, and new business submissions rose 6% (8% ex Commercial Property).
Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said London competition is creeping into long-tail occurrence lines and depressing Construction pricing.
The board added a $250M buyback authorization, bringing total capacity to $337M, which Kehoe described as the principal capital allocation while growth is limited.
Salmaan Allibhai, Chief Analytics and Technology Officer, said the accident year loss ratio could drift up over time as mix shifts away from property.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS was $5.54 versus $4.78 in Q2 2025, up 15.9%; net income rose 31.1% and net operating earnings rose 13.3%.
Combined ratio was 75.5%, including 4.5 points of favorable prior year development (vs 3.9) and 1.3 points of cat losses (vs under 1 point).
Expense ratio rose to 21.7% from 20.7%, while the other underwriting expense ratio fell to 10.3% from 10.6%.
Net written premium fell 1.4% while net earned premium rose 8.9%.
Net investment income rose 19.9%, float reached $3.4B versus $3.1B at end 2025, and new money yields are about 5.25% at a 4.25-year duration.
guidance: Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said the Q2 expense ratio of 21.7% is a good measure going forward, with a slight uptick in net commission possible after the June 1 reinsurance renewal.
Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, expects modestly easier GWP comparisons in Q3-Q4 2026 since 60% of Commercial Property Division premium was written in 1H25.
Buyback capacity totals $337M after an additional $250M authorization, up from about $87M remaining.
Stuart Winston, Chief Underwriting Officer, said 5 new products are launching imminently with 10 more in the pipeline.

qa.question: What drove the accident year loss ratio improvement versus 2Q25, and will the ceding commission rate rise after the reinsurance renewal?
qa.answer: Allibhai said losses came in below expectations amid normal variability and mix across a dozen statutory lines, with reserves as conservative as ever; Bryan Petrucelli, CFO, said treaties renewed June 1 so only one month was affected, a slight net commission uptick is possible partly offset by AI efficiency, and Q2's expense ratio is a good forward measure.

qa.question: Is Q2 the trough in commercial property, and what drives the 3.7% ex-property growth, including any shift to the admitted market?
qa.answer: Winston said there is no telling for 2027, citing pressure from London MGAs and traditional markets with large limits, said Kinsale will accept shrinking to meet return thresholds, noted London competition depressing Construction pricing, and said some flow to admitted is occurring but is not pervasive.
qa.read: Answered partially; no view on timing.

qa.question: Are inbound accounts rising from broker engagement or pricing, what are casualty loss trends and social inflation, and was the AY benefit all short-tail property?
qa.answer: Winston said both, citing an idle broker initiative, with hit ratios roughly unchanged; Salmaan Allibhai put casualty loss trend at mid-single digits with little social inflation given small accounts and low limits, and short-tail lines performing especially well; Michael Kehoe added IBNR releases slower in long-tail occurrence lines.

qa.question: How did property pricing move Q2 vs Q1, will the AY loss ratio drift up with mix shift, and what is buyback pacing?
qa.answer: Kehoe said equilibrium will come eventually as cats occur but gave no timing; Stuart Winston said Agribusiness Property and small business property are stable and growing while Inland Marine sees more competition; Salmaan Allibhai said the AY loss ratio could drift up; Kehoe said the first $100M buyback was exhausted, about $80M remains of a $250M program plus a new $250M, with growth taking priority when it accelerates.
qa.read: Answered partially; declined to time the property cycle.

qa.question: How much are E&S casualty ROEs compressing, and how are broker commissions evolving in the soft market?
qa.answer: Kehoe said all lines are managed to 20%+ ROE with most running ahead and 24.4% for the quarter, and that commission tension is normal but heightened in a soft market.
qa.read: Answered partially; no line-level ROE compression figure.

summary.overview: Eli Lilly's Q2 2026 revenue grew 48% year over year, with MOUNJARO and ZEPBOUND contributing $14.9 billion (+$6.3 billion) and non-GAAP EPS of $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D charges. Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $85-87 billion from $82-85 billion and the non-GAAP performance margin range to 49%-50.5%. The call centred on the U.S. Foundayo launch, which Ilya Yuffa, President of Lilly USA, said is now showing an inflection, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge rollout, and the retatrutide BLA pathway.
keyTakeaways: Ilya Yuffa, President of Lilly USA, said Foundayo volume almost doubled in the last week of July versus a month earlier, about one in four new starts are on Foundayo, and prescribers rose to 36,000 from about 8,000 at the last call.
Dave Ricks, Chair and CEO, said Lilly is seeking a BLA pathway for retatrutide with submission expected by Q1 2027, after a mixed first court decision and active litigation.

Lucas Montarce, CFO, said Q2 and recent quarters included one-off prior-period U.S. rebate adjustments not expected to recur in H2, and ZEPBOUND net price is expected to fall as CVS open access starts in Q4.
Ilya Yuffa said the Medicare Bridge program expands access to about 35% more Americans, with roughly 80% of treated patients on injectables and 60%-70% new patients previously lacking access.

Patrik Jonsson, President of Lilly International, said MOUNJARO TRx continues to grow in India and Brazil after generic semaglutide launches, and Foundayo's major ex-U.S. rollout begins in early 2027 with no supply gating.
financialHighlights: Revenue grew 48% versus Q2 2025, with U.S. revenue up 33% on volume and U.S. price down 3% (down 9% excluding rebate estimate adjustments).
Gross margin was 86.3%, up about 1.3 percentage points; non-GAAP performance margin was 54.8%, up 9 points.
Non-GAAP EPS was $8.38 including $3.03 of acquired IPR&D, versus $6.31 including $0.14 a year earlier.
Europe grew 55% constant currency including a $250 million Jardiance milestone; Japan 30%, China 93%, rest of world 136%.
Oncology, immunology and neuroscience key products grew 121%; Ebglyss sales more than doubled and Jaypirca grew 56%; Lilly paid $1.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $1.6 billion of shares.
guidance: Lucas Montarce, CFO, raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $85-87 billion from $82-85 billion, a $2.5 billion increase at midpoint.

Lucas Montarce raised the FY2026 non-GAAP performance margin range to 49%-50.5% from 47%-48.5%, and set non-GAAP EPS at $35.50-36.50 (up $2.78 at midpoint before $3.03 Q2 IPR&D charges) versus $35.50-37 previously.
Dan Skovronsky, Chief Scientific and Product Officer, expects the retatrutide U.S. BLA submission in Q1 2027; Dave Ricks expects Foundayo Type 2 diabetes U.S. regulatory action later this year.

Lucas Montarce expects Foundayo global rollout in all major markets in 2027 and the first OSA readout later this year; Dan Skovronsky expects lebrikizumab every-12-week dosing data in 2027 and EU approval of Onswik in coming months.
Lucas Montarce said H2 guidance factors non-recurring rebate adjustments, Europe Q3 vacation seasonality, U.S. T2D Q4 seasonality and a lower ZEPBOUND net price offset by volume.

qa.answer: Guidance rose $2.5 billion at midpoint; Q2 and recent quarters included one-off prior-period U.S. rebate adjustments not expected to recur, the 2025 base had a bolus of MOUNJARO country launches that won't repeat, and Europe Q3 and U.S. T2D Q4 seasonality are factored; H2 dollar growth is still expected to be significant.

With CVS access starting Q4, medical-exception, cash and competitor patients will shift, net price is expected to fall, which is embedded in guidance and more than offset by volume.

exchanges.question: How does Lilly envision expanding its consumer-driven obesity treatment opportunity, and how similar or different are the U.S. and international self-pay markets?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Obesity treatment utilization is still mid-single-digit in the U.S. and globally, leaving significant opportunity; access is improving via Bridge and state Medicaid going live or committing to next year. Q2 obesity TRxs were 3 million, driven by both injectable and oral new patients; about 55% of ZEPBOUND prescriptions are self-pay, and Lilly is investing in consumer awareness and expanding LillyDirect. OUS obesity remains mainly out of pocket; Lilly is replicating U.S. consumer practices and has launched versions of LillyDirect outside the U.S., with models varying by local regulation.

exchanges.question: Why has the U.S. Foundayo launch curve been slower than anticipated and when is an inflection expected; and how are competitive dynamics ex-U.S. evolving, including UAE share now that Novo's oral is there?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Three launch priorities are physician education, access/affordability, and consumer awareness; in the last 30 days CVS added Foundayo in June, Bridge launched July 1, and the full DTC campaign started. In the last week of July volume almost doubled versus a month ago and about one in four new starts are on Foundayo, so an inflection is now visible. OUS, UAE launched early May with a strong start; most patients are incretin-naive, Lilly's combined incretin share held steady after a second oral entered, Mexico and Saudi launch next, most launches come in 2027 with no supply gating, and competitor data cited is often sell-in data with inventory noise.

exchanges.question: What are the requirements and milestones for retatrutide to be accepted under the BLA pathway, and would subsequent incretins also qualify as BLAs?
exchanges.answer: Lilly believes retatrutide qualifies as a biologic under both the amino acid count rule and as analogous to a protein; there was a mixed first court decision and litigation is active. Lilly hopes to reach a conclusion with FDA to support a BLA, has all clinical data needed but must gather more CMC data, is in communication with the agency and will update investors on filing status. Submission is expected by Q1 next year.

exchanges.question: What are the early learnings and surprises from the Medicare obesity Bridge rollout, including the initial ramp and orals versus injectables?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Bridge expands access to about 35% more Americans; prior authorization is working well, criteria are clear, and LillyDirect can fulfill Bridge prescriptions. An inflection is visible for both ZEPBOUND and MOUNJARO over the last few weeks, partly from Bridge; around 80% of people getting treatment are on injectables, and approximately 60%-70% are new patients who lacked access before.

exchanges.question: Does Lilly need a commercial strategy to protect against unapproved retatrutide available today, and does retatrutide's higher efficacy open additional indications beyond tirzepatide's?
exchanges.answer: People are awaiting authentic retatrutide and are expected to embrace the guaranteed product once approved. Higher efficacy opens additional opportunities: knee osteoarthritis pain reduced by unprecedented amounts, 75%, in TRIUMPH-4 and TRIUMPH-1; a MASH/MASLD study is ongoing leveraging glucagon action; a chronic lower back pain study will read out next year; additional indications are being evaluated internally.

exchanges.question: What is the post-Verzenio breast cancer strategy, and is an all-oral combination of the SERD and oral PI3K inhibitor on the table?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: Lilly believes it has the best medicines against the three key breast cancer targets—estrogen receptor, CDK4/6, and PI3K alpha—and plans to combine them all. EMBER-4 adjuvant readout for imlunestrant/INLURIYO is next year; the tersolisib phase III program is about to begin, initially with existing endocrine therapies and investigator's choice CDK4/6, with later combination with INLURIYO envisioned as an all-oral regimen.

exchanges.question: Guidance implies a revenue deceleration in the back half versus Q2 despite Bridge and Foundayo access ramping—is something missed on price or is the team being conservative?
exchanges.answer: Guidance was raised $2.5 billion at midpoint for the full year. Recent quarters, including Q2, included one-off prior-period rebate and discount estimate adjustments in the U.S. that are not expected to recur in H2. The 2025 base included the bolus of MOUNJARO launches in many new countries, which will not repeat; future OUS growth is penetration-driven, and dollar growth in H2 is still expected to be significant. Guidance also factors Europe Q3 vacation seasonality and U.S. Type 2 diabetes Q4 seasonality.

exchanges.question: Which OUS regions are seeing the most MOUNJARO growth, and what is Lilly seeing in India with generic semaglutide launching?
exchanges.answer: MOUNJARO performs strongly almost everywhere with market leadership in many markets; China NRDL delivered category leadership after 16 months, and Korea, the U.K., Mexico and Germany are key growth drivers, with share in many markets similar to or above U.S. levels. In India and Brazil, MOUNJARO TRx continues to grow after generic semaglutide launches, driven by superiority data; in Canada tirzepatide TRx grows at the same pace as the total market; generic companies face significant supply constraints.

exchanges.question: How extensive is Foundayo sampling and is it dampening IQVIA prescription data; is the U.S. prescriber base expanding and can it be quantified?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities
exchanges.answer: Sampling covers the first 30 days of the first dose, similar to a typical oral small molecule, extensively across the prescriber base with full supply. Prescribers increased from about 8,000 at the last earnings call to 36,000, with week-on-week growth in adoption and improved perception of the profile.

exchanges.question: ZEPBOUND net price of about $580 per prescription is well above cash prices; how sustainable are medical exceptions driving this now that CVS is back on formulary, and are they behind the favorable rebate adjustments?
exchanges.answer: ZEPBOUND pricing is transparent: LillyDirect $299 to $449, Bridge at $245, plus commercial pricing. Script size and medical exceptions are drivers of per-prescription price; per-pack price is significantly lower. With CVS access starting in Q4, patients who went to medical exception, cash or competitor after CVS moved to 101 last year will shift; medical exception is short-term, open access is the goal, and the net price is expected to go down, which is embedded in guidance and will be more than offset by volume growth.

exchanges.question: Are psychiatry and vaccines areas Lilly intends to scale as high priorities, or are the recent deals one-offs driven by interest in the science?
exchanges.responderTitle: President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development
exchanges.answer: Both areas share immense unmet need, the through line of Lilly's internal and BD work; the deals were acquired at prices allowing discipline and long-term value creation and are not different from other deals year to date. Lilly will not forward-look on whether it builds further in infectious disease or psychiatry, remaining opportunistic.

exchanges.question: Which one or two non-obesity pipeline assets should the street pay more attention to?
exchanges.answer: Cardiovascular: PCSK9 gene editing and oral and injectable Lp(a)-lowering drugs. Neuroscience: psychiatry, sleep-wake disorders via Centessa, addiction and major depressive disorder potentially addressable with incretin science. Oncology: richest readout period ever, including Kelonia in vivo CAR T for multiple myeloma and AJ1-11095 JAK inhibitor. Immunology: lebrikizumab growth with new indications, plus combination ideas in IBD and psoriatic diseases.

exchanges.question: Given UAE Foundayo sales of $31 million versus $67 million in the U.S., what is the ex-U.S. obesity potential, and will Foundayo be better reimbursed by ex-U.S. governments for diabetes than tirzepatide?
exchanges.answer: UAE start is encouraging but early with noise and initial inventory build; the majority of patients are incretin-naive and there is significant opportunity. Major OUS rollout happens in the beginning of 2027. Lilly is probably slightly better positioned for Type 2 reimbursement with an oral and three head-to-head trials, but OUS reimbursement takes time; launch focus will be chronic weight management.

summary.overview: Deere reported fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues of $12.608B, up 5% YoY, with net income of $1.379B ($5.10 diluted EPS) and an equipment operations margin of 14.4%. Construction & Forestry sales rose 18% and Small Ag & Turf 12%, while Production & Precision Ag fell 6%; full-year net income guidance was raised to $4.75B-$5B. Deanna Kovar, President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, described model year 2027 early order program results as reinforcing the view that 2026 is the bottom of the ag cycle.
keyTakeaways: Planter and sprayer early order programs are up mid-single digits versus the prior-year program, per Deanna Kovar, President, Worldwide Agriculture & Turf.
See & Spray factory adoption is nearly doubling to about one-third of North American sprayers on order, and over 40% of NA MY2027 planters carry advanced technology.
Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, said C&F has four to five months of orders on hand versus a typical two to three, driven by infrastructure, data centers and rental fleets.
Brent Norwood, CFO, said tariffs will be a headwind in FY2027, with a run rate near ~$1B versus ~$750M net in FY2026.
Chris Seibert said PPA and C&F are underproducing retail by a couple of percentage points each in 2026.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues were $12.608B, up 5%, with equipment operations net sales of $10.999B, up 6%.
PPA sales fell 6% to $3.998B with a 13.2% margin ($527M operating profit).
SAT sales rose 12% to $3.383B with an 18.4% margin ($622M).
C&F sales rose 18% to $3.618B on 8 points of price, with a 12.1% margin ($436M).
Tariff refunds of $110M were recognized in Q3, bringing FY26 to date to $382M.
guidance: FY2026 net income attributable to Deere raised to $4.75B-$5B from $4.5B-$5.0B, and equipment operations cash flow to $5B-$5.5B from $4.5B-$5.5B, per Dan Pooley, Manager, Investor Communications.
PPA FY26 sales now down ~10% (bottom of prior 5%-10% range) with margin narrowed to 11%-12% from 11%-13%; SAT margin raised to 14.5%-15.5% from 13.5%-15%.
C&F FY26 sales up ~20% with price raised to 3 points from 2.5, and margin tightened to 10.5%-11.5% from 10%-12%.
Chris Seibert cut FY26 direct tariff expense excluding refunds to ~$1.1B from $1.2B, assuming no further refunds in Q4.
Brent Norwood expects Q4 PPA and C&F net sales similar to Q3, with PPA and SAT margins lower on seasonal R&D/SA&G and no refunds.

qa.question: What drove the tariff estimate change to $1.1B, and how is the Deere-designed excavator launch going?
qa.answer: The cut from $1.2B came mainly from the Section 232 rate on European imports falling from ~25% to 15% effective June 1, covering five of 12 months this year with further benefit in FY2027; three excavator models are in market with more over the next three to four years.

qa.question: Will net tariff impact be a headwind, tailwind or neutral in 2027 versus 2026?
qa.answer: A headwind: FY26 is ~$1.1B direct less $382M refunds, or ~$750M net, while the FY27 run rate is expected closer to ~$1B.

qa.question: Did shipments slip from Q3 to Q4, and was tractor inventory built ahead of the industry?
qa.answer: He pushed back, saying not to read much into Q3, as some demand was pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk and there is no inventory concern; NA tractor shipments started slowly and are catching up.

qa.question: Why does the C&F price guide imply low Q4 price after +8% in Q3, and what are dealer rental ambitions?
qa.answer: Q3's 8% partly reflects an easy comp against ~5% negative price in Q3 2025, the guide has moved 2.5%→3%→2.5%→3%, and 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as rental, with dealers wanting larger fleets that could boost inventory fill next year.

qa.question: What are the margin implications of EOP pricing for next year, and what does the FTC right-to-repair settlement mean for aftermarket targets?
qa.answer: Deere is taking measured inflationary price and is committed to covering inflation over time amid oil and supplier tariffs, but gave no margin direction; Brent Norwood, CFO, said the FTC agreement formalizes existing tools such as Operations Center PRO Service.

qa.question: How are 8 Series tractor orders trending, and would Europe respond to crop price recovery like the U.S.?
qa.answer: 8R orders are as expected with the MY2026 schedule closed, ~$5.05 corn is a good signal, Brazil is too early to call for 2027, Europe arable is challenged while dairy/livestock is stable, and there has been no recent step-up in order pace.

exchanges.question: Production vs retail by region for 2027 setup; 2027 pricing expectations given EOP up mid-single digits and farm equipment inflation concerns.
exchanges.answer: PPA and C&F modestly underproducing in 2026, a couple percentage points each; PPA due to South America caution, C&F due to retail growth with orders four to five months out. EOP pricing rolled out months ago, focused on covering inflation across EOP products and PPA portfolio into 2027.

exchanges.question: What drove tariff expense estimate change to $1.1B; update on Deere-designed excavator launch and adoption.
exchanges.answer: Prior FY26 run rate $1.2B now $1.1B excluding refunds, mainly from Section 232 rate dropping from ~25% to 15% on European imports, effective June 1, so five of 12 months this year; further tailwind in FY2027. Excavator: first models launched this spring, three models in market, very positive feedback; more models rolling out over next three to four years.

exchanges.question: Did shipments slip between Q3 and Q4; was tractor inventory built in Q3 ahead of industry?
exchanges.answer: Don't read much into Q3; some demand pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk, no inventory concern. Retail pace on trend with historical averages; North America tractor shipments started slowly, making up time. Q4 net sales similar to Q3 for PPA and C&F; no refunds in Q4 and seasonal high R&D/SA&G will compress PPA and SAT margins.

exchanges.question: How might higher technology sales affect mix in 2027 versus historic 2-3 point mix benefit?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell given uncertainty in ag inputs, commodities, Black Sea disruptions, EU and Brazil softness; construction growth and EOP tech adoption and outcome, plus combines, will drive mix. Encouraged by signals.

exchanges.question: Regional variability in EOP and whether mid-single-digit growth could end high single digits.
exchanges.answer: Couple weeks left on sprayer EOP, longer on planters. U.S. trending slightly better than Canada, which is limited in planters. Time will tell whether it turns more positive; See & Spray factory orders doubling, 40% of planters with advanced tech.

exchanges.question: Cadence of EOP orders; was improvement driven by grain prices or technology decisions?
exchanges.answer: Cadence as expected; tweaks to EOP gave dealers more choice. Pleasantly surprised by tech take rates; hopeful mid-single-digit increase extends.

exchanges.question: 8 Series tractor order trends; would Europe respond to crop price recovery like the U.S.?
exchanges.answer: 8R orders as expected; orders four to five months out, MY2026 schedule closed, collecting Q1 orders. Corn futures about $5.05 a good signal. Brazil takes three-month order book; too early for 2027, move financing at single-digit rates may help. Europe mixed: arable challenged, dairy/livestock stable. No step-up in order pace recently.

exchanges.question: How C&F orders are shaping up and how much is dealer rental fleet loading.
exchanges.answer: Four to five months of orders on hand vs typical two to three months. Drivers: infrastructure, data centers, independent rental channel, dealer-owned rental fleets. 2026 underproduction gives opportunity in 2027.

exchanges.question: Will net tariff impact be headwind, tailwind or neutral in 2027 vs 2026?
exchanges.answer: Headwind. FY26 ~$1.1B direct less $382M refunds ≈ $750M net; FY27 run rate expected closer to ~$1B.

exchanges.question: C&F price guide implies low Q4 price vs +8% in Q3; dealer rental aspirations and economics.
exchanges.answer: Price guide moved 2.5%→3%→2.5%→now 3%; Q3 8% partly easy comp vs ~5% negative price in Q3 2025 from incentives; Q4 nothing outsized, road building helps. 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as rental and growing; dealers want to expand rental fleets, could boost inventory fill next year.

exchanges.question: EOP merchandising incentives and margin implication of backlog for next year; FTC right-to-repair settlement implications for aftermarket and $2-3B lifecycle parts target.
exchanges.answer: Taking measured inflationary price, committed to cover inflation over time; dynamic environment with oil and supplier tariffs; no margin direction given. FTC agreement formalizes existing tools like Operations Center PRO Service (diagnostics, manuals, software updates); supports lifecycle solutions aspirations.

exchanges.question: Will EU CAP budget change in 2028 pull forward or delay European demand in 2027; directional 2027 Europe forecast.
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell; order book four to five months out. Arable sentiment depends on input costs and commodity prices; dairy and livestock stable.

exchanges.question: How Brazilian and U.S. farmers are positioning on input costs and effect on crop decisions.
exchanges.answer: Uncertainty everywhere; fertilizer impact differs by region. Farmers seeking alternatives but not seeing huge reduction in application; larger farmers have multiple years of inputs contracted; still focused on yield.

summary.overview: Chipotle reported Q2 2026 revenue of $3.3B, up 9.3% year-over-year, with comparable restaurant sales up 2.2% (transactions +1%, pricing ~1.6%) and adjusted diluted EPS of $0.33, flat to last year, while restaurant-level margin fell 220 bps to 25.2%. Adam Rymer, CFO, raised full-year comp guidance to low single digits from about flat but guided Q3 comps to around +1%, embedding a roughly 200 bps industry Cyclospora headwind that began in the second half of July. Scott Boatwright, CEO, framed the quarter as early days of the Recipe for Growth strategy, pointing to menu innovation, the HEAP rollout and the rewards relaunch.
keyTakeaways: Adam Rymer, CFO, said traffic improved through Q2 and into early July, then comps softened about 200 bps in the second half of July around the industry Cyclospora issue; Scott Boatwright, CEO, said Chipotle is not involved and the implicated products are not on its menu.
Rymer confirmed the Q3 guide of ~1% implies an underlying ~3% trend with the 200 bps headwind assumed to persist, and called Q3 the toughest lap of the year.

Boatwright said HEAP is in more than 1,000 restaurants, yields two to four labor hours reinvested in prep and peak line, and adds two to three entrees in Max 15, with 2,000 targeted by year-end and the full portfolio in 2027.

Digital sales reached $1.3B, 38.3% of sales versus 35.5% a year ago; Boatwright attributed the ~18% growth to the rewards relaunch and Summer of Extras, with a frictionless in-restaurant rewards pay pilot launching in August.

Rymer said younger and lower-income cohorts, previously most pressured, improved the most, and Boatwright cited the highest year-over-year wallet share gains since 2024 across all income and age groups.
financialHighlights: Revenue $3.3B, up 9.3% year-over-year; comps +2.2% with transaction comp +1% and pricing ~1.6%.
Restaurant-level margin 25.2%, down 220 bps, with cost of sales 29.7% (+~80 bps), labor 25% (+~30 bps), other operating 14.9% (+~90 bps) and marketing 3% (+~30 bps).
Adjusted diluted EPS $0.33, flat year-over-year; non-GAAP G&A $176M ($148M underlying).
Opened 101 restaurants (100 company-owned, 80 Chipotlanes, 1 international partner-operated); new unit productivity ~80% with ~60% year-two cash-on-cash returns.
Repurchased $631M in Q2 at $32.55 average and $1.3B+ year-to-date; $1.7B authorization remaining after a $1.3B addition, with cash and investments of $800M, down $1.3B year-over-year.
guidance: Adam Rymer, CFO, raised FY2026 comparable sales to low single-digit range from about flat; Q3 comps around +1% assuming the ~200 bps Cyclospora impact persists.
Rymer expects Q3 pricing in the mid 2% range against inflation of about 3%, with pricing and inflation expected to match from Q4 forward; full-year pricing near the high end of 1%-2%.
Q3 cost lines per Rymer: cost of sales just under 30%, labor mid 25%, other operating mid 15%, marketing low 3%, non-GAAP G&A around $180M; FY depreciation ~3% of sales and tax rate 24%-26%.
Scott Boatwright, CEO, reiterated approximately 350 openings in 2026, about 80% with Chipotlanes, and HEAP in ~2,000 restaurants by year-end with the full portfolio sometime in 2027.
Boatwright expects Seoul in 2026, Singapore early 2027, Mexico City 2027, Saudi Arabia in the near future, and a national catering/Build-Your-Own Chipotle launch in 2027.

qa.question: Color on the low single-digit comp guide, Q3 and recent softening trends.
qa.answer: Traffic improved through Q2 and into the first half of July; second-half July comps softened ~200 bps around the industry Cyclospora issue. Q3 comps expected around +1% assuming the impact continues, as duration is hard to predict; Q3 is the toughest lap of the year. Scott Boatwright added Chipotle is not involved and sources lettuce in California.

qa.question: Does the ~1% Q3 guide imply an underlying ~3% trend with a 200 bps headwind persisting, and where is Max 15 throughput ex-HEAP?
qa.answer: Yes; expense guidance assumes the impact continues through the quarter. HEAP restaurants do two or three more entrees in Max 15; in-store Max 15 is in the low 20s, digital (almost 40% of sales) mid-teens, combined low to mid-30s per restaurant per day.

qa.question: Margin outlook beyond Q3 and the narrowing pricing-inflation gap.
qa.answer: Gap was widest in H1 (pricing ~1% vs inflation low-to-mid 3%); Q3 inflation ~3% vs pricing mid 2%; from Q4 forward pricing and inflation expected to match, eliminating the dislocation.

qa.question: Why 350 openings per year versus the prior 400 ceiling, and what gates acceleration?
qa.answer: One restaurant per day is what the organization can support with ready-now leaders; above 350 risks opening quality. Incremental growth comes from company-owned Western Europe and partner markets; Alshaya is at 15 restaurants across three or four countries with meaningful acceleration planned for 2027.

qa.question: Any regional World Cup benefit, and what the rolling pricing rollout showed?
qa.answer: About 300 restaurants within ~10 miles of stadiums saw a 50-100 bps comp benefit, but overall quarter impact was under five basis points. Rolling pricing measures resistance market by market; consumer reads allowed continued pushing, and the dislocation was a timing impact.

qa.question: Chipotle is doing and spending a lot for 1%-2% comps; how can you be confident momentum builds into 2027?
qa.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflects early days of Recipe for Growth and HEAP/throughput/hospitality investment; additional levers (menu innovation, rewards, brand communication, group occasions) show green shoots and will build through H2 2026 into 2027. Digital and brand ideas were described as industry-changing but not detailed.

unanswered.question: How can you be confident comp momentum picks up into 2027 given the recent slowdown and tough comparisons?
unanswered.how: Scott Boatwright pointed to green shoots and unspecified industry-changing digital and brand work without quantifying any 2027 driver.

unanswered.question: Sizing of the remodel program, expected sales uplift and timeline.
unanswered.how: Boatwright gave the $100,000-$300,000 per-restaurant test cost but said he had nothing to report on returns or scale.

unanswered.how: Adam Rymer declined to give individual LTO lifts, offering only that lifts are typically hundreds of basis points.

whatChanged.toneShift: Prior call stressed remaining cautious on outlook with upside; this call raised the full-year comp but paired it with a quantified external headwind, with Adam Rymer citing heightened consumer caution and difficulty predicting duration while Scott Boatwright shifted to early-days momentum language.

exchanges.question: Do returning pantry LTOs (e.g., Chicken al Pastor) still deliver lifts as good or better than prior runs? And are value perceptions changing given generous portions and years of underpricing the industry?
exchanges.answer: Chipotle Honey Chicken performed better the second time around, as do many LTOs, though there is likely a point of diminishing returns around the fifth or sixth time; menu innovation has been ramped 4x versus a couple of years ago with new items coming in months ahead. Brand tracker showed solid progress on value perception across all income groups and age cohorts, with affordability scores the best in roughly the past couple of years. Value is about convenience, execution and menu innovation, not just price; the high-protein menu is contributing.

exchanges.question: Pushback: Chipotle seems to be doing and spending a lot to get 1%-2% comps; how can you be confident momentum picks up into 2027 given recent slowdown and tough comparisons?
exchanges.answer: Q2 transaction growth reflects early days of Recipe for Growth, especially menu innovation, plus investment in execution via HEAP, throughput and hospitality; early proof points in guest satisfaction, food quality and consistency confirm the path. Additional drivers (menu innovation, rewards engagement, brand communication, group occasions) are showing green shoots and will build through second half 2026 into 2027. Arlie's digital ideas and Fernando's brand work are described as industry-changing but not shared on the call.

exchanges.question: More color on the low single-digit 2026 comp guide, Q3 and recent trends including the softening, and cadence from here.
exchanges.answer: Traffic improved throughout Q2 and momentum continued into the first half of July; in the second half of July comps softened about 200 basis points around the industry Cyclospora issue. Q3 is the toughest lap of the year; Q3 comps expected around +1%, assuming the roughly 200 basis point impact continues since duration is hard to predict. Year-to-date performance plus Q3 setup and Q4 plans drove the raise to low single-digit full-year comps. Scott added Chipotle is impacted on sales but not involved in the Cyclospora issue; products implicated are not on its menu and lettuces are sourced in California.

exchanges.question: Update on sizing the store refresh/remodel program (three investment levels for ~1,000-1,500 stores), expected sales uplift and timeline; and whether partners could be leveraged in other international markets instead of owning stores.
exchanges.answer: No aesthetic remodel has been done in brand history; this year is a stage-gate test of a remodel refresh program with several locations across several geographies at $100,000-$300,000 per restaurant to measure consumer perception and returns. Nothing to report yet; work is in flight and management is optimistic but patient. Partnerships exist with Alshaya (Middle East), Alsea (Latin America) and SPC (Southeast Asia), via partner-operated and/or JVs; Western Europe will remain company-owned, rest of world partner-operated.

exchanges.question: Digital sales grew ~18% year-over-year; was there a catalyst that unlocked this four quarters ago, and is it linked to loyalty and payment changes at the register?
exchanges.answer: It is all linked; last year's Summer of Extras showed where the brand can win in digital and informed the rewards relaunch a couple of months ago, which removed friction and added flexibility on earning and redeeming. This year's Summer of Extras has accelerated digital revenue, aided by an emerging trend. Arlie is taking a holistic look at digital; innovation over the next weeks and months is expected to be game changing.

exchanges.question: Will HEAP labor efficiency all be reinvested into the production line, and could it drive positive traffic and customer satisfaction?
exchanges.answer: Yes; HEAP yields about two to four hours of labor efficiency depending on volume, which is kept in-restaurant for morning prep and peak line deployment. This translates to transaction gains in Max 15 throughput and total sales, plus better taste of food scores. Rollout targets 2,000 restaurants by year-end, with the entire portfolio hoped for sometime in 2027; all new restaurants come standard with HEAP.

exchanges.question: Why is 350 company-operated openings per year the right level versus the prior 400 ceiling, and what gates acceleration above 350?
exchanges.answer: One restaurant per day is meaningful growth the organization can support given white space and the ability to develop ready-now leaders; going beyond 350 risks diminishing returns in opening quality or fracturing the base. Incremental growth will come from Western Europe company-owned and partner-operated markets; the Alshaya partnership started a couple of years ago and is already at 15 restaurants across three or four countries with meaningful acceleration planned for 2027. Historical total growth targets still seen as achievable.

exchanges.question: With a new CMO, where should brand positioning go given the For Real campaign feels stale; will value and ingredient quality be highlighted more prominently versus limited-service competitors?
exchanges.answer: For Real was extraordinary and served the brand for many years; Fernando's work is the next evolution, not a 180 pivot. Messaging will show more fresh in-restaurant preparation, ingredient usage and cultivating a better world, with creative ambition to break through sameness on television. Value will be highlighted as best ingredients prepared fresh daily at abundance and speed at an approachable price, not discounting.

exchanges.question: Is the ~1% Q3 comp guide implying an underlying ~3% trend with a 200 basis point Cyclospora headwind assumed to persist? And where is system Max 15 throughput ex-HEAP?
exchanges.answer: Yes, that is correct; expense line guidance is based on the 1% comp guide and assumes the impact continues through the rest of the quarter. HEAP restaurants do about two or three more entrees in Max 15; overall in-store Max 15 is in the low 20 range, digital (almost 40% of sales) in the mid-teens, combined low to mid-30s per restaurant per day.

exchanges.question: Elaborate on in-restaurant loyalty promotion efforts, what is working and what can improve; do the ~80% of in-store transactions without loyalty over-index to lower income guests?
exchanges.answer: No, non-loyalty in-store transactions are broad-based, not skewed to lower income. Current experience is clunky (phone, app, card); in August Curt and team launch one-stop pay where paying earns rewards points automatically and guests can be enrolled, without relying on restaurant teams so throughput is protected. More consumer education on the in-restaurant program still needed.

exchanges.question: Elaborate on new menu items coming in months ahead: center-of-plate or sides?
exchanges.answer: Culinary team expanded to drive new news beyond pantry items; focus is center-of-the-plate items, with teams also on beverage, sides and desserts. Big ideas are in the stage-gate process and could appear on the calendar back half of 2026, certainly in 2027.

exchanges.question: Update on Q2 and 3Q-to-date trends by age and income cohort; are younger and lower-to-middle income guests improving relative to higher income?
exchanges.answer: The younger and lower income cohorts, previously under most pressure, have improved the most; results from Q1 into Q2 are broad-based with outsized gains in those groups, driven by menu innovation (Chipotle Honey Chicken, Cilantro Lime Sauce) and promotions like Matchday BOGO. Scott added the highest year-over-year wallet share gains last quarter since 2024, and share taken in each month of 2026 across all income cohorts and age groups.

exchanges.question: Margin outlook beyond Q3, and update on the gap between pricing and inflation narrowing toward year-end.
exchanges.answer: The price-inflation gap was widest in the first half (pricing ~1%, inflation low to mid 3%) and is easing with the rolling pricing strategy. Q3 inflation expected closer to about 3% with pricing in the mid 2% range; from Q4 forward pricing and inflation are expected to match, eliminating the dislocation.

exchanges.question: Any regional divergence showing a World Cup benefit? And what was learned from methodical pricing rollout that gives comfort trending toward the high end of the 1%-2% guide?
exchanges.answer: About 300 restaurants within roughly 10 miles of World Cup stadiums saw a 50 to 100 basis point comp benefit during the tournament, but overall quarter impact was less than five basis points. The rolling pricing strategy allows measuring resistance precisely market by market and adjusting to inflation; consumer reads allowed continued pushing forward, the strategy will continue, and the dislocation was a timing impact.

exchanges.question: Color on LTO contribution to frequency/traffic versus historical benchmarks; and do high-protein LTOs attract new guests or existing ones?
exchanges.answer: No specifics on individual LTO lifts, but Chipotle Honey Chicken and Chicken al Pastor drove transaction increases from most frequent guests visiting more often plus new guests; typically hundreds of basis points of transaction lift, most sustained through the promotion, with stickiness measured afterward; viewed as a multi-year AUV lever. Scott added LTOs bring new customers whose lifetime value rises materially, existing guests visit more; a couple more center-of-plate items, sides innovation and a meaningful beverage push are coming in the back half.
