summary.overview: Kinsale Capital Group reported fiscal Q2 2026 diluted operating EPS of $5.54, up 15.9% from $4.78, with an annualized operating ROE of 24.4% and a combined ratio of 75.5%. Gross written premium fell 5% as the Commercial Property Division continued to shrink, while GWP excluding that division grew 3.7% in the quarter and 4.8% in the first half. Michael Kehoe, Chairman, President and CEO, announced an additional $250 million buyback authorization, taking total capacity to $337 million.
keyTakeaways: Gross written premium fell 5% overall but rose 3.7% excluding the Commercial Property Division, where Kehoe said Kinsale is writing a shrinking volume in a buyer's market.
Pricing trend on the MS Amlin index worsened to -5.9% from -3.3% in Q1 2026, with Stuart Winston, CUO, citing London competition creeping into liability occurrence lines and Construction.
Combined ratio of 75.5% included 4.5 pts of favorable prior-year development (vs 3.9 pts) and 1.3 pts of cat losses (vs less than 1 pt).

Board added a $250 million buyback authorization on top of roughly $80 million remaining, for $337 million total; Kehoe called buybacks the principal capital allocation strategy alongside a small dividend.
New business submissions grew 6% (8% ex-Commercial Property), with 24 wholesale and 176 retail (Aspera) broker appointments and 9 product offerings or enhancements rolled out year to date.
financialHighlights: Diluted operating EPS $5.54, up 15.9% from $4.78 in Q2 2025; net income up 31.1% and net operating earnings up 13.3%.
Net written premium down 1.4%; net earned premium up 8.9%.
Expense ratio 21.7% vs 20.7% in Q2 2025; other underwriting expense ratio 10.3% vs 10.6%.
Net investment income up 19.9%; float $3.4 billion, up from $3.1 billion at end of 2025.
Annualized gross investment return 4.5% for 1H26 vs 4.3% last year; new money yields around 5.25% at 4.25-year duration.

summary.overview: Deere reported fiscal Q3 2026 net sales and revenues of $12.608 billion, up 5% year-over-year, with equipment operations net sales of $10.999 billion, up 6%, a 14.4% equipment operations margin, net income of $1.379 billion and diluted EPS of $5.10. Dan Pooley, Manager of Investor Communications, narrowed FY2026 net income guidance to $4.75 billion-$5 billion from $4.5 billion-$5 billion, while Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf, said model year 2027 early order program orders are up mid-single digits and reinforce the view that 2026 is the ag cycle bottom. Construction & Forestry grew 18% with 8 points of price, and Brent Norwood, CFO, flagged net tariff expense stepping up to around $1 billion in FY2027.
keyTakeaways: Model year 2027 planter and sprayer early order program orders are up mid-single digits, with See & Spray factory adoption nearly doubling to about one-third of North American sprayers on order and more than 40% of planters taking the most advanced technologies, per Deanna Kovar, President of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf.
Deanna Kovar described the EOP results as reinforcing 2026 as the ag cycle bottom but said fundamentals support a measured recovery rather than a sharp rebound in 2027.

Direct tariff expense for FY2026 was lowered to approximately $1.1 billion from $1.2 billion as Section 232 tariffs dropped from roughly 25% to 15% effective 1 June, but Brent Norwood, CFO, expects FY2027 net tariff expense of right around $1 billion versus approximately $750 million net this year.

Chris Seibert, Director of Investor Relations, said C&F has four to five months of orders on hand versus a typical two to three, driven by infrastructure, data center starts and rental channels, and PPA and C&F are each underproducing retail by a couple of percentage points in 2026.
Brent Norwood said Q4 PPA and C&F net sales should be similar to Q3, but margins will come in a little with no refund benefit and seasonally high R&D and SA&G in PPA and SAT.
financialHighlights: Net sales and revenues of $12.608 billion, up 5%; equipment operations net sales of $10.999 billion, up 6%; equipment operations margin 14.4%; net income $1.379 billion; diluted EPS $5.10.

Production & Precision Ag net sales of $3.998 billion, down 6% (price +2.5 points, currency slightly over +1.5 points), with operating profit of $527 million and a 13.2% margin, down on lower volumes and higher production costs.
Small Ag & Turf net sales of $3.383 billion, up 12%, with operating profit of $622 million and an 18.4% margin, up year-over-year.
Construction & Forestry net sales of $3.618 billion, up 18% (price +8 points, currency roughly +0.5 point), with operating profit of $436 million and a 12.1% margin.
Financial Services net income of $219 million, up on favorable financing spreads; tariff refunds of $110 million recognized in Q3, bringing the FY2026 total to $382 million.

exchanges.question: How to think about production versus retail by region for the 2027 setup, and what are pricing expectations for 2027 given the mid-single-digit EOP and inflationary cost concerns?
exchanges.answer: PPA and C&F are modestly underproducing retail this year, a couple percentage points for each segment; shipping plans are set for the full year and South America changes drive more caution. C&F underproduction reflects continuous retail growth and an order position four to five months out. EOP pricing was rolled out several months ago with focus on covering inflation, done across EOP products and the whole PPA portfolio heading into 2027.

exchanges.question: What is driving the tariff expense change to $1.1 billion, about $100 million lower than originally anticipated — July ag equipment relief or expected refunds? Also, update on the excavator launch and timing of broader adoption.
exchanges.answer: Previous FY2026 run rate was $1.2 billion, now $1.1 billion, excluding refunds; the change is mainly Section 232 tariffs dropping from roughly 25% to 15% on imported goods, particularly from Europe, effective 1st June so only five of 12 months impact this year, with a further tailwind in FY2027. Deere-designed excavator first models launched this spring, three models in market today, shipments just getting to customers with very positive feedback; the portfolio will roll out over the next three to four years.

exchanges.question: Did something slip between 3Q and 4Q, and why did tractor inventory build in 3Q ahead of the industry — is it offset by South America? What is the cadence exiting the year?
exchanges.answer: Don't read too much into Q3 changes; shipment plans are set and orders on hand, some demand pulled ahead to manage Q4 risk, nothing concerning on inventory. Factories are hitting forecasts; sold-ahead positions and retail pace across the Americas are on trend with historical averages, and North America tractor shipments started slowly so time is being made up. For 3Q to 4Q, PPA and C&F expect similar net sales in Q4 as Q3, but no refund benefit in Q4 and PPA and SAT have a seasonal high of R&D and SA&G in Q4, so margins will come in a little.

exchanges.question: How could mix, particularly higher technology sales in C&F and precision take rates in EOP, influence 2027 versus the historical 2- to 3-point mix benefit?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell given uncertainty in inputs, commodities and shipment disruptions such as the Black Sea; recent softness in the E.U. and Brazil needs to play out and South America can turn quickly. Construction growth could have a mix impact, as could EOP tech adoption, whether recovery is more than modest, and what combines do later this year. Encouraged by current signals.

exchanges.question: What regional variability did the early order program show, and could the mid-single-digit growth end up in the high single-digit range as programs wind down?
exchanges.answer: Sprayer EOP has a couple of weeks to go, planter EOP longer; U.S. is trending slightly better than Canada, which is a very limited part of the planter portfolio. Orders are up mid-single digit and time will tell whether that turns more positive. Best signals are technology take rates: a doubling of See & Spray on factory-installed sprayer orders and 40% of planters taking the most advanced technologies.

exchanges.question: What has the cadence of EOP orders been — did recent grain price improvement or technology decisions drive orders earlier?
exchanges.answer: Wouldn't read much into cadence; it has been as expected. Tweaks were made to the EOP this year to give dealers more choice and they came through as expected. Pleasantly surprised with technology take rates and hopeful the mid-single-digit increase extends well into the year.

exchanges.question: How are 8 Series tractor orders trending relative to the better EOPs, and how should Europe be viewed given heat and input cost stress — would it react like the U.S. to a crop price response?
exchanges.answer: 8R orders are as expected with orders four to five months out; model year 2026 shipment schedule is basically closed and orders are being collected for Q1; corn futures around $5.05 are a good signal. Brazil runs a three-month order book, Q4 orders on hand, too early to tell for 2027 though the move financing program at single-digit rates could help. Europe is mixed: arable farmers more challenged, Small Ag & Turf producers benefiting from strong dairy and livestock cash flows; overall order pace as expected with no step-up in the last one or two days.

exchanges.question: How are C&F order programs shaping up, and how much is dealer rental fleet loading and what is the outlook for that theme?
exchanges.answer: C&F order trends very positive with about four to five months of orders on hand, more than the typical two to three months. Drivers are large infrastructure projects, data center starts, participation in the independent rental channel and dealer-owned rental fleets. Underproduction in 2026 gives an opportunity entering 2027.

exchanges.question: With half-year 232 benefit this year and no further refunds in Q4, is the roughly $800 million net tariff impact a headwind, tailwind or neutral going into 2027?
exchanges.answer: Net tariffs will be a headwind next year. This year about $1.1 billion direct tariffs less $382 million of refunds gives net exposure of approximately $750-ish million. Next year the run rate is expected closer to right around $1 billion, so a step up in tariff expense versus this year.

exchanges.question: What explains C&F guidance implying roughly 50 bps price in Q4 versus +8% in Q3, and what are Deere's dealer rental fleet aspirations and how would they change business economics?
exchanges.answer: C&F price guide started the year at 2.5%, went to 3%, rounded down to 2.5%, now back to 3% full year; Q3's 8% reflected easy comps as Q3 2025 had about 5% negative price from incentives, and Q4 has no outsized year-over-year comp; road building contributes to pricing. On rental, 30%-35% of earthmoving transactions start as a rental and that is growing; dealer-owned rental fleets have grown with the market and dealers show increased appetite to expand, which could boost inventory fill next year.

exchanges.question: Are there merchandising incentives in the EOPs and does the backlog imply margins up, down or neutral next year? Also, what are the implications of the FTC right-to-repair settlement for the aftermarket and the $2 billion-$3 billion lifecycle parts target?
exchanges.answer: Deere is taking measured inflationary price in a challenging environment, committed to covering inflation over time, nothing outsized; pricing is taken at several points in the year and the inflationary environment is dynamic given oil prices and suppliers passing on tariffs. On the agreement, Deere has always supported customers' ability to repair their own equipment; the agreement formalizes tools like John Deere Operations Center PRO Service offering diagnostics, digital manuals and software updates, which supports long-term lifecycle solutions aspirations.

exchanges.question: Could the European cap budget policy change in 2028 pull demand forward into 2027 or cause delays, and any directional 2027 forecast for Europe?
exchanges.answer: Too early to tell; the order book is four to five months out so Q1 orders are just starting to be collected. Arable sentiment will depend on input costs and commodity prices; dairy and livestock look fairly stable. Unclear whether policy will pull demand forward or delay it.

exchanges.question: What are Brazilian and U.S. farmers saying about input cost trends and how that affects crop and purchase decisions?
exchanges.answer: Input price uncertainty exists everywhere, with fertilizer impact different in Brazil versus the U.S.; markets are reacting and farmers are seeking alternatives in product types, amounts and sources. Not seeing a huge reduction in intended application; larger farmers have multiple years of inputs contracted and are considering changes. Farmers remain resilient and focused on driving yield.
